Jump Game II (Greedy, Medium)

You get a 0-indexed integer array nums of length n. You start at index 0. The value nums[i] is the maximum length of a forward jump from index i. From index i you can jump to any index i + j where 0 <= j <= nums[i] and i + j < n. Return the minimum number of jumps to reach index n - 1. The test cases guarantee that index n - 1 is reachable.

Constraints:
1 <= nums.length <= 10^4
0 <= nums[i] <= 1000
It's guaranteed that you can reach nums[n - 1].

Name the technique and the memory hook. Then rebuild the solution.
column2:
Hook: BFS in windows: the next window runs from right + 1 to the farthest reach of this window.
Techniques: greedy, bfs-shortest-path

Approach: Use BFS by windows. The window [left, right] holds the indices whose minimum jump count is jumps. The next window starts at right + 1. It ends at the farthest i + nums[i] for i in the current window.

Rebuild:
  1. Set jumps = 0 and the window left = right = 0, because index 0 needs 0 jumps.
  2. Loop while right < n - 1, because the window does not yet cover the last index.
  3. Compute farthest = max(i + nums[i]) for i in left..right.
  4. Move the window: left = right + 1 and right = farthest.
  5. Add 1 to jumps for each new window.
  6. After the loop, return jumps.
Signals:
  • The problem asks for the minimum number of moves, and every move has the same cost. This is a shortest path in an unweighted graph, so think BFS.
  • Each position reaches a contiguous range of next positions (i + 1 to i + nums[i]). Then each BFS layer is also a contiguous range, so two indices describe it and no queue is necessary.
  • Moves only go forward along a line. One left-to-right scan visits the BFS layers in order.
  • n times the maximum jump length is large (here up to 10^7). Relaxing every edge is too slow in Python, so the solution must avoid enumerating individual jumps.
Key insight: When each state reaches a contiguous range of next states, every BFS layer is also a contiguous range. You can then run BFS with two boundaries instead of a queue: the end of the current layer and the farthest point of the next layer. The number of times you cross a layer boundary is the minimum number of moves.
Optimal: The optimal solution_code has the same O(n) time and O(1) space. It folds the inner window scan into one flat for loop. It closes a window when i equals cur_end. It needs no inner scan, but you must stop at index n - 2 and update farthest before you check cur_end. Without the reachability guarantee, both forms need a check. In the window form, return -1 when farthest <= right.
Approaches:
  • Brute-force recursion: O(max(nums)^n) (exponential) time, O(n) space (too slow)
  • DP or memoized recursion over all edges: O(n * max(nums)), up to about 10^7 time, O(n) space (too slow)
  • Backward greedy: O(n^2) time, O(1) space (too slow)
  • BFS by window (NeetCode style): O(n) time, O(1) space
  • Greedy implicit BFS in one loop (optimal, chosen): O(n) time, O(1) space
class Solution:
    def jump(self, nums: List[int]) -> int:
        jumps = 0
        left = right = 0  # window = indices whose fewest jumps is `jumps`
        while right < len(nums) - 1:
            farthest = max(i + nums[i] for i in range(left, right + 1))
            left, right = right + 1, farthest
            jumps += 1
        return jumps

Permutations (Backtracking, Medium)

You get an array nums of distinct integers. Return all possible permutations of nums. A permutation is an ordering that uses every element exactly once. You can return the permutations in any order.

Constraints:
1 <= nums.length <= 6
-10 <= nums[i] <= 10
All the integers of nums are unique.

Name the technique and the memory hook. Then rebuild the solution.
column2:
Hook: Pick one from the pool. Recurse on the rest. An empty pool means a finished permutation.
Techniques: backtracking-permutations

Approach: Pick from the pool. Take one item from the pool of remaining items, add it to the path, and recurse on the smaller pool. When the pool is empty, the path is one full permutation.

Rebuild:
  1. Make an empty result list and a helper build(path, remaining).
  2. Base case: if remaining is empty, append path to result and return.
  3. Loop over every index i of remaining.
  4. Recurse with path + [remaining[i]] and remaining[:i] + remaining[i + 1:].
  5. Call build([], nums) and return result.
Signals:
  • The task says return all orderings or all arrangements. The output has n! items, so enumeration is unavoidable.
  • The input size is tiny (n <= 6, so n! <= 720). A bound near 10 or less signals exhaustive search.
  • Every element must appear exactly once in each answer. You must track which elements are already used.
  • The elements are distinct, so every ordering is unique. If the input has duplicates, you must add sort plus skip pruning.
Key insight: A permutation is a sequence of n choices where each choice removes one item from the pool. Depth-first search over these choices, with a choose, explore, unchoose step, visits every ordering exactly once.
Optimal: The optimal solution_code keeps one shared path and a used array. It undoes each choice after the recursive call (choose, explore, unchoose). It does not allocate new lists at each call, so its auxiliary space is O(n) instead of O(n^2) along the recursion stack. Both run in O(n * n!) time. The shared-state form is better when the search tree is large and per-call copies cost too much. It is also the usual template for pruning searches such as N-Queens. For Permutations II, the pool form still works: sort nums, then skip remaining[i] when it equals remaining[i - 1].
Approaches:
  • Filter all index tuples: O(n * n^n) time, O(n * n!) space
  • Library call: O(n * n!) time, O(n * n!) space
  • Remove one, recurse on the rest (NeetCode reference): O(n * n!) time, O(n * n!) space
  • Iterative insertion: O(n * n!) time, O(n * n!) space
  • Backtracking with used flags: O(n * n!) time, O(n) auxiliary, O(n * n!) for the output space
  • In-place swap backtracking: O(n * n!) time, O(n) auxiliary, O(n * n!) for the output space
  • Iterative next permutation: O(n * n!) time, O(n) auxiliary for the working copy, O(n * n!) for the output space
from typing import List


class Solution:
    def permute(self, nums: List[int]) -> List[List[int]]:
        result = []

        def build(path, remaining):
            if not remaining:
                result.append(path)
                return
            for i in range(len(remaining)):
                build(path + [remaining[i]], remaining[:i] + remaining[i + 1:])

        build([], nums)
        return result

Rotate Image (Math & Geometry, Medium)

You get an n x n 2D matrix that represents an image. Rotate the image by 90 degrees clockwise. You must rotate the image in-place: modify the input 2D matrix directly. Do not allocate another 2D matrix to do the rotation. The function returns nothing.

Constraints:
n == matrix.length == matrix[i].length
1 <= n <= 20
-1000 <= matrix[i][j] <= 1000

Name the technique and the memory hook. Then rebuild the solution.
column2:
Hook: Flip on the diagonal, then flip each row.
Techniques: matrix-manipulation

Approach: Transpose, then reverse each row. Swap each cell with its mirror cell across the main diagonal. Then reverse every row. The two flips together turn the grid 90 degrees clockwise.

Rebuild:
  1. Write the target map for one cell: (i, j) goes to (j, n-1-i).
  2. Set n = len(matrix).
  3. Transpose: for i in range(n), for j in range(i + 1, n), swap matrix[i][j] and matrix[j][i]. Start j at i + 1 so that each pair swaps only once.
  4. Mirror: for row in matrix, call row.reverse().
  5. Return nothing, because the change is in place.
Signals:
  • The task asks for a geometric transform of a square grid (rotate, flip, mirror, transpose).
  • Each cell goes to a new position that depends only on its own coordinates. The transform is a fixed permutation of the cells.
  • The statement says in-place and forbids a second matrix. You need swaps or short cycles instead of a copy.
  • The input is square. A transpose keeps the same shape, so all swaps stay inside the matrix.
Key insight: A rotation equals the composition of two reflections. Each reflection is a set of disjoint pair swaps, so you can do it in place with no extra buffer.
Approaches:
  • Copy into a new matrix: O(n^2) time, O(n^2) space (too slow)
  • Transpose then reverse each row: O(n^2) time, O(1) space
  • Flip upside down then transpose: O(n^2) time, O(1) space
  • Layer-by-layer 4-way cycle: O(n^2) time, O(1) space
class Solution:
    def rotate(self, matrix: List[List[int]]) -> None:
        n = len(matrix)
        # 1) Transpose: swap across the main diagonal (upper triangle only).
        for i in range(n):
            for j in range(i + 1, n):
                matrix[i][j], matrix[j][i] = matrix[j][i], matrix[i][j]
        # 2) Mirror: reverse every row.
        for row in matrix:
            row.reverse()

Group Anagrams (Arrays & Hashing, Medium)

You get an array of strings strs. Put the strings that are anagrams of each other into the same group. Two strings are anagrams when one is a rearrangement of the letters of the other, using every letter the same number of times. Return a list of the groups. The order of the groups and the order of strings inside a group do not matter. Every input string appears in exactly one group, and duplicate strings go into the same group. The empty string is a valid input and forms a group with other empty strings. All strings contain only lowercase English letters.

Constraints:
1 <= strs.length <= 10^4
0 <= strs[i].length <= 100
strs[i] consists of lowercase English letters.

Name the technique and the memory hook. Then rebuild the solution.
column2:
Hook: Sort each word, group by the sorted word.
Techniques: grouping-by-canonical-key, hash-map-lookup, counting-frequency, sorting

Approach: Sorted string as key. Sort the letters of each string to get its key. Put the string into a dict of lists under that key. Anagrams sort to the same string.

Rebuild:
  1. Import defaultdict from collections.
  2. Make groups = defaultdict(list).
  3. Loop over each string s in strs.
  4. Compute key = "".join(sorted(s)).
  5. Append s to groups[key].
  6. After the loop, return list(groups.values()).
Signals:
  • The task asks you to group or cluster items that are equal under some equivalence rule, not under plain equality.
  • The equivalence ignores one detail of each item, such as the order of letters. This points to a canonical form that removes that detail.
  • The output order does not matter. You only need the buckets, so a hash map from key to list is enough.
  • The alphabet is small and fixed (26 lowercase letters). A fixed-size count vector is a cheap, exact fingerprint.
Key insight: When items are equal under a rule that ignores some detail, map each item to a canonical form that removes that detail. Then group by the canonical form in a hash map. One hash lookup per item replaces all pairwise comparisons.
Optimal: The solution_code uses a 26-letter count tuple as the key. That key costs O(k + 26) per string instead of O(k log k), so it is asymptotically better. In CPython the sorted key is still as fast or faster, because sorted runs in C and the count loop runs in Python. At max size both take about 0.11 s of CPU time. With one string of 10^6 letters, the sorted key also wins (0.17 s against 0.22 s). Use the count key when you must show O(k) work per string. Use the sorted key in all other cases, and also when the alphabet is large or unknown.
Approaches:
  • Pairwise comparison with group representatives: O(n^2 * k) time, O(n * k) space (too slow)
  • Sorted string as key: O(n * k log k) time, O(n * k) space
  • Letter-count tuple as key (chosen): O(n * (k + 26)), which is O(n * k) for a fixed alphabet time, O(n * (k + 26)), which is O(n * k) for a fixed alphabet space
  • Prime product as key: O(n * k^2) time, O(n * k) space
from collections import defaultdict
from typing import List


class Solution:
    def groupAnagrams(self, strs: List[str]) -> List[List[str]]:
        groups = defaultdict(list)
        for s in strs:
            key = "".join(sorted(s))
            groups[key].append(s)
        return list(groups.values())

Pow(x, n) (Math & Geometry, Medium)

Implement pow(x, n). It returns x raised to the power n, that is x^n. x is a real number with -100.0 < x < 100.0. n is an integer from -2^31 to 2^31 - 1, so n can be negative or zero. A negative n means the reciprocal: x^-n = 1 / x^n. Either x is not zero or n > 0, so the input never has x = 0 together with n <= 0. The true answer x^n always lies between -10^4 and 10^4.

Constraints:
-100.0 < x < 100.0
-2^31 <= n <= 2^31-1
n is an integer.
Either x is not zero or n > 0.

Name the technique and the memory hook. Then rebuild the solution.
column2:
Hook: Square the half, add one x if odd.
Techniques: fast-exponentiation, bit-manipulation, divide-and-conquer

Approach: Recursive halving (divide and conquer). Compute the half power x^(n//2) once, square it, and multiply by one more x when n is odd. A negative n becomes a positive n with base 1/x.

Rebuild:
  1. If n is negative, return myPow(1 / x, -n).
  2. If n is 0, return 1.0.
  3. Compute half = myPow(x, n // 2) one time only.
  4. If n is even, return half * half.
  5. If n is odd, return half * half * x.
Signals:
  • A repeat count or exponent can reach 2^31 or more, so one step per repetition is too slow and you need O(log n) steps.
  • The repeated operation is associative (multiplication, matrix product, function composition), so you can group repetitions into blocks.
  • The task says compute x^n, apply an operation k times, or find the k-th term of a linear recurrence with a huge k.
  • The task asks you to build a power function yourself instead of calling the built-in one. The interviewer wants repeated squaring.
Key insight: Do not apply an associative operation n times one by one. Square the base to double the block size, and combine only the blocks that match the set bits of n. This turns n steps into about log2(n) steps.
Optimal: The optimal solution_code is the iterative bit loop. It has the same O(log |n|) time but uses O(1) space instead of about 34 stack frames. Use it when a task forbids recursion or asks for O(1) space. It is also the usual template for modular power and matrix power loops.
Approaches:
  • Repeated multiplication: O(|n|) time, O(1) space (too slow)
  • Recursive halving (divide and conquer): O(log |n|) time, O(log |n|) space
  • Iterative binary exponentiation (repeated squaring): O(log |n|) time, O(1) space
  • Built-in power or logarithm identity: O(1) time, O(1) space
class Solution:
    def myPow(self, x: float, n: int) -> float:
        if n < 0:
            return self.myPow(1 / x, -n)
        if n == 0:
            return 1.0
        half = self.myPow(x, n // 2)
        if n % 2 == 0:
            return half * half
        return half * half * x

column1:
N-Queens (Backtracking, Hard)

Place n queens on an n x n chessboard so that no two queens attack each other. Two queens attack each other when they share a row, a column, or a diagonal (in either direction). Given an integer n, return all distinct solutions. Each solution is a board given as a list of n strings of length n, where 'Q' marks a queen and '.' marks an empty cell. You may return the solutions in any order.

Constraints:
1 <= n <= 9

Name the technique and the memory hook. Then rebuild the solution.
column2:
Hook: One queen per row. Block the column, r minus c and r plus c.
Techniques: backtracking-constraint-search, hash-set-membership, string-parsing-building

Approach: Row-by-row backtracking with three sets. Put one queen in each row, skip a column when its column, its r - c diagonal or its r + c diagonal is already used, and undo the marks after the recursive call.

Rebuild:
  1. Make empty sets cols, diag and anti. Make empty lists queens and res.
  2. Define backtrack(r). If r == n, build one string for each column c in queens: c dots, then Q, then n - c - 1 dots. Append this new board to res and return.
  3. Loop c over range(n). Skip c if c is in cols, r - c is in diag or r + c is in anti.
  4. Add c to cols, r - c to diag and r + c to anti. Append c to queens.
  5. Call backtrack(r + 1). Then pop queens and remove the three keys from the sets.
  6. Call backtrack(0) and return res.
Signals:
  • The problem asks for ALL valid configurations, not a count or an optimum. Listing every solution means a full search, usually backtracking.
  • The input is tiny (here n <= 9). Exponential or factorial search is acceptable.
  • The answer is a sequence of choices under pairwise conflict rules. A partial assignment can already break a rule, so you can prune early.
  • The rules force exactly one item per slot (here one queen per row). You can then make one decision per level of recursion.
Key insight: Make one decision per level so that one constraint holds by construction (one queen per row). Then turn every remaining conflict line into a hashable key (column c, diagonal r - c, anti-diagonal r + c). This gives an O(1) is-safe check and lets you prune a partial board as soon as it breaks a rule.
Approaches:
  • Choose any n cells: O(C(n^2, n) * n^2) time, O(n^2) space (too slow)
  • One queen per row, any column: O(n^n * n^2) time, O(n) space (too slow)
  • Column permutations, check at the end: O(n! * n^2) time, O(n) space
  • Row-by-row backtracking with a linear safety scan: O(n! * n^2) loose bound, plus O(S * n^2) to build S boards time, O(n) plus output space
  • Row-by-row backtracking with column and diagonal sets (optimal, standard): O(n! * n) loose bound, plus O(S * n^2) to build S boards time, O(n) plus output space
  • Bitmask backtracking: O(n!) search, plus O(S * n^2) to build S boards time, O(n) plus output space
from typing import List


class Solution:
    def solveNQueens(self, n: int) -> List[List[str]]:
        cols = set()
        diag = set()      # r - c is constant on a "\" diagonal
        anti = set()      # r + c is constant on a "/" diagonal
        queens = []       # queens[r] = column of the queen in row r
        res = []

        def backtrack(r: int) -> None:
            if r == n:
                res.append(["." * c + "Q" + "." * (n - c - 1) for c in queens])
                return
            for c in range(n):
                if c in cols or r - c in diag or r + c in anti:
                    continue
                cols.add(c)
                diag.add(r - c)
                anti.add(r + c)
                queens.append(c)
                backtrack(r + 1)
                queens.pop()
                cols.remove(c)
                diag.remove(r - c)
                anti.remove(r + c)

        backtrack(0)
        return res

column1:
Maximum Subarray (Greedy, Medium)

You get an integer array nums. Find the subarray with the largest sum and return that sum. A subarray is a contiguous, non-empty sequence of elements of the array. Elements can be negative, so the answer can be negative. You return only the sum, not the indices.

Constraints:
1 <= nums.length <= 10^5
-10^4 <= nums[i] <= 10^4
Follow-up: If you have figured out the O(n) solution, try coding another solution using the divide and conquer approach, which is more subtle.

Name the technique and the memory hook. Then rebuild the solution.
column2:
Hook: A negative running sum only hurts, so drop it and restart.
Techniques: kadane, dp-1d-linear, greedy, prefix-suffix-accumulation, divide-and-conquer

Approach: Kadane's algorithm (extend or restart). Scan once and keep cur, the best sum of a subarray that ends at the current element. If cur is negative, drop it and restart at the current element, then update the best answer.

Rebuild:
  1. Set best = nums[0] because the subarray must be non-empty.
  2. Set cur = 0 to stand for no previous run.
  3. For each x in nums, set cur = max(cur, 0) + x to extend a positive run or restart at x.
  4. After each step, set best = max(best, cur).
  5. Return best.
Signals:
  • The task asks for the best (max or min) sum over contiguous segments of an array.
  • Values can be negative, so a variable sliding window has no monotone rule to shrink it.
  • Only the best value is needed, not the list of all segments, so one rolling state can be enough.
  • n is up to 10^5, so O(n^2) pair enumeration is too slow and you need O(n) or O(n log n).
Key insight: A segment with a negative sum never helps a segment that extends it to the right. So you drop it and start fresh at the next element. Put another way: the best segment that ends at i either extends the best segment that ends at i-1 or starts at i.
Approaches:
  • Brute force over all pairs with inner sum: O(n^3) time, O(1) space (too slow)
  • Fixed start with running sum: O(n^2) time, O(1) space (too slow)
  • Prefix sums with minimum prefix so far: O(n) time, O(1) space
  • Divide and conquer (crossing sum scan): O(n log n) time, O(log n) space
  • Divide and conquer returning four values: O(n) time, O(log n) space
  • Kadane's algorithm (optimal, standard): O(n) time, O(1) space
class Solution:
    def maxSubArray(self, nums: List[int]) -> int:
        best = nums[0]  # start at nums[0], not 0, so all-negative input works
        cur = 0         # best sum of a subarray ending at the previous index
        for x in nums:
            # A negative running sum only hurts; drop it and restart at x.
            cur = max(cur, 0) + x
            best = max(best, cur)
        return best
column3: greedy kadane dp-1d-linear greedy prefix-suffix-accumulation divide-and-conquer

Spiral Matrix (Math & Geometry, Medium)

You get an m x n matrix. Return all elements of the matrix in spiral order. Spiral order starts at the top-left cell and moves right along the top row. When the next cell is outside the matrix or already visited, it turns clockwise: right, then down, then left, then up. It keeps turning inward until it visits every cell exactly once. The output is a flat list of m * n values.

Constraints:
m == matrix.length
n == matrix[i].length
1 <= m, n <= 10
-100 <= matrix[i][j] <= 100

Name the technique and the memory hook. Then rebuild the solution.
column2:
Hook: Walk straight, turn right when blocked.
Techniques: matrix-manipulation, simulation

Approach: Direction walk with a turn rule. Walk straight in the current direction and record each cell. When the next cell is outside the grid or already visited, turn clockwise and continue, for exactly rows * cols steps.

Rebuild:
  1. Write directions as right, down, left, up: (0, 1), (1, 0), (0, -1), (-1, 0).
  2. Set rows and cols from the matrix. Start at r = c = 0 with direction index d = 0, an empty visited set and an empty result.
  3. Loop rows * cols times: append matrix[r][c] and add (r, c) to visited.
  4. Compute the next cell with directions[d]. If it is out of bounds or visited, set d = (d + 1) % 4 and compute the next cell again with the new direction. One turn is always enough.
  5. Move to the next cell, and return the result after the loop.
Signals:
  • The problem asks for a fixed visiting order over a grid, not for a computed value. This points to simulation with careful index control.
  • The order follows the outer ring and then moves inward. This points to four shrinking boundaries, one per side.
  • The output must contain every cell exactly once, and the grid is small (m, n <= 10). Any correct traversal is O(m * n) and optimal, so the hard part is index correctness, not speed.
  • The matrix can be non-square, a single row, or a single column. This signals that the last layer can be a single row or column and needs guards.
Key insight: The unvisited cells always form one rectangle. Each straight side of the spiral consumes one edge of that rectangle. So you only need four bounds that move inward, and you do not need to track visited cells. Use this idea whenever a walk eats a grid from the outside in.
Optimal: The optimal solution_code keeps four shrinking bounds (top, bottom, left, right) instead of a visited set. It uses O(1) extra space instead of O(m * n). It needs two guards so that a single leftover row or column is not read twice. Use it only when a task asks for constant extra space or does not let you mark cells. With m, n <= 10, both run in O(m * n) time and are fast.
Approaches:
  • Direction simulation with visited marks: O(m * n) time, O(m * n) space
  • Rotate and pop: O(m * n * min(m, n)) time, O(m * n) space
  • Layer peeling with four shrinking boundaries: O(m * n) time, O(1) extra, excluding the output space
class Solution:
    def spiralOrder(self, matrix: List[List[int]]) -> List[int]:
        rows, cols = len(matrix), len(matrix[0])
        directions = [(0, 1), (1, 0), (0, -1), (-1, 0)]  # right, down, left, up
        visited = set()
        result = []
        r, c, d = 0, 0, 0
        for _ in range(rows * cols):
            result.append(matrix[r][c])
            visited.add((r, c))
            nr, nc = r + directions[d][0], c + directions[d][1]
            if not (0 <= nr < rows and 0 <= nc < cols) or (nr, nc) in visited:
                d = (d + 1) % 4  # blocked: turn clockwise
                nr, nc = r + directions[d][0], c + directions[d][1]
            r, c = nr, nc
        return result

column1:
Jump Game (Greedy, Medium)

You get an integer array nums. You start at index 0. The value nums[i] is the maximum jump length from index i. From index i you can move to any index from i + 1 to i + nums[i] that lies inside the array. Return true if you can reach the last index. Otherwise return false. Only reachability matters. The number of jumps does not matter.

Constraints:
1 <= nums.length <= 10^4
0 <= nums[i] <= 10^5

Name the technique and the memory hook. Then rebuild the solution.
column2:
Hook: Walk forward; if you pass farthest you are stuck, else stretch farthest.
Techniques: greedy, dp-1d-linear, prefix-suffix-accumulation

Approach: Greedy farthest reach, forward scan. Walk left to right and keep farthest, the right edge of the reachable prefix. If an index lies past farthest, there is a gap, so return false. Otherwise, stretch farthest to i + nums[i] when that is larger.

Rebuild:
  1. Set farthest = 0, because you stand on index 0.
  2. Loop over i, jump in enumerate(nums).
  3. If i > farthest, nothing reaches i, so return False.
  4. Else set farthest = max(farthest, i + jump).
  5. After the loop, return True, because no gap appeared.
Signals:
  • Each value gives a maximum step, so every shorter step is also allowed.
  • The question asks only yes or no for reachability, not a path or a count.
  • Moves go only forward along a line of positions, so one left-to-right scan can see every move.
  • n reaches 10^4 and one jump can span the whole array, so expanding each jump target separately costs O(n^2) and is too slow in Python.
Key insight: When a move allows any step up to a maximum, the reachable positions always form a contiguous prefix. So you track one number, the farthest reachable index, instead of a set of positions.
Approaches:
  • Plain recursion (try every jump): O(2^n) time, O(n) space (too slow)
  • Memoized DFS (top-down DP): O(n^2) time, O(n) space (too slow)
  • Bottom-up DP over good indices: O(n^2) time, O(n) space (too slow)
  • Greedy farthest reach, forward scan (chosen): O(n) time, O(1) space
  • Greedy goal shift, backward scan (NeetCode): O(n) time, O(1) space
class Solution:
    def canJump(self, nums: List[int]) -> bool:
        farthest = 0                      # right edge of the reachable prefix
        for i, jump in enumerate(nums):
            if i > farthest:              # gap: nothing reaches index i
                return False
            farthest = max(farthest, i + jump)
        return True

column1:
Merge Intervals (Intervals, Medium)

You get an array intervals where intervals[i] = [start_i, end_i]. Merge all overlapping intervals. Return an array of the non-overlapping intervals that cover all the intervals in the input. Example 2 shows that two intervals that share only an endpoint, such as [1,4] and [4,5], count as overlapping. Example 3 shows that the input is not necessarily sorted. The source does not state an output order. The standard answer returns the intervals sorted by start.

Constraints:
1 <= intervals.length <= 10^4
intervals[i].length == 2
0 <= start_i <= end_i <= 10^4

Name the technique and the memory hook. Then rebuild the solution.
column2:
Hook: Sort, then extend the last one or append a new one.
Techniques: intervals-sort-sweep, sorting, greedy

Approach: Sort by start and sweep. Sort the intervals, then walk them once and either extend the last merged interval or start a new one.

Rebuild:
  1. Sort the intervals so starts go up.
  2. Make an empty list merged.
  3. For each start, end: if merged is not empty and start <= merged[-1][1], set merged[-1][1] = max(merged[-1][1], end).
  4. Else append a new list [start, end].
  5. Return merged.
Signals:
  • The input is a collection of [start, end] ranges. The task asks for their union, their overlaps, or a consolidated cover.
  • The answer depends only on the set of intervals and not on their input order. So you are free to sort them.
  • The words overlap or merge appear together with intervals, time slots, ranges, or segments.
  • The input size is about 10^4 or more. A check of every pair is then too slow in Python, so an O(n log n) sort is the budget.
Key insight: Sorting by start turns a pairwise overlap relation into a linear scan. After the sort, a new interval can only overlap the group that is still open, so you compare it with one interval and not with all of them.
Approaches:
  • Repeated pairwise merge to a fixpoint: O(n^3) time, O(n) space (too slow)
  • Overlap graph with union-find or DFS: O(n^2) time, O(n^2) with an edge list, O(n) with union-find space (too slow)
  • Coverage difference array on a doubled coordinate line: O(n + V) time, O(V) space
  • Sort by start and sweep (optimal, standard): O(n log n) time, O(n) space
  • Event sweep with an active counter: O(n log n) time, O(n) space
from typing import List


class Solution:
    def merge(self, intervals: List[List[int]]) -> List[List[int]]:
        intervals.sort()
        merged = []
        for start, end in intervals:
            if merged and start <= merged[-1][1]:
                merged[-1][1] = max(merged[-1][1], end)
            else:
                merged.append([start, end])
        return merged

column1:
Insert Interval (Intervals, Medium)

You get a list of non-overlapping intervals. Each interval is [start_i, end_i]. The list is sorted in ascending order by start_i. You also get one new interval newInterval = [start, end]. Two intervals overlap if they share at least one point. So [1,2] and [2,3] overlap, but [1,2] and [3,4] do not. Insert newInterval into the list. Merge the intervals that overlap, if necessary. The result must stay sorted by start and must have no overlapping intervals. Return the resulting list. You can build and return a new list. You do not need to change the input in place. The input list can be empty.

Constraints:
0 <= intervals.length <= 10^4
intervals[i].length == 2
0 <= starti <= endi <= 10^5
intervals is sorted by starti in ascending order.

Name the technique and the memory hook. Then rebuild the solution.
column2:
Hook: Left stays left, right stays right, the middle melts into one.
Techniques: intervals-sort-sweep, binary-search-index

Approach: Three buckets in one loop. An interval that ends before the new start goes to left. An interval that starts after the new end goes to right. Any other interval overlaps, so it melts into the new interval. Return left + [merged] + right.

Rebuild:
  1. Unpack start, end = newInterval and make two empty lists, left and right.
  2. Loop for s, e in intervals.
  3. If e < start, the interval is fully left: append it to left.
  4. Elif s > end, the interval is fully right: append it to right.
  5. Else it overlaps: set start = min(start, s) and end = max(end, e).
  6. Return left + [[start, end]] + right.
Signals:
  • The input is a sorted list of disjoint items, and one new item breaks that state.
  • The task adds one item to a sorted structure and asks you to restore an invariant, such as sorted order with no overlap. This points to one linear pass, not a full re-sort.
  • The task asks you to merge overlapping intervals. This points to the interval sweep family. Two closed intervals overlap when each one starts at or before the end of the other.
  • The statement defines overlap as sharing at least one point. So touching endpoints merge, and the choice between strict and non-strict comparisons matters.
Key insight: When a sorted, disjoint collection receives one new element, the old elements split into three contiguous blocks by their relation to it: entirely before, overlapping, and entirely after. Copy the first block, collapse the middle block into one element, and copy the last block. No sort is necessary.
Optimal: The record's solution_code uses the same three-block idea and the same O(n) time. It moves one index through two while loops. It copies the right block with one slice, intervals[i:], so it skips the tests for that block. This changes only a constant factor. Use it when an interviewer asks for the classic three-phase form. Append, sort and merge is also correct and fast enough here, but it costs O(n log n) and ignores the sorted input. If the search must be O(log n), as in Range Module, use bisect on the starts and ends to find the middle block, then splice it.
Approaches:
  • Append, sort, merge: O(n log n) time, O(n) space
  • Coverage array on doubled coordinates: O(n + R) where R is the coordinate range time, O(R) space
  • Three-phase linear scan (optimal, standard): O(n) time, O(n) for the output, O(1) extra space
  • Binary search for the overlap block: O(log n) search + O(n) to build the result time, O(n) space
from typing import List


class Solution:
    def insert(self, intervals: List[List[int]], newInterval: List[int]) -> List[List[int]]:
        start, end = newInterval
        left, right = [], []
        for s, e in intervals:
            if e < start:
                # Ends before the new interval starts: it stays on the left.
                left.append([s, e])
            elif s > end:
                # Starts after the new interval ends: it stays on the right.
                right.append([s, e])
            else:
                # It overlaps: swallow it into the new interval.
                start = min(start, s)
                end = max(end, e)
        return left + [[start, end]] + right

column1:
Unique Paths (2-D Dynamic Programming, Medium)

A robot is on an m x n grid. The robot starts at the top-left corner, grid[0][0]. The robot wants to reach the bottom-right corner, grid[m - 1][n - 1]. At each step the robot moves either one cell down or one cell right. No other moves are allowed. Given the integers m and n, return the number of unique paths from the top-left corner to the bottom-right corner. The test cases guarantee that the answer is less than or equal to 2 * 10^9.

Constraints:
1 <= m, n <= 100

Name the technique and the memory hook. Then rebuild the solution.
column2:
Hook: Fill the grid with ones, then each cell equals up plus left.
Techniques: dp-2d-grid, memoized-dfs, math-number-theory

Approach: Bottom-up 2-D DP table filled with ones. Each inner cell holds the paths from above plus the paths from the left, and the answer is the bottom-right cell.

Rebuild:
  1. Make ways = [[1] * n for _ in range(m)]. The first row and the first column stay 1.
  2. Loop r over range(1, m). This skips row 0.
  3. Inside it, loop c over range(1, n). This skips column 0.
  4. Set ways[r][c] = ways[r - 1][c] + ways[r][c - 1]. The first term is the cell above. The second term is the cell to the left.
  5. Return ways[m - 1][n - 1].
Signals:
  • The question asks for the number of ways, not for the paths themselves. Counting questions point to DP or combinatorics, not to enumeration.
  • Moves go only down or right. The moves form a DAG on the grid, so each cell depends only on cells above it and to its left.
  • Many different paths pass through the same cell. Overlapping subproblems mean memoization or a bottom-up table removes repeated work.
  • The grid has no obstacles or weights. A uniform grid with fixed step types often has a closed-form binomial answer.
Key insight: The number of ways to reach a cell equals the sum of the ways to reach each cell that can step into it. This holds because the last move splits the paths into disjoint groups.
Optimal: The optimal solution_code keeps one row of length n instead of the full table. It updates row[j] += row[j - 1] from left to right, where the old row[j] is the cell above. This cuts space from O(m * n) to O(n) with the same time. The binomial C(m + n - 2, m - 1) gives O(min(m, n)) time and O(1) space. You need these only when a follow-up asks for less memory or the grid is very large. At 100 x 100 the full table uses only 10^4 cells.
Approaches:
  • Brute-force recursion: O(2^(m+n)) time, O(m + n) space (too slow)
  • Top-down memoized DFS: O(m * n) time, O(m * n) space
  • Bottom-up 2-D DP table: O(m * n) time, O(m * n) space
  • Bottom-up DP with one rolling row: O(m * n) time, O(n) space
  • Combinatorics (binomial coefficient): O(min(m, n)) time, O(1) space
class Solution:
    def uniquePaths(self, m: int, n: int) -> int:
        # ways[r][c] = number of paths from (0, 0) to (r, c).
        # Start with all 1s: the first row and first column have one straight path.
        ways = [[1] * n for _ in range(m)]
        for r in range(1, m):
            for c in range(1, n):
                ways[r][c] = ways[r - 1][c] + ways[r][c - 1]  # from above + from left
        return ways[m - 1][n - 1]

column1:
Plus One (Math & Geometry, Easy)

You get a large integer as an integer array digits. Each digits[i] is the i-th digit of the integer. The digits go from most significant to least significant in left-to-right order. The large integer does not contain any leading 0's. Increment the large integer by one and return the resulting array of digits.

Constraints:
1 <= digits.length <= 100
0 <= digits[i] <= 9
digits does not contain any leading 0's.

Name the technique and the memory hook. Then rebuild the solution.
column2:
Hook: From the right, each 9 becomes 0 until a digit can take the +1. If all digits are 9, put a 1 in front.
Techniques: simulation, math-number-theory

Approach: Early-exit carry loop (add 1 by hand). Walk from the right. A 9 becomes 0, and the carry moves left. The first digit below 9 gets plus one, and the function returns. If every digit was 9, put a 1 in front.

Rebuild:
  1. Loop i from the last index down to 0 with range(len(digits) - 1, -1, -1).
  2. If digits[i] < 9, add 1 to it and return digits at once.
  3. Else set digits[i] = 0, because 9 + 1 = 10 writes 0 and carries 1 to the left.
  4. After the loop, every digit was 9 and is now 0, so return [1] + digits.
  5. Check with 1299 -> 1300 and 99 -> 100.
Signals:
  • A number is stored as an array, string or linked list of digits, so it can be longer than a machine integer.
  • The task is an arithmetic operation (add, increment, multiply) on that digit representation.
  • The digits are ordered most significant first, so the arithmetic must start at the right end.
  • The added amount is small, such as one. The carry is then at most 1, and it stops at the first digit below the maximum digit.
Key insight: Adding a small constant to a digit array only changes a suffix. The carry moves left through a run of maximum digits (9s) and stops at the first digit that can absorb it. The length grows only when the whole number is made of maximum digits.
Approaches:
  • Convert to integer and back: O(n^2) in CPython in general, because decimal string to int conversion and back is quadratic. For n <= 100 the cost is negligible. time, O(n) space
  • General carry loop (full adder): O(n) time, O(1) extra, O(n) only for a new leading digit space
  • Early-exit carry loop (optimal): O(n) worst case, O(1) when the last digit is not 9 time, O(1) extra, O(n) only for the all-9s case space
  • Find last non-9 digit: O(n) time, O(1) extra, O(n) only for the all-9s case space
class Solution:
    def plusOne(self, digits: List[int]) -> List[int]:
        # Walk from the right, like adding 1 by hand: 1299 + 1 = 1300.
        for i in range(len(digits) - 1, -1, -1):
            if digits[i] < 9:
                digits[i] += 1      # this digit absorbs the carry
                return digits       # nothing to the left changes
            digits[i] = 0           # 9 + 1 = 10: write 0, carry 1 left
        return [1] + digits         # all digits were 9: 999 + 1 = 1000

column1:
Climbing Stairs (1-D Dynamic Programming, Easy)

You climb a staircase. The top is n steps away. Each move climbs either 1 step or 2 steps. Return the number of distinct ways to reach the top. Two ways are different when their sequences of moves are different, so order matters (1+2 and 2+1 are two ways). You must land exactly on step n.

Constraints:
1 <= n <= 45

Name the technique and the memory hook. Then rebuild the solution.
column2:
Hook: The last move is a 1-step or a 2-step, so add the ways for the two steps below.
Techniques: dp-1d-linear, memoized-dfs, math-number-theory, fast-exponentiation

Approach: Bottom-up DP table. Set ways[0] = 1 and ways[1] = 1. Fill ways[i] = ways[i-1] + ways[i-2] for i from 2 to n. Return ways[n].

Rebuild:
  1. Define ways[i] as the number of ways to stand exactly on step i.
  2. Make a list ways of n+1 zeros.
  3. Set ways[0] = 1 for the empty climb. Set ways[1] = 1 for one 1-step. Index 1 exists because n >= 1.
  4. Loop i from 2 to n and set ways[i] = ways[i-1] + ways[i-2].
  5. Return ways[n].
Signals:
  • The question asks "how many distinct ways" to reach a target. Counting questions with a choice at each step point to DP.
  • Each move comes from a small fixed set of options (here 1 or 2). The count for a position is the sum of the counts for the positions that lead into it.
  • Order of moves matters. This means you count sequences (compositions), not sets, so the outer loop runs over positions.
  • The plain recursion calls the same subproblem many times. Overlapping subproblems signal memoization or tabulation.
Key insight: Split the count by the last move. The ways to reach a state equal the sum of the ways to reach each state that can move into it. The cases do not overlap, so the sum counts each way exactly once.
Optimal: The optimal solution keeps only the last two values in prev and curr, so it uses O(1) memory instead of O(n). Both run in O(n) time. Use the rolling form when a problem asks for constant space. To get it, notice that ways[i] reads only ways[i-1] and ways[i-2]. Then replace the table with prev, curr = curr, prev + curr and run the loop n-1 times.
Approaches:
  • Brute-force recursion: O(phi^n), about O(1.618^n) time, O(n) recursion stack space (too slow)
  • Top-down memoized DFS: O(n) time, O(n) space
  • Bottom-up DP table: O(n) time, O(n) space
  • Two rolling variables (optimal, standard): O(n) time, O(1) space
  • Combinatorics: O(n^2) with math.comb, O(n) with incremental binomials time, O(1) space
  • Matrix exponentiation: O(log n) time, O(1) space
  • Binet closed form: O(1) time, O(1) space
class Solution:
    def climbStairs(self, n: int) -> int:
        # ways[i] = number of ways to stand exactly on step i
        ways = [0] * (n + 1)
        ways[0] = 1  # the empty climb
        ways[1] = 1  # one 1-step
        for i in range(2, n + 1):
            # the last move came from step i-1 (1-step) or step i-2 (2-step)
            ways[i] = ways[i - 1] + ways[i - 2]
        return ways[n]

column1:
Edit Distance (2-D Dynamic Programming, Medium)

You get two strings word1 and word2. Return the minimum number of operations needed to convert word1 into word2. Three operations are permitted on a word, and each costs 1: insert a character, delete a character, or replace a character. Either string can be empty. Both strings contain only lowercase English letters.

Constraints:
0 <= word1.length, word2.length <= 500
word1 and word2 consist of lowercase English letters.

Name the technique and the memory hook. Then rebuild the solution.
column2:
Hook: Look at the last chars: same is free diagonal, else 1 plus min of up, left, diagonal.
Techniques: dp-two-sequences, dp-2d-grid, memoized-dfs

Approach: Bottom-up 2-D table over prefixes. dp[i][j] is the edit cost from word1[:i] to word2[:j]. If the last chars are equal, take the diagonal for free. Else take 1 plus the min of up (delete), left (insert) and diagonal (replace).

Rebuild:
  1. Make dp of size (m+1) by (n+1). dp[i][j] is the cost to turn word1[:i] into word2[:j].
  2. Fill the edges: dp[i][0] = i (delete all) and dp[0][j] = j (insert all).
  3. Loop i from 1 to m and j from 1 to n.
  4. If word1[i-1] == word2[j-1], copy the diagonal dp[i-1][j-1].
  5. Else set 1 + min(dp[i-1][j] delete, dp[i][j-1] insert, dp[i-1][j-1] replace).
  6. Return dp[m][n].
Signals:
  • Two sequences are given and the answer is a minimum cost to transform or align one into the other.
  • Each allowed operation changes one character at a time: insert, delete, or replace. So you can reason about the last character of each prefix.
  • Both lengths are small (hundreds to a few thousand), so an O(m*n) table of prefix pairs fits.
  • Greedy choices fail because a local match or mismatch decision changes what is possible later.
Key insight: In an optimal edit script, the last character of word1 pairs with the last character of word2 (match or replace), or one of them pairs with nothing (delete or insert). So the answer for two prefixes depends only on three smaller prefix pairs: drop one char from the first, drop one char from the second, or drop one from each. This turns an exponential search over scripts into a table indexed by prefix lengths.
Optimal: The record solution uses the same recurrence but keeps only two rows, prev and cur. This cuts space from O(m*n) to O(n), or to O(min(m, n)) if you pass the shorter string as word2. Time stays O(m*n). Use it when the strings are too long for the full table, or when the task asks for less space. To get it from the table, note that row i reads only row i-1 and row i. Build a new cur list for each row, set cur[0] = i, and set prev = cur at the end of the row.
Approaches:
  • Brute force recursion: O(3^(m+n)) time, O(m+n) space (too slow)
  • BFS over strings: Exponential, roughly O(26^L * 52L) with L = max(m, n) time, Exponential, roughly O(26^L) space (too slow)
  • Top-down memoized DFS: O(m*n) time, O(m*n) space
  • Bottom-up 2-D table: O(m*n) time, O(m*n) space
  • Bottom-up with two rolling rows (chosen): O(m*n) time, O(n) space
  • Bit-parallel Myers algorithm: O(m*n/w) time, O(sigma * m / w) space
class Solution:
    def minDistance(self, word1: str, word2: str) -> int:
        m, n = len(word1), len(word2)
        # dp[i][j] = edits to turn word1[:i] into word2[:j]
        dp = [[0] * (n + 1) for _ in range(m + 1)]
        for i in range(m + 1):
            dp[i][0] = i  # delete all i chars
        for j in range(n + 1):
            dp[0][j] = j  # insert all j chars
        for i in range(1, m + 1):
            for j in range(1, n + 1):
                if word1[i - 1] == word2[j - 1]:
                    dp[i][j] = dp[i - 1][j - 1]  # same last char: free
                else:
                    dp[i][j] = 1 + min(
                        dp[i - 1][j],      # delete word1[i-1]
                        dp[i][j - 1],      # insert word2[j-1]
                        dp[i - 1][j - 1],  # replace word1[i-1]
                    )
        return dp[m][n]

column1:
Set Matrix Zeroes (Math & Geometry, Medium)

You get an m x n integer matrix. If a cell holds 0, set every cell in its row and every cell in its column to 0. Only zeros that exist in the original matrix trigger this. Zeros that you write do not spread further. You must change the matrix in place. The function returns nothing.

Constraints:
m == matrix.length
n == matrix[0].length
1 <= m, n <= 200
-2^31 <= matrix[i][j] <= 2^31 - 1
Follow-up: A straightforward solution using O(mn) space is probably a bad idea. A simple improvement uses O(m + n) space, but still not the best solution. Could you devise a constant space solution?

Name the technique and the memory hook. Then rebuild the solution.
column2:
Hook: Mark zero rows and zero columns first, then clear.
Techniques: matrix-manipulation, index-as-hash-in-place-marking

Approach: Two sets, read then write. Pass 1 only reads and puts the index of each row and each column that holds a zero into two sets. Pass 2 only writes and sets a cell to 0 when its row or its column is in a set.

Rebuild:
  1. Get m and n from len(matrix) and len(matrix[0]).
  2. Make two empty sets: zero_rows and zero_cols.
  3. Pass 1: loop over every cell. If the cell is 0, add i to zero_rows and j to zero_cols.
  4. Do not write anything in pass 1, so new zeros never spread.
  5. Pass 2: loop over every cell again. If i is in zero_rows or j is in zero_cols, set the cell to 0.
  6. Return nothing, because the matrix changes in place.
Signals:
  • The task says to modify a grid in place, and a change at one cell affects a whole row or column.
  • Writes made during a scan can be confused with original values. This means you must separate the read phase from the write phase.
  • The follow-up asks for O(1) extra space, and some cells of the input have a final value that you can predict. This points to storing the bookkeeping inside the input.
  • The needed bookkeeping is one bit per row and one bit per column. A row and a column of the matrix have exactly that shape.
Key insight: When you need per-row and per-column flags but have no extra space, borrow one row and one column of the input to hold them. This is safe because a borrowed cell is only overwritten with the value it gets at the end anyway. Save the original state of the borrowed row and column first, and restore or apply it last.
Optimal: The intuitive version uses O(m + n) extra space for the two sets. The record's solution_code reaches O(1) extra space, which the follow-up asks for. It stores zero_cols in row 0 and zero_rows in column 0, because those cells become 0 anyway when they are marked. To build it from the intuitive version, first save two booleans: does row 0 hold a zero, and does column 0 hold a zero. Then run both passes on the inner block only (i and j start at 1). Clear row 0 and column 0 last, from the two booleans. Use it only when constant extra space is required. Time is O(mn) in both versions.
Approaches:
  • Copy the matrix: O(mn(m + n)) time, O(mn) space
  • Collect zero positions: O(mn(m + n)) time, O(mn) space
  • Row and column flag arrays: O(mn) time, O(m + n) space
  • First row and first column as markers with two flags: O(mn) time, O(1) space
  • Markers with one flag (NeetCode style): O(mn) time, O(1) space
from typing import List


class Solution:
    def setZeroes(self, matrix: List[List[int]]) -> None:
        m, n = len(matrix), len(matrix[0])
        zero_rows = set()
        zero_cols = set()

        # Pass 1: only read. Remember every row and column that holds a zero.
        for i in range(m):
            for j in range(n):
                if matrix[i][j] == 0:
                    zero_rows.add(i)
                    zero_cols.add(j)

        # Pass 2: only write. Clear a cell if its row or its column is marked.
        for i in range(m):
            for j in range(n):
                if i in zero_rows or j in zero_cols:
                    matrix[i][j] = 0

column1:
Search a 2D Matrix (Binary Search, Medium)

You get an m x n integer matrix and an integer target. Each row is sorted in non-decreasing order. The first integer of each row is greater than the last integer of the previous row. Return true if target is in the matrix. Otherwise return false. The solution must run in O(log(m * n)) time.

Constraints:
m == matrix.length
n == matrix[i].length
1 <= m, n <= 100
-10^4 <= matrix[i][j], target <= 10^4

Name the technique and the memory hook. Then rebuild the solution.
column2:
Hook: The grid is one sorted list cut into rows, so binary search the flat index and divmod by cols.
Techniques: binary-search-index, matrix-manipulation

Approach: Single binary search on the virtual flat array. Read the grid row by row as one sorted list of length rows * cols, and run the standard binary search on flat indices with divmod(mid, cols) to find the cell.

Rebuild:
  1. Get rows and cols from the matrix. Set lo = 0 and hi = rows * cols - 1.
  2. Loop while lo <= hi. Set mid = (lo + hi) // 2.
  3. Convert mid to a cell with r, c = divmod(mid, cols). Read val = matrix[r][c].
  4. Return True if val equals target.
  5. If val is smaller than target, set lo = mid + 1. Otherwise, set hi = mid - 1.
  6. After the loop, return False.
Signals:
  • The statement requires O(log(...)) time on sorted data. A log bound on sorted data points to binary search.
  • Each row is sorted, and each row starts above the end of the previous row. Read row by row, the whole grid is one sorted sequence.
  • The question is a membership test on sorted data: is the value present or not.
  • A 2D container with a total order across all cells suggests that you can treat it as 1D through an index mapping.
Key insight: When a multi-dimensional structure is totally ordered in its natural traversal order, it is a sorted 1D array in disguise. Binary search the flat index and convert the index to coordinates on demand with divmod.
Approaches:
  • Brute force scan: O(m * n) time, O(1) space (too slow)
  • Binary search each row: O(m log n) time, O(1) space (too slow)
  • Staircase search from the top-right corner: O(m + n) time, O(1) space (too slow)
  • Two binary searches: row, then column: O(log m + log n) = O(log(m * n)) time, O(1) space
  • Single binary search on the virtual flat array (optimal, chosen): O(log(m * n)) time, O(1) space
class Solution:
    def searchMatrix(self, matrix: List[List[int]], target: int) -> bool:
        rows, cols = len(matrix), len(matrix[0])
        lo, hi = 0, rows * cols - 1
        while lo <= hi:
            mid = (lo + hi) // 2
            r, c = divmod(mid, cols)
            val = matrix[r][c]
            if val == target:
                return True
            if val < target:
                lo = mid + 1
            else:
                hi = mid - 1
        return False

column1:
Minimum Window Substring (Sliding Window, Hard)

You get two strings s and t with lengths m and n. Return the shortest contiguous non-empty substring of s that contains every character of t, including duplicates. A character that appears k times in t must appear at least k times in the window. The window can contain extra characters that are not in t. Characters are case-sensitive. If no such substring exists, return the empty string. The test cases guarantee that the answer is unique.

Constraints:
m == s.length
n == t.length
1 <= m, n <= 10^5
s and t consist of uppercase and lowercase English letters.
Follow-up: Could you find an algorithm that runs in O(m + n) time?

Name the technique and the memory hook. Then rebuild the solution.
column2:
Hook: Grow right until have equals required, then shrink left while it holds.
Techniques: sliding-window-variable, two-pointers, counting-frequency, hash-map-lookup

Approach: Expand-then-shrink sliding window with a have/required counter. Grow the window to the right until every character of t has its count, then shrink from the left while the window stays valid and record the shortest one.

Rebuild:
  1. If len(t) > len(s), return the empty string.
  2. Set need = Counter(t) and window = Counter(). Set have = 0 and required = len(need).
  3. Set best_len = float("inf"), best_start = 0 and left = 0.
  4. For each right, c in enumerate(s), add 1 to window[c]. If c is in need and window[c] == need[c], add 1 to have.
  5. While have == required, record the window. If right - left + 1 < best_len, set best_len to that length and best_start to left.
  6. Still in the while loop, set out = s[left] and subtract 1 from window[out]. If out is in need and window[out] < need[out], subtract 1 from have. Then add 1 to left.
  7. After the scan, return the empty string if best_len is still infinity. Otherwise return s[best_start:best_start + best_len].
Signals:
  • The answer is a contiguous substring or subarray, and the task asks for the shortest one that satisfies a condition.
  • The condition is monotone in the window: if a window satisfies it, every larger window that contains it also satisfies it.
  • The condition is about multiset coverage: the window must contain required items with required counts, and extra items are allowed.
  • The input length is up to 10^5, so O(m^2) substrings are too many and you need a linear or near-linear scan.
Key insight: For a shortest window that must satisfy a monotone coverage condition, the best left end never moves backward as the right end moves forward. So expand right until the window is valid, then shrink left while it stays valid. Track validity with a counter of satisfied requirements so that each step costs O(1).
Approaches:
  • Brute force over all substrings: O(m^2 * (m + |Sigma|)) time, O(|Sigma|) space (too slow)
  • Fix left end, extend right end incrementally: O(m^2) time, O(|Sigma|) space (too slow)
  • Binary search on window length plus fixed sliding window: O(m log m + n) time, O(|Sigma|) space
  • Variable sliding window with satisfied-distinct counter (optimal): O(m + n) time, O(|Sigma|) space
  • Single missing-count variant: O(m + n) time, O(|Sigma|) space
  • Filtered sliding window: O(m + n) time, O(m) space
from collections import Counter


class Solution:
    def minWindow(self, s: str, t: str) -> str:
        if len(t) > len(s):
            return ""
        need = Counter(t)
        window = Counter()
        have, required = 0, len(need)
        best_len, best_start = float("inf"), 0
        left = 0
        for right, c in enumerate(s):
            window[c] += 1
            if c in need and window[c] == need[c]:
                have += 1
            while have == required:
                if right - left + 1 < best_len:
                    best_len = right - left + 1
                    best_start = left
                out = s[left]
                window[out] -= 1
                if out in need and window[out] < need[out]:
                    have -= 1
                left += 1
        if best_len == float("inf"):
            return ""
        return s[best_start:best_start + best_len]

Subsets (Backtracking, Medium)

You get an integer array nums. All elements of nums are unique. Return all possible subsets of nums (the power set). The result must not contain duplicate subsets. The empty subset is part of the answer. You can return the subsets in any order.

Constraints:
1 <= nums.length <= 10
-10 <= nums[i] <= 10
All the numbers of nums are unique.

Name the technique and the memory hook. Then rebuild the solution.
column2:
Hook: Each number doubles the list. Keep the old subsets and add each one plus the number.
Techniques: backtracking-subsets, bit-manipulation

Approach: Iterative cascade (doubling). Start with only the empty subset. For each number, keep every subset you have and add a copy of each subset with the number appended.

Rebuild:
  1. Set res = [[]], because the empty subset is always an answer.
  2. Loop over each number x in nums.
  3. In the loop, write res += [subset + [x] for subset in res]. Python builds the full new list first, so the comprehension reads only the old subsets.
  4. Do not use res.extend with a generator or append inside a loop over res. Then the loop also sees the new subsets and does not stop.
  5. After the loop, return res. It holds 2^n subsets.
Signals:
  • The task says return all possible subsets, combinations or selections. You must list every answer, so exponential output is expected.
  • n is very small (about 10 to 20). This allows 2^n enumeration.
  • Each element is either in or out of an answer. This is one binary decision per element.
  • The order inside the answer does not matter. Fix the element order to avoid counting the same set twice.
Key insight: A subset is a sequence of independent include or exclude decisions, one for each element, made in a fixed order. Enumerate all decision sequences and you get every subset exactly once. The fixed order is what prevents duplicates.
Optimal: The record's solution_code uses backtracking with take or skip and one shared path. It has the same O(n * 2^n) time, so you do not need it for speed here. Learn it as the template for related problems. Subsets II, Combinations, Combination Sum and Permutations all use the same append, recurse and pop pattern with pruning. The cascade builds every subset and cannot prune, so it is a weaker template for those problems.
Approaches:
  • Ordered generation plus dedupe (naive): O(n! * n log n) time, O(n * 2^n) space (too slow)
  • Iterative cascade: O(n * 2^n) time, O(n * 2^n) for the output, O(1) extra space
  • Bitmask enumeration: O(n * 2^n) time, O(n * 2^n) for the output, O(1) extra space
  • Backtracking with include or exclude (chosen): O(n * 2^n) time, O(n) extra for the recursion and the path, O(n * 2^n) for the output space
  • Backtracking with a start index (for-loop template): O(n * 2^n) time, O(n) extra for the recursion and the path, O(n * 2^n) for the output space
class Solution:
    def subsets(self, nums: List[int]) -> List[List[int]]:
        res = [[]]                      # the empty subset
        for x in nums:
            # every old subset stays; a copy of it with x is new
            res += [subset + [x] for subset in res]
        return res

Word Search (Backtracking, Medium)

You get an m x n grid of characters board and a string word. Return true if word exists in the grid, else return false. The word must be built from the letters of sequentially adjacent cells. Adjacent cells are horizontal or vertical neighbors only. Diagonal cells are not adjacent. One path may not use the same cell more than once. Board and word contain only lowercase and uppercase English letters. A letter matches only the identical character, so 'a' does not match 'A'.

Constraints:
m == board.length
n = board[i].length
1 <= m, n <= 6
1 <= word.length <= 15
Follow-up: Could you use search pruning to make your solution faster with a larger board?

Name the technique and the memory hook. Then rebuild the solution.
column2:
Hook: Check the cell, mark it, try four neighbors, unmark it. Speed-up: fill can-finish cells from the back first.
Techniques: backtracking-constraint-search, grid-flood-fill, in-place-visited-marking, counting-frequency, dp-2d-grid

Approach: Backtracking DFS with a can-finish guard table. First fill can[i], the cells that could spell word[i:] if a path could reuse cells. Then run the usual mark, recurse, unmark DFS with a used set, and step only on cells in can[i].

Rebuild:
  1. List all cells. Write neighbors(r, c) that returns the 4 moves. Set last = len(word) - 1.
  2. Make can as one empty set per letter of word.
  3. For i from last down to 0, add a cell to can[i] if its letter is word[i] and (i == last or a neighbor is in can[i + 1]).
  4. Make an empty set used for the cells on the current path.
  5. Write dfs(r, c, i). Return False if (r, c) is not in can[i] or is in used. Return True if i == last.
  6. Add (r, c) to used. Set found = any(dfs(nr, nc, i + 1)) over the 4 neighbors. Remove (r, c) from used. Return found.
  7. Return any(dfs(r, c, 0)) over all cells.
Signals:
  • The task asks if a sequence can be traced through a grid or graph by moving between neighbors.
  • A rule forbids reuse of a cell inside one path. The state then depends on the whole path, not only on the current cell.
  • The limits are tiny (here at most 36 cells and at most 15 letters). An exponential search with pruning is acceptable.
  • The answer is a yes/no existence question. The search can stop at the first success.
Key insight: Grow the path one matched letter at a time and drop a branch as soon as the next letter does not match. Handle the no-reuse rule by marking a cell on the way down and unmarking it on the way back. Then one shared grid always shows exactly the current path. For speed, solve the easy version that allows reuse with a small DP table. A cell that fails the easy version also fails the real one, so the search skips it.
Optimal: The record's solution_code uses the same table and DFS. It adds two O(m*n + L) prunes before the search: a letter count check and a reversal that starts from the rarer end of the word. It also marks used cells in place with '#' and starts the DFS only from cells in ok[0]. These make easy rejections instant (for example a word that needs more copies of a letter than the board has) and save a small constant factor. They do not change the worst case found. Rows BBBBBB and five rows of AAAAAA with word 'A'*13 + 'BA' make about 1.2 million dfs calls in both versions (about 0.64 s CPU intuitive, 0.58 s CPU record). The reversal does help on some boards. AAAAAB/AAAAAA/BAAAAA/AAAAAA/AAAAAA/AABAAB with word 'A'*12 + 'BAB' makes about 0.9 million calls (about 0.5 s) without it and 60 calls with it. Add them when you want the fastest constant factor or when the board can be much larger than 6x6.
Approaches:
  • Enumerate ordered cell sequences: O((m*n)!/(m*n-L)! * L) time, O(L) space (too slow)
  • Enumerate all simple walks, then compare: O(m*n*3^L*L) time, O(L) space (too slow)
  • Plain backtracking DFS (visited set or in-place mark): O(m*n*3^L) time, O(L) space (too slow)
  • Backtracking DFS with count and reversal prunes (NeetCode reference): O(m*n*3^L) time, O(L) space (too slow)
  • Count and reversal prunes plus an adjacent letter pair check: O(m*n*3^L) time, O(m*n + L) space (too slow)
  • Count and reversal prunes plus a reachability table (chosen): O(m*n*L + m*n*3^L) time, O(m*n*L) space
from typing import List


class Solution:
    def exist(self, board: List[List[str]], word: str) -> bool:
        rows, cols = len(board), len(board[0])
        cells = [(r, c) for r in range(rows) for c in range(cols)]
        last = len(word) - 1

        def neighbors(r: int, c: int):
            return [(r + 1, c), (r - 1, c), (r, c + 1), (r, c - 1)]

        # Guard table: can[i] holds the cells that could spell word[i:]
        # if a path were allowed to reuse cells. It is the DFS below
        # without the used set, filled from the last letter to the first.
        can = [set() for _ in word]
        for i in range(last, -1, -1):
            for r, c in cells:
                if board[r][c] == word[i] and (
                    i == last or any(nb in can[i + 1] for nb in neighbors(r, c))
                ):
                    can[i].add((r, c))

        used = set()  # cells on the current path

        def dfs(r: int, c: int, i: int) -> bool:
            # can[i] holds only in-bounds cells that match word[i],
            # so this one test checks bounds, letter and future.
            if (r, c) not in can[i] or (r, c) in used:
                return False
            if i == last:
                return True
            used.add((r, c))
            found = any(dfs(nr, nc, i + 1) for nr, nc in neighbors(r, c))
            used.remove((r, c))
            return found

        return any(dfs(r, c, 0) for r, c in cells)

Largest Rectangle in Histogram (Stack, Hard)

You get an array of integers heights. Each value is the height of one bar in a histogram. Each bar has width 1, and the bars stand next to each other in array order. Return the area of the largest rectangle in the histogram. The rectangle covers a contiguous run of bars. Its height cannot exceed the shortest bar in that run. Heights can be 0.

Constraints:
1 <= heights.length <= 10^5
0 <= heights[i] <= 10^4

Name the technique and the memory hook. Then rebuild the solution.
column2:
Hook: Each bar is the shortest: stretch it to the nearest shorter bar on both sides.
Techniques: monotonic-stack, reverse-thinking, divide-and-conquer

Approach: Nearest shorter bar on each side, found with one monotonic stack helper called twice. Treat each bar as the shortest bar of its rectangle. Find the closest strictly shorter bar on its left and on its right. The area is the bar height times the gap between those two bars.

Rebuild:
  1. Set n = len(heights).
  2. Define nearest_smaller(order, default). Make result = [default] * n and an empty stack of indices.
  3. For each i in order, pop while heights[stack[-1]] >= heights[i]. The pop leaves only strictly shorter bars.
  4. If the stack is not empty, set result[i] = stack[-1]. Push i. After the loop, return result.
  5. Call left = nearest_smaller(range(n), -1). The default -1 means no shorter bar on the left.
  6. Call right = nearest_smaller(range(n - 1, -1, -1), n). The default n means no shorter bar on the right.
  7. Return the max of heights[i] * (right[i] - left[i] - 1) over all i.
Signals:
  • The score of a contiguous range is the minimum (or maximum) element of the range times the range length.
  • Each element can be the limiting value, and its reach ends at the nearest smaller element on each side.
  • A brute force needs the first element to the left or right that is smaller than the current one, for every index.
  • The input is a row of bars or buildings, and a shorter item stops a taller item's span from going further.
Key insight: Enumerate the limiting element instead of the range. If a bar is the shortest bar of the rectangle, the rectangle is as wide as the gap between the nearest strictly shorter bars on its left and right. A monotonic stack finds all those nearest-smaller boundaries in one linear pass, because the moment a bar is popped is the moment its right boundary appears.
Optimal: The record solution_code does the same work in one pass. It keeps (start, height) pairs, and a popped bar gets its area at the moment the shorter bar arrives. The new bar inherits the start of the last popped bar, and a final loop flushes the bars that reach the end. It saves the two helper arrays and one pass. Both versions are O(n) time and O(n) space. Use it when you need a single pass or shorter code. The two-pass version is easier to rebuild and to adapt to counting problems such as Sum of Subarray Minimums.
Approaches:
  • Brute force over all ranges: O(n^2) time, O(1) space (too slow)
  • Expand from each bar: O(n^2) time, O(1) space (too slow)
  • Divide and conquer on the minimum: O(n log n) average, O(n^2) worst case with a linear minimum search time, O(n) recursion depth in the worst case space (too slow)
  • Two passes for nearest smaller on each side: O(n) time, O(n) space
  • One-pass monotonic stack with start index (chosen): O(n) time, O(n) space
  • One-pass monotonic stack with sentinels: O(n) time, O(n) space
class Solution:
    def largestRectangleArea(self, heights: List[int]) -> int:
        n = len(heights)

        def nearest_smaller(order, default):
            # For each i, the index of the closest strictly shorter bar seen before i in this order.
            result = [default] * n
            stack = []  # indices; heights strictly increase from bottom to top
            for i in order:
                while stack and heights[stack[-1]] >= heights[i]:
                    stack.pop()
                if stack:
                    result[i] = stack[-1]
                stack.append(i)
            return result

        left = nearest_smaller(range(n), -1)
        right = nearest_smaller(range(n - 1, -1, -1), n)

        best = 0
        for i in range(n):
            width = right[i] - left[i] - 1
            best = max(best, heights[i] * width)
        return best

Subsets II (Backtracking, Medium)

You get an integer array nums. The array can contain duplicate values. Return all possible subsets of nums (the power set). The result must not contain duplicate subsets. Two subsets are duplicates when they contain the same values with the same counts, no matter which indices the values came from. The empty subset is part of the answer. You can return the subsets in any order.

Constraints:
1 <= nums.length <= 10
-10 <= nums[i] <= 10

Name the technique and the memory hook. Then rebuild the solution.
column2:
Hook: Count each value. Every old subset takes 0 to count copies of it.
Techniques: backtracking-subsets, sorting

Approach: Iterative cascade over distinct values. It is the Subsets I cascade with counts. Count each value. Start with only the empty subset. For each value with count c, replace the list with every old subset plus 0, 1, ..., c copies of the value.

Rebuild:
  1. Start with only the empty subset: res = [[]].
  2. Count each value with Counter(nums). Sort the (value, count) pairs. The sort is not needed for correctness, but each subset then comes out in sorted order.
  3. Loop over each value and its count.
  4. Build a new list. For each old subset and each k from 0 to count, add subset + [value] * k.
  5. Assign the new list to res. Do not extend res in place, because k = 0 already keeps every old subset.
  6. After the loop, return res.
Signals:
  • The task asks for all subsets, all combinations or the power set. This means you must enumerate, so use backtracking.
  • The input length is very small (n <= 10 or n <= 20). An exponential output of 2^n items is acceptable.
  • The input may contain duplicates, but the output must not contain duplicate groups. This means you must deduplicate by value, not by index.
  • Order inside a group does not matter. Sort the input so that equal values sit next to each other and each group has one canonical order.
Key insight: Duplicates come from equal values at different indices. Sort the input so that equal values are adjacent. Then, at one decision point, try each distinct value only once. Equal values give identical subtrees, so the first branch already covers them.
Optimal: The record's solution_code sorts nums and uses start-index backtracking with the skip rule j > start and nums[j] == nums[j - 1]. It has the same O(n * 2^n) time, so you do not need it for speed here. Learn it as the template for Combination Sum II and Permutations II. In Combination Sum II, the search must stop when the sum exceeds the target, and the cascade cannot prune. In Permutations II, the order of the values matters, so counts alone do not describe an answer. The skip rule tries each value only once at one level of the search.
Approaches:
  • Brute force: all index subsets plus a set of sorted tuples: O(n * 2^n * log n) time, O(n * 2^n) space
  • Sort, then backtracking with a for-loop and skip of equal siblings (chosen): O(n * 2^n) time, O(n) extra for the recursion and the path, plus the output space
  • Sort, then include or exclude with a jump over the equal block (NeetCode style): O(n * 2^n) time, O(n) extra plus the output space
  • Counter of distinct values, choose a count for each: O(n * 2^n) time, O(n) extra plus the output space
  • Iterative build with the size of the previous step: O(n * 2^n) time, O(1) extra plus the output space
  • Bitmask with a canonical-choice filter: O(n * 2^n) time, O(n) extra plus the output space
from collections import Counter
from typing import List


class Solution:
    def subsetsWithDup(self, nums: List[int]) -> List[List[int]]:
        res = [[]]                                   # the empty subset
        for value, count in sorted(Counter(nums).items()):
            # every old subset takes 0, 1, ..., count copies of value
            res = [subset + [value] * k for subset in res for k in range(count + 1)]
        return res
