Reorder List (Linked List, Medium)

You get the head of a singly linked list L0 -> L1 -> ... -> Ln-1 -> Ln. Reorder the list into the form L0 -> Ln -> L1 -> Ln-1 -> L2 -> Ln-2 -> ... The result takes nodes alternately from the front and from the back, starting with the front. You must not change the values in the nodes. You may only change the nodes themselves, that is, their next links. Modify the list in place and return nothing. The head node stays the head.

Constraints:
The number of nodes in the list is in the range [1, 5 * 10^4].
1 <= Node.val <= 1000

Name the technique and the memory hook. Then rebuild the solution.
column2:
Hook: Put the nodes in an array, take front then back, chain them, end with None.
Techniques: linked-list-pointer-rewiring, two-pointers-fast-slow, linked-list-reversal, prev-curr-pointers, linked-list-merge

Approach: Array of nodes, then relink in order. Copy the node references into an array, list them in the order front, back, front, back with two indices that move inward, and then chain the nodes in that order.

Rebuild:
  1. Walk the list and append each node to an array called nodes.
  2. Make an empty array called order. Set left to 0 and right to len(nodes) - 1.
  3. While left <= right, append nodes[left] to order. Append nodes[right] to order only if left < right. Then add 1 to left and subtract 1 from right.
  4. For each adjacent pair a, b in order, set a.next = b.
  5. Set the next link of the last node in order to None.
Signals:
  • The output alternates between the front and the back of a sequence: first, last, second, second-to-last, and so on.
  • In a list of n nodes with 0-based indices, node i pairs with its mirror node n-1-i.
  • The input is a singly linked list, so you can only move forward, but the task needs access from both ends.
  • The task forbids changes to node values and asks for an in-place change. This points to pointer rewiring. An O(1) extra space answer is possible and is the expected one.
Key insight: The target order reads the list from both ends at the same time. A singly linked list only reads forward. Reverse the back half in place, so its last node becomes a head you can read forward. The problem then becomes an alternating merge of two forward lists.
Optimal: The record solution_code uses O(1) extra space instead of O(n). It finds the end of the front half with slow and fast pointers, cuts the list, reverses the back half in place, and weaves the two halves. Both solutions run in O(n) time. The statement asks only for in-place rewiring of the nodes, and the array solution does that. Use the optimal form when O(1) extra space is required. It is also the shared pattern for palindrome linked list and maximum twin sum.
Approaches:
  • Repeated tail removal: O(n^2) time, O(1) space (too slow)
  • Recursion with a front pointer: O(n) time, O(n) call stack space (too slow)
  • Array of nodes with converging pointers: O(n) time, O(n) space
  • Stack of nodes: O(n) time, O(n) space
  • Find middle, reverse second half, merge alternately: O(n) time, O(1) space
class Solution:
    def reorderList(self, head: Optional[ListNode]) -> None:
        """
        Do not return anything, modify head in-place instead.
        """
        # 1. Copy the node references into an array.
        nodes = []
        node = head
        while node:
            nodes.append(node)
            node = node.next

        # 2. Build the target order: front, back, front, back, ...
        order = []
        left, right = 0, len(nodes) - 1
        while left <= right:
            order.append(nodes[left])
            if left < right:
                order.append(nodes[right])
            left += 1
            right -= 1

        # 3. Chain the nodes in that order and end the list.
        for a, b in zip(order, order[1:]):
            a.next = b
        order[-1].next = None

LRU Cache (Linked List, Medium)

Design a data structure that follows the rules of a Least Recently Used (LRU) cache. Implement the class LRUCache. LRUCache(capacity) creates the cache with a positive capacity. get(key) returns the value of key if key exists, else it returns -1. put(key, value) updates the value of key if key exists, else it adds the key-value pair to the cache. If the number of keys becomes larger than capacity after a put, the cache evicts the least recently used key. A successful get and every put count as a use of that key. get and put must each run in O(1) average time.

Constraints:
1 <= capacity <= 3000
0 <= key <= 10^4
0 <= value <= 10^5
At most 2 * 10^5 calls will be made to get and put.

Name the technique and the memory hook. Then rebuild the solution.
column2:
Hook: Ordered dict: move to end on use, pop the front on overflow.
Techniques: hashmap-plus-linked-list, hash-map-lookup, design-data-structure, dummy-node, linked-list-pointer-rewiring

Approach: Use collections.OrderedDict as the cache. The dict keeps keys from oldest to newest, so on every use you move the key to the end, and on overflow you pop the first key.

Rebuild:
  1. In __init__, store the capacity and create an empty OrderedDict. Its front is the oldest key and its end is the newest key.
  2. In get, return -1 if the key is not in the dict.
  3. Else call move_to_end(key), because a get is a use, and return the value.
  4. In put, assign cache[key] = value and call move_to_end(key), because a put is a use.
  5. If len(cache) is larger than capacity, call popitem(last=False) to drop the oldest key.
Signals:
  • The problem asks you to design a class, and each operation must run in O(1) time.
  • Words like cache, capacity, evict and recently used appear in the statement.
  • You must find an item by key and also keep the items in an order that changes on every access.
  • An accessed item must move from any position in the order to one end.
Key insight: When you need O(1) lookup by key and O(1) reordering or removal from the middle of a sequence, store the items in a doubly linked list and keep a hash map from key to node. The map finds the node, and the prev and next pointers let you unlink it without a search.
Optimal: The record's solution_code builds the same structure by hand: a dict from key to node plus a doubly linked list with left and right sentinels. The big-O is the same. In CPython, OrderedDict is about 1.5 to 2 times faster, because its linked list is written in C. You need the hand-built version when an interviewer forbids OrderedDict, asks you to show the linked list, or uses a language without an ordered map. Hook for it: map finds the node, list keeps the order, remove then insert at the right, evict left.next. Remember to store the key in each node so eviction can delete the map entry. Do not replace OrderedDict with a plain dict and next(iter(d)), because eviction is not O(1) in CPython.
Approaches:
  • Hash map plus timestamps: O(1) get, O(capacity) put when it evicts time, O(capacity) space (too slow)
  • Hash map plus ordered Python list of keys: O(capacity) per operation time, O(capacity) space (too slow)
  • Hash map plus doubly linked list with sentinels: O(1) per operation time, O(capacity) space
  • collections.OrderedDict: O(1) per operation time, O(capacity) space
  • Plain dict insertion order: O(1) average for get and for put without eviction, O(capacity) amortized per eviction in CPython time, O(capacity) space
from collections import OrderedDict


class LRUCache:

    def __init__(self, capacity: int):
        self.capacity = capacity
        self.cache = OrderedDict()  # oldest key first, newest key last

    def get(self, key: int) -> int:
        if key not in self.cache:
            return -1
        self.cache.move_to_end(key)  # a get is a use
        return self.cache[key]

    def put(self, key: int, value: int) -> None:
        self.cache[key] = value
        self.cache.move_to_end(key)  # a put is a use
        if len(self.cache) > self.capacity:
            self.cache.popitem(last=False)  # drop the oldest key

column1:
Evaluate Reverse Polish Notation (Stack, Medium)

You get an array of strings tokens. The array is an arithmetic expression in Reverse Polish Notation (postfix): each operator comes after its two operands. Evaluate the expression and return its integer value. The valid operators are '+', '-', '*' and '/'. Each operand is an integer or another expression. Division between two integers truncates toward zero. No division by zero occurs. The input is always a valid RPN expression. The answer and all intermediate results fit in a 32-bit signed integer.

Constraints:
1 <= tokens.length <= 10^4
tokens[i] is either an operator: "+", "-", "*", or "/", or an integer in the range [-200, 200].

Name the technique and the memory hook. Then rebuild the solution.
column2:
Hook: Push numbers. An operator pops b, then a, and pushes a op b. Divide with int(a / b).
Techniques: stack-matching-parsing, simulation

Approach: Operand stack, one pass. Push each number. On an operator, pop the right operand, then the left operand, and push the result.

Rebuild:
  1. Make an empty list called stack and loop over the tokens.
  2. Compare the whole token with the set of four operators, so that '-11' stays a number.
  3. For an operator, pop b first (right operand), then pop a (left operand).
  4. Push a + b, a - b or a * b, and push int(a / b) for division so that it truncates toward zero.
  5. For a number, push int(tok).
  6. After the loop, return stack[0], the single value left.
Signals:
  • The input is a postfix or prefix token stream. Each operator comes after (or before) the values it acts on.
  • Each operator uses the most recent values that no operator has used yet. Newest first is last in, first out, so a stack fits.
  • The result of one step is an input to a later step. You must keep partial results until an operator needs them.
  • Some tokens close a unit of work and consume items that came before them. A token that reduces earlier pending items points to a stack.
Key insight: In postfix order, every operator acts on the most recent pending results. A stack of pending values gives exactly this last-in, first-out access. One left-to-right pass evaluates the expression with no precedence or bracket logic.
Approaches:
  • Repeated collapse of the first num-num-op triple: O(n^2) time, O(n) space (too slow)
  • Recursive descent from the end (expression tree): O(n) time, O(n) recursion depth space
  • Operand stack, single pass (optimal, standard): O(n) time, O(n) space
  • In-place stack inside the tokens array: O(n) time, O(1) extra space
class Solution:
    def evalRPN(self, tokens: List[str]) -> int:
        stack = []
        for tok in tokens:
            if tok in {"+", "-", "*", "/"}:
                b = stack.pop()  # right operand is on top
                a = stack.pop()  # left operand is below it
                if tok == "+":
                    stack.append(a + b)
                elif tok == "-":
                    stack.append(a - b)
                elif tok == "*":
                    stack.append(a * b)
                else:
                    stack.append(int(a / b))  # truncate toward zero
            else:
                stack.append(int(tok))
        return stack[0]

column1:
Maximum Product Subarray (1-D Dynamic Programming, Medium)

You get an integer array nums. Find a non-empty contiguous subarray that has the largest product. Return that product. The product of a single-element subarray is the value of that element. The values can be negative, zero or positive. The test cases guarantee that the answer fits in a 32-bit integer, and the product of any subarray of nums fits in a 32-bit integer.

Constraints:
1 <= nums.length <= 2 * 10^4
-10 <= nums[i] <= 10
The product of any subarray of nums is guaranteed to fit in a 32-bit integer.

Name the technique and the memory hook. Then rebuild the solution.
column2:
Hook: Kadane, but carry the biggest and the smallest, because a negative swaps them.
Techniques: kadane, dp-1d-linear, prefix-suffix-accumulation

Approach: Max and min product ending here (Kadane with two states). Carry the biggest and the smallest product of a subarray that ends at the current value, because a negative value turns the smallest into the biggest.

Rebuild:
  1. Set best = nums[0] and big = small = 1, the empty product.
  2. Loop over each x in nums.
  3. Build the three candidates: x alone, big * x and small * x.
  4. Set big, small = max(candidates), min(candidates) in one assignment, so both use the old values.
  5. Update best = max(best, big) inside the loop.
  6. Return best after the loop.
Signals:
  • The problem asks for the best value of an aggregate over a contiguous, non-empty subarray. This points to a 'best ending at index i' scan (Kadane style).
  • The aggregate is a product and the values can be negative. A negative factor reverses the order of candidates, so the largest can become the smallest and the reverse.
  • Zeros can occur. A zero sets every running product to 0 and acts as a barrier between independent segments.
  • n is up to 2 * 10^4. O(n^2) is about 2 * 10^8 steps and is too slow in CPython, so you need one linear pass.
Key insight: When the step that extends a partial result can reverse order, such as a multiplication by a negative number, the best result at the next step can come from the worst result at this step. Carry both the maximum and the minimum ending here. A monotone step maps extremes to extremes, so these two values are sufficient.
Approaches:
  • Brute force over all subarrays: O(n^3) time, O(1) space (too slow)
  • Brute force with running product: O(n^2) time, O(1) space (too slow)
  • Max and min product ending here (Kadane variant): O(n) time, O(1) space
  • Prefix and suffix product scan: O(n) time, O(1) space
  • Split by zeros and count negatives: O(n) time, O(1) space
class Solution:
    def maxProduct(self, nums: List[int]) -> int:
        best = nums[0]
        big = small = 1  # largest and smallest product that ends here (empty product to start)
        for x in nums:
            # a subarray that ends at x is x alone, or an old one times x
            candidates = (x, big * x, small * x)
            big, small = max(candidates), min(candidates)  # update both from the OLD values
            best = max(best, big)
        return best

Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array (Binary Search, Medium)

An array of length n is sorted in ascending order and then rotated between 1 and n times. For example, nums = [0,1,2,4,5,6,7] becomes [4,5,6,7,0,1,2] after 4 rotations. It becomes [0,1,2,4,5,6,7] again after 7 rotations. Rotating [a[0], a[1], a[2], ..., a[n-1]] one time gives [a[n-1], a[0], a[1], a[2], ..., a[n-2]]. You get the sorted rotated array nums of unique elements. Return the minimum element of this array. You must write an algorithm that runs in O(log n) time.

Constraints:
n == nums.length
1 <= n <= 5000
-5000 <= nums[i] <= 5000
All the integers of nums are unique.

Name the technique and the memory hook. Then rebuild the solution.
column2:
Hook: Low run means at most the last value; find the first one.
Techniques: binary-search-rotated, binary-search-index

Approach: First-true binary search against the last element. The test nums[i] <= nums[-1] is false on the high run and true on the low run, so the minimum is the first index where the test is true.

Rebuild:
  1. Save last = nums[-1]. The low run holds every value <= last.
  2. Set lo = 0 and hi = n - 1. The last index is always in the low run.
  3. Loop while lo < hi and take the lower midpoint mid = (lo + hi) // 2.
  4. If nums[mid] <= last, set hi = mid, because mid can be the answer.
  5. Else set lo = mid + 1, because mid is in the high run.
  6. Return nums[lo] when lo == hi.
Signals:
  • The input is a sorted array that was rotated or shifted. A rotated sorted array is two sorted runs, so binary search still applies.
  • The statement demands O(log n) time on an array. This rules out a scan and points to binary search.
  • The elements are unique. Then one comparison with an end value always tells which half to keep. With duplicates, a tie can block that decision.
  • You look for a boundary or turning point, not a given target value. Search for the first index where a yes/no property becomes true.
Key insight: A rotated sorted array splits into two sorted runs. Every value in the first run is greater than the last element, and every value in the second run is not. So the comparison nums[i] <= nums[-1] is a monotone false-then-true predicate, and the minimum is the first true index. Binary search finds that boundary.
Optimal: The optimal solution_code compares nums[mid] with nums[hi] instead of the fixed nums[-1]. It has the same O(log n) time and O(1) space and gives the same result on unique values. It adds nothing you need for this problem. The nums[hi] form is the one that extends to problem 154 with duplicates, where a tie nums[mid] == nums[hi] lets you do hi -= 1.
Approaches:
  • Linear scan: O(n) time, O(1) space (too slow)
  • Find the drop by scanning: O(n) time, O(1) space (too slow)
  • Binary search, compare mid with right end: O(log n) time, O(1) space
  • Binary search with running minimum (NeetCode style): O(log n) time, O(1) space
  • Binary search with a fixed last-element pivot: O(log n) time, O(1) space
class Solution:
    def findMin(self, nums: List[int]) -> int:
        # Low run: every value <= the last value. High run: every value > it.
        # Find the first index in the low run (first True).
        last = nums[-1]
        lo, hi = 0, len(nums) - 1
        while lo < hi:
            mid = (lo + hi) // 2
            if nums[mid] <= last:
                hi = mid          # mid is in the low run; it can be the answer
            else:
                lo = mid + 1      # mid is in the high run; answer is to the right
        return nums[lo]

Min Stack (Stack, Medium)

Design a stack class MinStack that supports push, pop, top and retrieval of the minimum element. MinStack() creates an empty stack. push(val) puts the integer val on top of the stack. pop() removes the top element. top() returns the top element. getMin() returns the smallest element that is currently in the stack. Each method must run in O(1) time. pop, top and getMin are always called on a non-empty stack. Values are 32-bit signed integers, and there are at most 3 * 10^4 calls in total.

Constraints:
-2^31 <= val <= 2^31 - 1
Methods pop, top and getMin operations will always be called on non-empty stacks.
At most 3 * 10^4 calls will be made to push, pop, top, and getMin.

Name the technique and the memory hook. Then rebuild the solution.
column2:
Hook: Push the pair (value, min so far). Pop removes both.
Techniques: design-data-structure, prefix-suffix-accumulation

Approach: Use one stack of (value, min so far) pairs. Each pair stores a value and the minimum of that value and all values below it. top reads the value in the last pair. getMin reads the minimum in the last pair.

Rebuild:
  1. In __init__, set self.stack to an empty list. Each entry is a (value, min_so_far) pair.
  2. In push, set min_so_far to min(val, self.stack[-1][1]) when the stack has entries. Else set min_so_far to val.
  3. In push, append the pair (val, min_so_far) to self.stack.
  4. In pop, call self.stack.pop() once. The pair below already holds the old minimum.
  5. In top, return self.stack[-1][0].
  6. In getMin, return self.stack[-1][1].
Signals:
  • The task is to design a container that answers an aggregate query, such as min or max, in O(1) next to its normal operations.
  • Removals happen only at one end in LIFO order. So every earlier state of the container comes back exactly after a pop.
  • The aggregate is easy to update when an element is added. It is impossible to undo by arithmetic when an element leaves, because min and max have no inverse.
  • The statement demands O(1) per operation. This rules out a scan, and it also rules out a heap or a sorted structure.
Key insight: When removals follow LIFO order, every earlier state returns exactly. So store a snapshot of the aggregate with each push, and undo becomes a pop of that snapshot. This works even for aggregates like min and max that you cannot reverse by arithmetic.
Optimal: The record solution_code uses the same prefix-minimum idea. It has the same O(1) time per operation and O(n) space. It only splits each pair into two parallel lists, stack and min_stack. So pop must remove from both lists. The split adds nothing that this problem needs.
Approaches:
  • Brute force scan: O(1) push/pop/top, O(n) getMin time, O(n) space (too slow)
  • Single cached minimum with rescan on pop: O(1) push/top/getMin, O(n) worst-case pop time, O(n) space (too slow)
  • Heap or sorted container with lazy deletion: O(log n) amortized per operation time, O(n) space (too slow)
  • Parallel prefix-minimum stack (optimal, standard): O(1) per operation time, O(n) space
  • Lean minimum stack (store only new minima): O(1) per operation time, O(n) worst case space
  • Difference encoding with one minimum variable: O(1) per operation time, O(1) extra beyond the stored elements space
class MinStack:

    def __init__(self):
        self.stack = []  # each entry is (value, min of this entry and all below it)

    def push(self, val: int) -> None:
        if self.stack:
            min_so_far = min(val, self.stack[-1][1])
        else:
            min_so_far = val
        self.stack.append((val, min_so_far))

    def pop(self) -> None:
        self.stack.pop()

    def top(self) -> int:
        return self.stack[-1][0]

    def getMin(self) -> int:
        return self.stack[-1][1]

column1:
Two Sum II - Input Array Is Sorted (Two Pointers, Medium)

You get a 1-indexed array of integers numbers that is already sorted in non-decreasing order. Find two numbers that add up to a specific target number. Let these two numbers be numbers[index1] and numbers[index2], where 1 <= index1 < index2 <= numbers.length. Return the indices index1 and index2, each incremented by one (so 1-based), as an integer array [index1, index2] of length 2. The tests are generated such that there is exactly one solution. You may not use the same element twice. Your solution must use only constant extra space.

Constraints:
2 <= numbers.length <= 3 * 10^4
-1000 <= numbers[i] <= 1000
numbers is sorted in non-decreasing order.
-1000 <= target <= 1000

Name the technique and the memory hook. Then rebuild the solution.
column2:
Hook: Sorted pair sum: start at both ends. Too small, move left up. Too big, move right down.
Techniques: two-pointers-converging, binary-search-index

Approach: Use two pointers from both ends. Start left at the smallest value and right at the largest value. If the sum is too small, move left up. If the sum is too large, move right down. Stop when the sum equals target.

Rebuild:
  1. Put one pointer at each end: left = 0 and right = len(numbers) - 1.
  2. Loop while left < right, so the two pointers never use the same element.
  3. Compute total = numbers[left] + numbers[right].
  4. If total == target, return [left + 1, right + 1] (1-based).
  5. If total < target, do left += 1. Otherwise do right -= 1.
  6. After the loop, return []. The one-solution guarantee means this line never runs.
Signals:
  • The input array is sorted, and the task asks for a pair whose sum meets a target (equal to it, closest to it, or below it).
  • The problem demands O(1) extra space, so a hash map of seen values is not allowed. The sorted order must do the work of the hash map.
  • The pair sum never decreases when either index moves toward larger values. So one comparison can rule out a whole row or a whole column of the pair table.
  • A sum that is too small tells you to raise the smaller value. A sum that is too large tells you to lower the larger value. One clear move per comparison points to converging pointers.
Key insight: In a sorted range, the pair (smallest, largest) tells you which element to discard. If their sum is too small, the smallest element is useless, because no partner is larger than the current largest. If their sum is too large, the largest element is useless by the same argument. So each comparison shrinks the search range by one, and the search becomes linear.
Approaches:
  • Brute force over all pairs: O(n^2) time, O(1) space (too slow)
  • Hash map of complements (original Two Sum): O(n) time, O(n) space (too slow)
  • Binary search for each complement: O(n log n) time, O(1) space
  • Two pointers converging from both ends (optimal): O(n) time, O(1) space
class Solution:
    def twoSum(self, numbers: List[int], target: int) -> List[int]:
        left, right = 0, len(numbers) - 1
        while left < right:
            total = numbers[left] + numbers[right]
            if total == target:
                return [left + 1, right + 1]
            if total < target:
                left += 1     # sum too small: need a bigger left value
            else:
                right -= 1    # sum too big: need a smaller right value
        return []

Reverse Bits (Bit Manipulation, Easy)

Reverse the bits of a given 32-bit signed integer n. Treat n as a fixed-width 32-bit value, including its leading zeros. Bit i of n moves to bit 31 - i of the result. Return the integer that the reversed bit pattern represents. The constraints keep n in the range 0 to 2^31 - 2 and require n to be even. So bit 0 and bit 31 of n are both 0. The result is then also an even value from 0 to 2^31 - 2, and no sign bit is involved. The leading zeros count: a value with few significant bits becomes a large value after the reversal.

Constraints:
0 <= n <= 2^31 - 2
n is even.
Follow-up: If this function is called many times, how would you optimize it?

Name the technique and the memory hook. Then rebuild the solution.
column2:
Hook: Peel the low bit off n, push it onto res, 32 times.
Techniques: bit-manipulation, divide-and-conquer

Approach: Use peel and push for exactly 32 steps. Read the lowest bit of n and push it onto the low end of res. Then drop that bit from n. The first bit that you read ends at the top.

Rebuild:
  1. Set res to 0.
  2. Loop exactly 32 times, not while n is above zero.
  3. Shift res left by 1, then OR in n & 1 to push the lowest bit of n.
  4. Shift n right by 1 to peel that bit off.
  5. Return res.
Signals:
  • The problem states a fixed bit width, such as 32 bits. Leading zeros then count as real digits.
  • The output is a rearrangement of the bit positions of the input, not an arithmetic result.
  • The problem asks for a positional transform of the binary form of an integer, such as reverse, rotate, or swap of bits.
  • A follow-up asks about many calls on small fixed-width values. This points to a precomputed table over small chunks, such as bytes.
Key insight: You can read the bits of a number from its low end and write them into a new number with a left shift and an OR. This reverses the order. It is the same loop that reverses decimal digits with a remainder by 10 and a multiply by 10. With a fixed width, run the loop for every position, because leading zeros become trailing zeros.
Approaches:
  • String reversal: O(32) = O(1) time, O(32) = O(1) space
  • Bit-by-bit shift and append (standard): O(32) = O(1) time, O(1) space
  • Bit-by-bit with explicit target position (NeetCode): O(32) = O(1) time, O(1) space
  • Byte lookup table (follow-up): O(1) per call after O(256) setup time, O(256) space
  • Divide-and-conquer mask swaps: O(log w) for width w, so 5 steps for 32 bits = O(1) time, O(1) space
class Solution:
    def reverseBits(self, n: int) -> int:
        res = 0
        for _ in range(32):
            res = (res << 1) | (n & 1)  # push the lowest bit of n onto res
            n >>= 1                     # peel that bit off n
        return res

column1:
Number of 1 Bits (Bit Manipulation, Easy)

You get a positive integer n. Return the number of set bits (bits equal to 1) in the binary representation of n. This count is also called the Hamming weight. The input is always positive and fits in a signed 32-bit integer.

Constraints:
1 <= n <= 2^31 - 1
Follow-up: If this function is called many times, how would you optimize it?

Name the technique and the memory hook. Then rebuild the solution.
column2:
Hook: Read the last bit, then shift it away.
Techniques: bit-manipulation

Approach: Check every bit with shift and mask. Add the last bit (n & 1) to a counter, then shift n right by one to drop that bit, and repeat until n is 0.

Rebuild:
  1. Start count at 0.
  2. Loop while n > 0.
  3. Add n & 1 to count, because n & 1 is the last bit.
  4. Shift n right by one with n >>= 1 to drop the last bit.
  5. When the loop ends, n is 0. Return count.
Signals:
  • The statement asks about the bits of an integer (set bits, binary representation, Hamming weight). This points to bitwise operators, not arithmetic on decimal digits.
  • The input fits in a fixed width of 32 bits. Any loop over bit positions is bounded by a constant, so brute force over bits is already fast.
  • The task is to count or visit only the 1 bits. An operation that jumps from one set bit to the next beats a scan over every position.
  • A follow-up says the function is called many times. This signals precomputation: a lookup table over small chunks, or a cache.
Key insight: Subtracting 1 from a number flips its lowest set bit and every bit below it. So x & (x - 1) deletes exactly the lowest set bit. Use this operation to step from one set bit to the next and skip all zero bits.
Optimal: The optimal solution uses n &= n - 1 to clear the lowest set bit in each step. It loops once per 1 bit instead of once per bit position, so it skips all the 0 bits. For 32-bit input this saves at most 30 cheap steps (for example n = 2^30 has 31 bit positions but only 1 set bit), so you need it only to show the trick or when most bits are 0 in very wide numbers. For the follow-up with many calls, use a 256-entry byte lookup table or n.bit_count(). Both loops need a mask n &= 0xFFFFFFFF first if the input can be negative.
Approaches:
  • Binary string count: O(log n) time, O(log n) space
  • Check every bit with shift and mask: O(log n), at most 31 steps time, O(1) space
  • Brian Kernighan: clear the lowest set bit: O(k), k = number of set bits time, O(1) space
  • Lookup table over bytes (follow-up): O(1) per call after O(256) setup time, O(256) space
  • Parallel bit count (SWAR, divide and conquer): O(1) time, O(1) space
  • Built-in popcount: O(log n), effectively O(1) time, O(1) space
class Solution:
    def hammingWeight(self, n: int) -> int:
        count = 0
        while n > 0:
            count += n & 1  # read the last bit
            n >>= 1         # drop the last bit
        return count

column1:
House Robber (1-D Dynamic Programming, Medium)

You get an integer array nums. nums[i] is the amount of money in house i. The houses stand in a line on a street. You can rob any set of houses, but you must not rob two adjacent houses on the same night, because adjacent houses have connected security systems that call the police. Return the maximum total amount of money you can rob without alerting the police. Robbing no house is allowed, so the answer is at least 0.

Constraints:
1 <= nums.length <= 100
0 <= nums[i] <= 400

Name the technique and the memory hook. Then rebuild the solution.
column2:
Hook: Skip it and keep the last best, or rob it and add its money to the best two back.
Techniques: dp-1d-linear, dp-state-machine, memoized-dfs

Approach: Growing best list (bottom-up DP without index math). Start with best = [0, 0] for no houses. For each house, append max(skip it: best[-1], rob it: best[-2] + money), and return best[-1].

Rebuild:
  1. Start best = [0, 0] so two earlier answers always exist.
  2. Loop over each money value in nums.
  3. Set skip = best[-1] because leaving the house keeps the best so far.
  4. Set take = best[-2] + money because robbing it forces the previous house to stay empty.
  5. Append max(skip, take) to best.
  6. After the loop, return best[-1].
Signals:
  • The task asks for a maximum or minimum total over a sequence of items.
  • Each item has a binary choice: take it or skip it.
  • A local rule links neighbors: taking one item forbids taking the next one (or the next k items).
  • Greedy choices fail on small counterexamples, such as [2,1,1,2] where taking every other item is not optimal.
Key insight: Decide about the last item only. Either you skip it and inherit the best answer of the shorter prefix, or you take it and inherit the best answer of the prefix that excludes its forbidden neighbor. The best answer of a prefix is all you need, not which items it used.
Optimal: The optimal solution_code keeps only the last two entries of the best list in two variables (prev2, prev1). This gives O(1) extra space instead of O(n). The time is O(n) in both. With n <= 100 the list costs nothing. Use the two-variable form only when the task asks for constant extra space. To convert, replace best[-2] and best[-1] with prev2 and prev1, and update both in one tuple assignment.
Approaches:
  • Brute force over subsets: O(2^n * n) time, O(1) space (too slow)
  • Plain recursion (rob or skip): O(phi^n), about O(1.618^n) time, O(n) space (too slow)
  • Memoized recursion (top-down DP): O(n) time, O(n) space
  • Bottom-up DP table: O(n) time, O(n) space
  • Bottom-up DP with two variables (optimal): O(n) time, O(1) space
  • Two-state machine (rob / skip): O(n) time, O(1) space
class Solution:
    def rob(self, nums: List[int]) -> int:
        # best[-1] = most money from the houses seen so far.
        # Two zeros stand for "no houses yet", so best[-2] always exists.
        best = [0, 0]
        for money in nums:
            skip = best[-1]          # leave this house: keep the best so far
            take = best[-2] + money  # rob it: the house before must stay empty
            best.append(max(skip, take))
        return best[-1]

column1:
Binary Tree Right Side View (Trees, Medium)

You get the root of a binary tree. Imagine that you stand on the right side of the tree. Return the values of the nodes that you can see, ordered from top to bottom. At each depth you see exactly one node: the rightmost node at that depth. That node can be in the left subtree when the right subtree is shorter. The tree can be empty; then return an empty list.

Constraints:
The number of nodes in the tree is in the range [0, 100].
-100 <= Node.val <= 100

Name the technique and the memory hook. Then rebuild the solution.
column2:
Hook: Level-order BFS; the last node of each level is the one you see.
Techniques: tree-bfs-level-order, tree-dfs-top-down

Approach: BFS by level, take the last node of each level. Process the queue one level at a time. Before you drain a level, the last node in the queue is the rightmost node of that depth, so you record its value.

Rebuild:
  1. If the root is None, return an empty list.
  2. Make an empty result list. Put the root in a deque.
  3. While the queue is not empty, append the value of queue[-1] to the result. The queue holds exactly one level, left to right, so queue[-1] is the node you see.
  4. Loop range(len(queue)) times. The range reads the level size once, before you push any child.
  5. In each pass, pop a node from the left. Push its left child, then its right child, if they exist.
  6. Return the result list.
Signals:
  • The answer has one value per depth of a tree. Think of a level-order traversal or a DFS that carries the depth.
  • The word 'view' (right, left, top, bottom) means you pick one extreme node per level or per column.
  • The output is ordered top to bottom. BFS produces levels in that order for free.
  • A node is visible only if no other node at the same depth is further right. This is a per-level comparison, not a path property.
Key insight: A side view is a per-level extreme. Group the nodes by depth with level-order BFS, then pick the first or last node of each level. In DFS form, visit the preferred side first, and the first node that reaches a new depth is the answer for that depth.
Approaches:
  • Brute force: one depth-limited search per depth: O(n*h), O(n^2) for a chain time, O(h) space
  • Full level-order lists, then take the last of each: O(n) time, O(n) space
  • BFS by level, record the last node (optimal, standard): O(n) time, O(w), w = maximum level width, O(n) worst case space
  • BFS that enqueues null children (NeetCode version): O(n) time, O(w) space
  • DFS right-first with depth check: O(n) time, O(h), O(n) for a skewed tree space
from collections import deque
from typing import List, Optional


class Solution:
    def rightSideView(self, root: Optional[TreeNode]) -> List[int]:
        if not root:
            return []
        view = []
        queue = deque([root])
        while queue:
            # The queue holds exactly one level, left to right.
            view.append(queue[-1].val)  # last node of the level = the one you see
            for _ in range(len(queue)):  # drain exactly this level
                node = queue.popleft()
                if node.left:
                    queue.append(node.left)
                if node.right:
                    queue.append(node.right)
        return view

column1:
Number of Islands (Graphs, Medium)

You get an m x n 2D grid named grid. Each cell holds the character '1' (land) or '0' (water). Land cells connect only when they are adjacent horizontally or vertically. Diagonal neighbors do not connect. An island is a maximal group of connected land cells, surrounded by water. All four edges of the grid are surrounded by water. Return the number of islands.

Constraints:
m == grid.length
n == grid[i].length
1 <= m, n <= 300
grid[i][j] is '0' or '1'.

Name the technique and the memory hook. Then rebuild the solution.
column2:
Hook: Count each new land cell, then sink its whole island.
Techniques: grid-flood-fill, union-find

Approach: Scan and sink with a stack-based DFS. Scan every cell, and each time you find a '1', add one island and sink its whole island to '0' with a stack that pushes all four neighbors and checks each cell only when it pops.

Rebuild:
  1. Set rows and cols to the grid height and width.
  2. Define sink(r, c). Start a stack that holds (r, c).
  3. Pop from the stack until it is empty.
  4. After each pop, skip the cell if it is out of bounds or not '1'.
  5. Otherwise, set the cell to '0' and push its four neighbors.
  6. Set islands to 0. Loop over every row r and every column c.
  7. If grid[r][c] is '1', add one to islands and call sink(r, c).
  8. Return islands.
Signals:
  • A 2D grid where each cell links to its 4 (or 8) neighbors is an implicit graph. Each cell is a node. Each adjacency is an edge.
  • The question asks how many separate groups, regions, or blobs exist. That is a count of connected components.
  • A phrase such as 'connected horizontally or vertically' defines the edge set. It tells you which neighbor offsets to use.
  • The grid has at most 300 x 300 = 90,000 cells. One pass that touches each cell a constant number of times fits easily. Repeated full passes do not.
Key insight: A grid region count is a connected-component count on an implicit graph. Scan all cells, and each time you meet an unvisited node, count it and flood-fill its whole component so you never count it again.
Optimal: The optimal code uses BFS with a deque and sinks each cell when it enters the queue. So each cell enters the queue at most once. The stack version can push the same cell up to four times. It also pushes water cells and off-grid positions, and the check after the pop discards them. Both are O(m*n) in time and space, and both fit easily. The BFS form matters when you need distances or levels, such as shortest path or rotting oranges, because BFS visits cells in order of distance.
Approaches:
  • Label propagation (brute force): O((m*n)^2) worst case time, O(m*n) space (too slow)
  • Recursive DFS flood fill: O(m*n) time, O(m*n) recursion depth space
  • Iterative BFS flood fill (chosen): O(m*n) time, O(m*n) worst case for the queue space
  • Union-find: O(m*n * alpha(m*n)) time, O(m*n) space
from typing import List


class Solution:
    def numIslands(self, grid: List[List[str]]) -> int:
        rows, cols = len(grid), len(grid[0])

        def sink(r, c):
            # Iterative DFS: push blindly, check when you pop.
            stack = [(r, c)]
            while stack:
                i, j = stack.pop()
                if 0 <= i < rows and 0 <= j < cols and grid[i][j] == "1":
                    grid[i][j] = "0"
                    stack += [(i + 1, j), (i - 1, j), (i, j + 1), (i, j - 1)]

        islands = 0
        for r in range(rows):
            for c in range(cols):
                if grid[r][c] == "1":
                    islands += 1
                    sink(r, c)
        return islands

Happy Number (Math & Geometry, Easy)

You get a positive integer n. Repeatedly replace the number with the sum of the squares of its decimal digits. The process either reaches 1 and stays there, or it loops forever in a cycle that does not contain 1. A number is happy if the process ends in 1. Return true if n is happy and false if not.

Constraints:
1 <= n <= 2^31 - 1

Name the technique and the memory hook. Then rebuild the solution.
column2:
Hook: Walk until you hit 1 or a repeat. A seen set catches the repeat.
Techniques: floyd-cycle-detection, two-pointers-fast-slow, hash-set-membership, math-number-theory, simulation

Approach: Hash set of seen values. Walk the sequence and remember every value. Stop when the value is 1 (happy) or when a value repeats (a loop without 1).

Rebuild:
  1. Make an empty set called seen.
  2. Loop while n is not 1 and n is not in seen.
  3. Inside the loop, add n to seen.
  4. Replace n with the sum of int(d) ** 2 for each digit d in str(n).
  5. After the loop, return n == 1.
Signals:
  • The statement applies a fixed function to a value again and again: x -> f(x). This sequence is a walk in a functional graph, where each node has exactly one outgoing edge.
  • The statement says the process ends at a target or loops endlessly. Any deterministic process on a finite state set must eventually repeat a state, so the question is cycle detection.
  • The step function shrinks large inputs fast (a d-digit number maps to at most 81d). This shows the reachable state set is small and finite, so the walk must cycle.
  • The target value (1) is a fixed point: f(1) = 1. Reaching it means the walk enters a cycle of length 1, so the answer is a test of which cycle you enter.
Key insight: Repeatedly applying a function to a value on a finite state set always ends in a cycle. So reframe the question as cycle detection on an implicit linked list: the target is reached exactly when the cycle you enter is the fixed point.
Optimal: The record solution uses Floyd fast/slow pointers instead of a set. Floyd uses O(1) extra memory. The set uses O(log n) memory, and here it never holds more than 20 values. Use Floyd when the problem asks for constant extra space, or when you must show the linked-list cycle pattern. Both run in about 10 to 15 microseconds of CPU time per call near the maximum n.
Approaches:
  • Simulation with a step cap: O(log n) time, O(1) space
  • Hash set of seen values: O(log n) time, O(log n) space
  • Floyd fast/slow pointers: O(log n) time, O(1) space
  • Known-cycle check: O(log n) time, O(1) space
class Solution:
    def isHappy(self, n: int) -> bool:
        seen = set()
        while n != 1 and n not in seen:
            seen.add(n)
            n = sum(int(d) ** 2 for d in str(n))
        return n == 1
column3: math-geometry floyd-cycle-detection two-pointers-fast-slow hash-set-membership math-number-theory simulation

Reverse Linked List (Linked List, Easy)

You get the head of a singly linked list. Reverse the list and return the head of the reversed list. The list can be empty; then return an empty list (None).

Constraints:
The number of nodes in the list is the range [0, 5000].
-5000 <= Node.val <= 5000
Follow-up: A linked list can be reversed either iteratively or recursively. Could you implement both?

Name the technique and the memory hook. Then rebuild the solution.
column2:
Hook: Save next, flip the arrow, step both, return prev.
Techniques: linked-list-reversal, linked-list-pointer-rewiring, prev-curr-pointers

Approach: Iterative prev/curr reversal. Walk the list once and flip each next pointer to point back at the previous node, saving the forward link first.

Rebuild:
  1. Set prev = None and curr = head.
  2. Loop while curr is not None.
  3. Save nxt = curr.next before you change anything.
  4. Flip the arrow: curr.next = prev.
  5. Step both pointers: prev = curr, then curr = nxt.
  6. After the loop, return prev, because curr is None and prev is the old tail.
Signals:
  • The task asks you to change the order or direction of the links in a singly linked list, not to compute a value.
  • Each node knows only its successor, so you cannot walk backward. You must flip each next pointer while you still hold a reference to the rest of the list.
  • The output must contain the same nodes in a new order, and you need O(1) extra space. This points to in-place pointer rewiring.
  • A list problem needs access from the tail end, for example to compare both ends or to add digits from the least significant end. Reversing the list, or one part of it, in place gives this access in O(1) space.
Key insight: To reverse a singly linked list, you do not move nodes. You flip each next pointer to point backward. Save the forward link before you overwrite it, because it is the only way to reach the rest of the list.
Approaches:
  • Copy values to array and rewrite: O(n) time, O(n) space
  • Stack of nodes: O(n) time, O(n) space
  • Recursive reversal: O(n) time, O(n) call stack space
  • Head insertion with a dummy node: O(n) time, O(1) space
  • Iterative three-pointer reversal (optimal): O(n) time, O(1) space
class Solution:
    def reverseList(self, head: Optional[ListNode]) -> Optional[ListNode]:
        prev = None          # head of the reversed part
        curr = head          # head of the part still to reverse
        while curr:
            nxt = curr.next  # 1. save the rest of the list
            curr.next = prev # 2. flip the arrow backward
            prev = curr      # 3. step prev forward
            curr = nxt       # 4. step curr forward
        return prev

Course Schedule (Graphs, Medium)

There are a total of numCourses courses that you must take. They are labeled from 0 to numCourses - 1. You get an array prerequisites. Each entry prerequisites[i] = [ai, bi] means that you must take course bi first if you want to take course ai. For example, the pair [0, 1] means that to take course 0 you must first take course 1. Return true if you can finish all courses. Otherwise, return false.

Constraints:
1 <= numCourses <= 2000
0 <= prerequisites.length <= 5000
prerequisites[i].length == 2
0 <= ai, bi < numCourses

Name the technique and the memory hook. Then rebuild the solution.
column2:
Hook: Take what is ready, free its dependents, check that you took everything.
Techniques: topological-sort, cycle-detection, graph-building

Approach: Kahn's algorithm: take the courses that are ready. Count the unmet prerequisites of each course. Take any course with zero unmet prerequisites. Each taken course frees the courses that depend on it. You can finish all courses if and only if you take all of them.

Rebuild:
  1. Make graph as one empty list per course and indegree as one zero per course.
  2. For each pair [course, pre], append course to graph[pre] and add 1 to indegree[course].
  3. Put every course with indegree 0 into a deque. Set taken to 0.
  4. While the queue is not empty, pop a course from the left and add 1 to taken.
  5. For each dependent of that course, subtract 1 from its indegree. Push the dependent when its indegree becomes 0.
  6. After the loop, return taken == numCourses.
Signals:
  • The input gives pairwise rules of the form 'do B before A' over a set of labeled items. Each rule is a directed edge.
  • The question asks if all items can be completed, or if a valid order exists. That is a feasibility question about a dependency graph.
  • The input is a node count plus an edge list, not an adjacency structure. This points to a graph problem where you build an adjacency list first.
  • Node and edge counts are in the thousands. This rules out trying all orders. A linear O(V + E) traversal fits easily.
Key insight: A set of 'X before Y' rules can be satisfied if and only if the directed rule graph has no cycle. Kahn's algorithm checks this constructively. In an acyclic graph, some node always has zero unmet requirements, so it can go next. If the process stalls before it covers every node, the remaining nodes lie on a cycle or depend on one.
Approaches:
  • Brute force: try every order: O(n! * (n + m)) time, O(n) space (too slow)
  • DFS cycle check without memoization: Exponential in the worst case time, O(n + m) space (too slow)
  • Repeated full scans (naive peeling): O(n * (n + m)) time, O(n + m) space (too slow)
  • DFS with three colors (white, gray, black): O(n + m) time, O(n + m) space
  • Kahn's algorithm (BFS topological sort): O(n + m) time, O(n + m) space
from collections import deque
from typing import List


class Solution:
    def canFinish(self, numCourses: int, prerequisites: List[List[int]]) -> bool:
        graph = [[] for _ in range(numCourses)]
        indegree = [0] * numCourses
        for course, pre in prerequisites:
            graph[pre].append(course)
            indegree[course] += 1

        queue = deque(c for c in range(numCourses) if indegree[c] == 0)
        taken = 0
        while queue:
            pre = queue.popleft()
            taken += 1
            for course in graph[pre]:
                indegree[course] -= 1
                if indegree[course] == 0:
                    queue.append(course)
        return taken == numCourses

Implement Trie (Prefix Tree) (Tries, Medium)

A trie, or prefix tree, is a tree data structure that stores and retrieves keys in a set of strings efficiently. Applications include autocomplete and spell checkers. Implement the Trie class. Trie() initializes the trie object. insert(word) inserts the string word into the trie. search(word) returns true if the string word is in the trie (that is, it was inserted before), and false otherwise. startsWith(prefix) returns true if a previously inserted string word has the prefix prefix, and false otherwise. A word counts as a prefix of itself. Inserts and queries arrive mixed in any order, and each query must reflect all inserts made before it. All strings are non-empty and use only lowercase English letters.

Constraints:
1 <= word.length, prefix.length <= 2000
word and prefix consist only of lowercase English letters.
At most 3 * 10^4 calls in total will be made to insert, search, and startsWith.

Name the technique and the memory hook. Then rebuild the solution.
column2:
Hook: One node per prefix: walk the letters, flag the word end.
Techniques: trie, design-data-structure, hash-map-lookup

Approach: Trie with dict children and an end flag. Each node maps a letter to a child node and has an is_end flag. One helper walks a string down from the root, and search and startsWith differ only in the final check.

Rebuild:
  1. Write TrieNode with children = {} and is_end = False. Trie holds one root TrieNode.
  2. insert: start at the root. For each letter, create the child if it is missing, then move to it. Set is_end to True on the last node.
  3. _walk: start at the root. For each letter, move to the child with children.get. Return None when the child is missing. Otherwise, return the last node.
  4. search: return True only when _walk gives a node and that node has is_end set to True.
  5. startsWith: return True when _walk gives any node.
Signals:
  • The task stores many strings and asks whether some stored string starts with a given prefix.
  • Queries come online and mix with inserts, so a one-time precomputation does not work.
  • The alphabet is small and fixed, so each step down a tree has a bounded number of choices.
  • The task asks two questions about one string: is it a whole stored key, and is it the start of some stored key. One walk answers both when the last node carries an end-of-key flag.
Key insight: When many queries ask about prefixes of stored strings, store the strings as paths in a tree that shares common beginnings. Each node then stands for exactly one prefix, so a prefix query is a walk of length L. An end-of-word flag on the node separates 'is a prefix' from 'is a whole stored word'.
Approaches:
  • List of words with linear scan: O(1) insert, O(n * L) per query, n = stored words time, O(T), T = total inserted characters space (too slow)
  • Hash set of words plus hash set of all prefixes: O(L^2) insert, O(L) per query time, O(sum of L^2) space (too slow)
  • Sorted unique list plus binary search: O(n + L log n) insert (list shift), O(L log n) per query time, O(T) space
  • Trie with a fixed 26-slot child array: O(L) per query; O(26 * L) worst-case insert, because each new node allocates 26 slots time, O(26 * T) pointers space
  • Trie with a dict of children (chosen): O(L) per call time, O(T) nodes space
class TrieNode:
    def __init__(self):
        self.children = {}
        self.is_end = False


class Trie:

    def __init__(self):
        self.root = TrieNode()

    def insert(self, word: str) -> None:
        node = self.root
        for ch in word:
            if ch not in node.children:
                node.children[ch] = TrieNode()
            node = node.children[ch]
        node.is_end = True

    def _walk(self, s: str):
        node = self.root
        for ch in s:
            node = node.children.get(ch)
            if node is None:
                return None
        return node

    def search(self, word: str) -> bool:
        node = self._walk(word)
        return node is not None and node.is_end

    def startsWith(self, prefix: str) -> bool:
        return self._walk(prefix) is not None

Course Schedule II (Graphs, Medium)

There are a total of numCourses courses that you must take. They are labeled 0 to numCourses - 1. You get an array prerequisites where prerequisites[i] = [ai, bi]. This pair means that you must take course bi first if you want to take course ai. For example, the pair [0, 1] means that you must take course 1 before course 0. Return an ordering of courses that lets you finish all courses. If many valid orders exist, return any of them. If you cannot finish all courses, return an empty array.

Constraints:
1 <= numCourses <= 2000
0 <= prerequisites.length <= numCourses * (numCourses - 1)
prerequisites[i].length == 2
0 <= ai, bi < numCourses

Name the technique and the memory hook. Then rebuild the solution.
column2:
Hook: Count unmet prerequisites. Take any course at zero. A short order means a cycle.
Techniques: topological-sort, cycle-detection, graph-building

Approach: Kahn's algorithm (peel off free courses). Keep a count of unmet prerequisites for each course, and repeatedly take a course whose count is 0. If some courses never become free, a cycle blocks them, so return an empty list.

Rebuild:
  1. Make an empty adjacency list and an indegree of 0 for each course.
  2. For each pair [course, pre], append course to graph[pre] and add 1 to indegree[course].
  3. Put every course with indegree 0 into a deque. Start an empty order list.
  4. While the deque is not empty, pop a course from the left and append it to order.
  5. For each dependent of that course, subtract 1 from its indegree. Push the dependent when its indegree reaches 0.
  6. Return order if len(order) == numCourses. Otherwise, return [].
Signals:
  • The input is a list of pairs that say "X must happen before Y". These pairs are directed edges of a dependency graph.
  • The task asks for an order that respects every dependency. This order is a topological order.
  • The task says to return an empty result when no order exists. No order exists exactly when the dependency graph has a directed cycle.
  • The task accepts any valid order. You do not need a special order, so a plain BFS or DFS topological sort is enough. A required order, such as the lexicographically smallest one, needs a min-heap instead of a queue.
Key insight: A node with no unmet dependencies can always go next. Removing it can only free more nodes. So you peel off indegree-0 nodes layer by layer. If you cannot peel off every node, the leftover nodes contain a cycle.
Approaches:
  • Brute force over permutations: O(V! * (V + E)) time, O(V + E) space (too slow)
  • Repeated scan for a free course: O(V * (V + E)) time, O(V + E) space (too slow)
  • Kahn's algorithm (BFS on indegrees): O(V + E) time, O(V + E) space
  • DFS postorder with three colors: O(V + E) time, O(V + E) space
from collections import deque
from typing import List


class Solution:
    def findOrder(self, numCourses: int, prerequisites: List[List[int]]) -> List[int]:
        # Edge b -> a means "take b before a".
        graph = [[] for _ in range(numCourses)]
        indegree = [0] * numCourses
        for course, pre in prerequisites:
            graph[pre].append(course)
            indegree[course] += 1

        # Start with every course that has no prerequisites.
        queue = deque(c for c in range(numCourses) if indegree[c] == 0)
        order = []
        while queue:
            course = queue.popleft()
            order.append(course)
            for nxt in graph[course]:
                indegree[nxt] -= 1
                if indegree[nxt] == 0:
                    queue.append(nxt)

        # A cycle leaves some courses with indegree > 0 forever.
        return order if len(order) == numCourses else []

Design Add and Search Words Data Structure (Tries, Medium)

Design a class WordDictionary that stores words and tells whether a query matches a stored word. WordDictionary() creates an empty structure. addWord(word) stores word so that later searches can match it. search(word) returns true if any stored word matches word. Otherwise it returns false. A query can contain dots. Each dot matches any one letter. Every other character must equal the letter at the same position. A match covers the whole stored word, so the lengths must be equal. A stored word that only starts with the query does not match. Added words contain only lowercase English letters. Queries contain lowercase letters and dots. Each word has length 1 to 25. A query has at most 2 dots. There are at most 10^4 calls in total, and adds and searches can interleave.

Constraints:
1 <= word.length <= 25
word in addWord consists of lowercase English letters.
word in search consist of '.' or lowercase English letters.
There will be at most 2 dots in word for search queries.

Name the technique and the memory hook. Then rebuild the solution.
column2:
Hook: Mask one letter on add, fill one dot on search.
Techniques: trie, design-data-structure, backtracking-constraint-search

Approach: One-dot pattern set. Store each word and each copy of it with one letter replaced by a dot in one set. A query with at most one dot is one lookup, and a query with more dots fills its first dot with each letter and searches again.

Rebuild:
  1. Keep one set named patterns.
  2. addWord(word): add word, then for each index i add word[:i] + '.' + word[i + 1:].
  3. search(word): if word.count('.') <= 1, return word in patterns.
  4. Else let i = word.index('.'), the first dot.
  5. Return any(self.search(word[:i] + letter + word[i + 1:]) for letter in 'abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz').
Signals:
  • The task asks you to design a structure that stores many strings and answers match or prefix queries about them. A trie is the default candidate.
  • A query contains a wildcard that matches any single character. One query then stands for many strings, so plain hashing of the query does not work directly.
  • The alphabet is small (26 lowercase letters) and strings are short (length 25 or less). Trie nodes stay cheap and the depth stays small.
  • The statement bounds the number of wildcards per query (here at most 2). The bound caps the branching to alphabet^k paths and makes branching search or explicit enumeration affordable.
Key insight: Index the stored strings in a trie so that one walk compares a query against all strings at once. A fixed character follows one edge, and a wildcard follows every edge at that depth. The search cost then depends on the number of wildcards and the trie shape, not directly on the number of stored strings.
Optimal: The record solution_code is a trie with DFS on dots. It is the standard answer when the question asks for a trie. The same walk solves Word Search II, prefix queries and autocomplete. With many dots, a trie search never visits more than all trie nodes. Its worst case is slow in CPython: a crafted input with all 676 two-letter prefixes takes about 24 s of CPU time for 9324 searches. Use the trie when a trie is required, when you also need prefix queries, or when the dot limit is large. In CPython the trie does not save memory here. Each node is an object with its own dict. For 10^4 random words of length 25, the trie used 58 MiB and the pattern set used 24 MiB. The pattern set search cost grows as 26^(k-1) lookups for k dots, so it suits only a small dot limit.
Approaches:
  • List of words with linear scan: addWord O(L); search O(N * L) time, O(N * L) space (too slow)
  • Buckets by length with linear scan: addWord O(L); search O(N * L) worst case time, O(N * L) space (too slow)
  • Precompute all wildcard patterns: addWord O(L^3) for up to 2 dots; search O(L) time, O(N * L^3) space (too slow)
  • Hash set with dot expansion: addWord O(L); search O(26^k * L), k <= 2 time, O(N * L) space
  • Trie with DFS on dots (optimal, standard): addWord O(L); search O(L) without dots, O(26^k * L) with k dots (at most about 1.7e4 node steps here), and never more than the trie size; about 1.5e8 node steps over all calls on a crafted worst case time, O(total characters inserted) nodes; recursion depth k + 1, because the code recurses only at dots space
  • Trie with BFS frontier: addWord O(L); search O(26^k * L) time, O(total characters) plus O(26^k) frontier space
  • One-dot pattern sets (fast worst case, depends on k <= 2): addWord O(L^2); search O(L) for 0 or 1 dots, O(26 * L) for 2 dots time, O(N * L^2) space
class WordDictionary:

    def __init__(self):
        # Every stored word, plus every copy of it with one letter replaced by '.'.
        self.patterns = set()

    def addWord(self, word: str) -> None:
        self.patterns.add(word)
        for i in range(len(word)):
            self.patterns.add(word[:i] + "." + word[i + 1:])

    def search(self, word: str) -> bool:
        if word.count(".") <= 1:
            return word in self.patterns
        i = word.index(".")
        return any(self.search(word[:i] + letter + word[i + 1:])
                   for letter in "abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz")

column1:
Word Search II (Tries, Hard)

You get an m x n board of lowercase letters and a list of unique lowercase words. Return every word that appears on the board. A word appears if you can spell it along a sequence of cells where each next cell is horizontally or vertically adjacent to the current cell. Diagonal moves are not allowed. A single cell may not be used more than once within one word. Different words may use the same cells. Each found word appears once in the result. LeetCode accepts the result in any order.

Constraints:
m == board.length
n == board[i].length
1 <= m, n <= 12
board[i][j] is a lowercase English letter.

Name the technique and the memory hook. Then rebuild the solution.
column2:
Hook: Word Search I, but walk a trie instead of one word, and cut empty leaves on the way back.
Techniques: trie, backtracking-constraint-search, in-place-visited-marking

Approach: Trie plus the Word Search I grid DFS. Put all words in a trie. Run the usual grid DFS from every cell. Each step into a cell also steps one trie edge. The DFS returns at once when the cell letter is not a child of the current trie node. On the way back, the DFS deletes a trie node that has no children left.

Rebuild:
  1. Build a trie. Each node has a children dict and a word field. Store the full word at its end node.
  2. Set rows and cols, and make an empty found list.
  3. Define dfs(r, c, parent). Return if the cell is off the board or its letter is not in parent.children.
  4. Set node = parent.children[letter]. If node.word is set, append it to found and set it to None.
  5. Mark the cell '#'. Call dfs on the 4 neighbors with node. Then restore the letter.
  6. If node has no children left, delete it from parent.children.
  7. Call dfs(r, c, root) from every cell. Return found.
Signals:
  • Many query strings are matched against one shared search space. A separate search per query repeats the work for shared prefixes.
  • The answer strings grow one step at a time along a path in a grid or graph. The search can stop as soon as the current path is not a prefix of any query.
  • The number of queries is large (here up to 3 * 10^4), so one full search per query is too slow.
  • Each query is short (here at most 10 letters) and the grid is small, so a depth-limited DFS from every cell is affordable when it is pruned.
Key insight: When many patterns are searched in the same space, merge the patterns into a trie and run one search that advances in the trie as it extends the path. A missing trie child proves that no pattern can continue, so the search stops at once. Shared prefixes are then explored only once for all patterns.
Optimal: The algorithm and the complexity are the same: a trie, a backtracking DFS, and leaf pruning. Only the code form changes. The record's solution_code checks bounds and the trie child before each call, so it makes fewer function calls that return at once. In CPython this gives no clear gain here: both took about 0.85 s to 0.95 s CPU time on the all-'a' worst cases. Its prune test also checks node.word is None, but that check is always true after the visit, because the DFS clears the word on entry. Keep the leaf prune in both forms: without it, the all-'a' board with words 'a' to 'aaaaaaaaaa' took about 2 s CPU time in the guard-at-top form (1.97 s and 2.03 s in two runs).
Approaches:
  • Word Search I once per word: O(W * m * n * 4 * 3^(L-1)) where W is the number of words and L is the maximum word length time, O(L) recursion depth space (too slow)
  • Enumerate all board paths and look them up in a word set: O(S + m * n * 4 * 3^(L-1) * L) time, O(S) for the set, where S is the total number of letters in words space
  • Prefix hash set with pruned DFS: O(S * L + m * n * 4 * 3^(L-1) * L) time, O(S * L) for the stored prefixes space
  • Trie plus backtracking DFS with leaf pruning (optimal, standard): O(S + m * n * 4 * 3^(L-1)); at most 1883664 DFS calls on a 12x12 board with L = 10, and pruning makes real runs much smaller time, O(S) for the trie plus O(L) recursion depth space
  • Trie with input heuristics: O(S + m * n * 4 * 3^(L-1)) time, O(S + L) space
from typing import List


class TrieNode:
    def __init__(self):
        self.children = {}  # letter -> TrieNode
        self.word = None  # the full word that ends at this node, if any


class Solution:
    def findWords(self, board: List[List[str]], words: List[str]) -> List[str]:
        # 1. Put every word in a trie. Store the full word at its end node.
        root = TrieNode()
        for word in words:
            node = root
            for ch in word:
                node = node.children.setdefault(ch, TrieNode())
            node.word = word

        rows, cols = len(board), len(board[0])
        found = []

        # 2. Word Search I DFS, but each step walks one trie edge.
        def dfs(r, c, parent):
            if r < 0 or c < 0 or r == rows or c == cols:
                return  # off the board
            ch = board[r][c]
            if ch not in parent.children:
                return  # no word goes on with this letter ('#' = used cell)
            node = parent.children[ch]
            if node.word:
                found.append(node.word)
                node.word = None  # report each word once
            board[r][c] = "#"  # mark the cell as used on this path
            dfs(r + 1, c, node)
            dfs(r - 1, c, node)
            dfs(r, c + 1, node)
            dfs(r, c - 1, node)
            board[r][c] = ch  # backtrack: restore the cell
            if not node.children:
                del parent.children[ch]  # prune: nothing left to find here

        for r in range(rows):
            for c in range(cols):
                dfs(r, c, root)
        return found

House Robber II (1-D Dynamic Programming, Medium)

You are a professional robber who plans to rob houses along a street. Each house has an amount of money in it. The houses are arranged in a circle, so the first house is the neighbor of the last house. Adjacent houses have a connected security system. The system automatically contacts the police if two adjacent houses are broken into on the same night. The integer array nums gives the amount of money in each house. Return the maximum amount of money you can rob tonight without alerting the police.

Constraints:
1 <= nums.length <= 100
0 <= nums[i] <= 1000

Name the technique and the memory hook. Then rebuild the solution.
column2:
Hook: Drop the first or drop the last, rob each row, take the max.
Techniques: dp-1d-linear, cycle-breaking-case-split, memoized-dfs

Approach: Drop one end and reuse House Robber I. The first house and the last house are neighbors. So every valid plan leaves at least one of them unrobbed. Run House Robber I on nums[1:] and on nums[:-1]. Return the larger result. One house has no neighbor, so return nums[0] in that case.

Rebuild:
  1. If there is one house, return nums[0].
  2. Inside rob, write the helper rob_row(houses). Set two_back and one_back to 0. two_back is the best total two houses back. one_back is the best total up to the previous house.
  3. For each money value, set two_back, one_back = one_back, max(one_back, two_back + money).
  4. Return one_back from rob_row.
  5. Return max(rob_row(nums[1:]), rob_row(nums[:-1])).
Signals:
  • You pick a subset of items in a sequence, and two neighboring items cannot both be picked. This points to the take-or-skip linear DP.
  • The goal is a best total over valid selections, not the list of selections. This points to DP, not backtracking.
  • The items form a circle, so the first item and the last item are neighbors. A wrap-around constraint usually means you cut the circle into one or more straight lines.
  • The problem is a known linear problem plus one extra constraint between the two ends. Reuse the linear solver and remove the extra constraint by case analysis.
Key insight: A circle is a line plus one extra edge between the two ends. Remove that edge by case analysis: either the first item is unused or the last item is unused. Each case is the linear problem you already know, so the answer is the better of two linear runs.
Optimal: The optimal code uses the same algorithm. It passes index bounds (lo, hi) instead of slices, so it makes no list copies and uses O(1) extra space. The slices cost O(n) extra memory. This does not matter for n <= 100. Use index bounds only when you must avoid copies of a very large array.
Approaches:
  • Brute force over all subsets: O(n * 2^n) time, O(1) space (too slow)
  • Plain recursion with a first-house flag: O(1.618^n) time, O(n) space (too slow)
  • Memoized DFS on state (index, first_robbed): O(n) time, O(n) space
  • Two linear DP tables (drop first, drop last): O(n) time, O(n) space
  • Two linear passes with two rolling variables (optimal): O(n) time, O(1) space
  • Case split on house 0 (equivalent alternative): O(n) time, O(1) space
from typing import List


class Solution:
    def rob(self, nums: List[int]) -> int:
        # One house: it has no neighbor, so rob it.
        if len(nums) == 1:
            return nums[0]

        def rob_row(houses: List[int]) -> int:
            # House Robber I on a straight row.
            # two_back = best total up to the house before the previous one
            # one_back = best total up to the previous house
            two_back, one_back = 0, 0
            for money in houses:
                two_back, one_back = one_back, max(one_back, two_back + money)
            return one_back

        # The first and last houses touch, so one of them stays unrobbed.
        # Drop the first house, or drop the last house, and keep the better row.
        return max(rob_row(nums[1:]), rob_row(nums[:-1]))

Kth Largest Element in an Array (Heap / Priority Queue, Medium)

You get an integer array nums and an integer k. Return the kth largest element in the array. The rank counts duplicates: it is the kth element in sorted (descending) order, not the kth distinct value. The problem asks if you can solve it without sorting.

Constraints:
1 <= k <= nums.length <= 10^5
-10^4 <= nums[i] <= 10^4
Follow-up: Can you solve it without sorting?

Name the technique and the memory hook. Then rebuild the solution.

Hook: Top k in a min-heap: push, trim to k, return the root.
Techniques: heap-top-k, quickselect, sorting

Approach: Min-heap of size k, push then trim. Push every value into a min-heap. When the heap holds more than k values, pop the smallest. At the end, the root is the kth largest.

Rebuild:
  1. Import heapq. Make an empty list top_k to use as a min-heap.
  2. For each x in nums, heappush x into top_k.
  3. If len(top_k) > k, heappop to drop the smallest value.
  4. After the loop, top_k holds the k largest values.
  5. Return top_k[0], the smallest of them, which is the kth largest.
Signals:
  • The question asks for one value at a given rank (kth largest, kth smallest, median), not for the whole order.
  • The text asks you to avoid a full sort. A full O(n log n) order then does more work than needed.
  • k can be much smaller than n. A structure of size k can summarize everything that matters.
  • Values lie in a small fixed range (here 2*10^4 + 1 values). A count array over the value range is then possible.
Key insight: To find the kth largest, you only need to remember the k largest values. Keep them in a min-heap so the weakest of them sits at the root. The root is the threshold a new value must beat, and at the end the root is the answer.
Optimal: The record solution_code uses the same size-k min-heap. It adds a gate: it pushes only while the heap has fewer than k values, and after that it calls heapreplace only when x > heap[0]. A value that cannot enter then costs O(1) instead of a push and a pop. Big-O stays O(n log k) time and O(k) space. Use the gate when you want fewer heap operations on long streams. Use quickselect when you need O(n) average time, and counting when the value range is small.
Approaches:
  • Sort: O(n log n) time, O(n) space
  • Repeated max removal: O(n*k) time, O(1) space (too slow)
  • Heapify all then pop: O(n + (n-k) log n) time, O(1) extra if done in place on nums space
  • Min-heap of size k (chosen): O(n log k) time, O(k) space
  • Quickselect with three-way partition: O(n) average, O(n^2) worst case time, O(n) average for the list version, O(n^2) worst case because each level keeps its lists alive. O(1) extra for an iterative in-place version. space
  • Counting over the value range: O(n + R) where R = max - min + 1 <= 20001 time, O(R) space
import heapq
from typing import List


class Solution:
    def findKthLargest(self, nums: List[int], k: int) -> int:
        top_k = []  # min-heap that keeps the k largest values seen so far
        for x in nums:
            heapq.heappush(top_k, x)
            if len(top_k) > k:
                heapq.heappop(top_k)  # drop the smallest, it cannot be in the top k
        return top_k[0]  # smallest of the k largest = kth largest

Contains Duplicate (Arrays & Hashing, Easy)

You get an integer array nums. Return true if any value appears at least twice in the array. Return false if every element is distinct. Only the yes or no answer matters. You do not return the duplicate value or its indices.

Constraints:
1 <= nums.length <= 10^5
-10^9 <= nums[i] <= 10^9

Name the technique and the memory hook. Then rebuild the solution.
column2:
Hook: Ask the set if you saw it, then add it.
Techniques: hash-set-membership, sorting

Approach: Seen-before hash set. Walk the array once. Keep a set of the values that you already saw. If the current value is already in the set, you found a duplicate.

Rebuild:
  1. Make an empty set called seen.
  2. Loop over each value x in nums.
  3. If x is in seen, return True.
  4. Otherwise add x to seen.
  5. After the loop, return False.
Signals:
  • The question asks if any value repeats, or if all values are distinct.
  • For each element, the answer depends on whether an equal value appeared earlier. You need fast lookup of what you already saw.
  • n goes up to 10^5. An O(n^2) pair check is too slow, so you need O(n) or O(n log n).
  • Values go up to 10^9 in absolute value. A fixed-size counting array is not practical, so a hash set is the right container. If values are small and bounded, a boolean array indexed by value also works.
Key insight: Replace the inner loop of a pair search with a lookup structure. For each element, ask the hash set if you saw this value before. The set remembers the whole prefix, so one pass is enough.
Approaches:
  • Brute force all pairs: O(n^2) time, O(1) space (too slow)
  • Sort and compare neighbors: O(n log n) time, O(n). A sorted copy needs O(n) memory. An in-place sort avoids the copy, but Timsort can still use up to n/2 scratch slots. space
  • Hash set with early exit: O(n) average, because each set lookup and insert is O(1) on average time, O(n) space
  • Set size comparison: O(n) average time, O(n) space
class Solution:
    def containsDuplicate(self, nums: List[int]) -> bool:
        seen = set()
        for x in nums:
            if x in seen:
                return True
            seen.add(x)
        return False
