Reconstruct Itinerary (Advanced Graphs, Hard)

You get a list of airline tickets. Each ticket tickets[i] = [from_i, to_i] gives the departure airport and the arrival airport of one flight. Reconstruct the itinerary in order and return it. All tickets belong to one man who departs from "JFK", so the itinerary must begin with "JFK". If more than one valid itinerary exists, return the itinerary that has the smallest lexical order when read as a single string. For example, the itinerary ["JFK", "LGA"] has a smaller lexical order than ["JFK", "LGB"]. You may assume that all tickets form at least one valid itinerary. You must use all the tickets once and only once.

Constraints:
1 <= tickets.length <= 300
tickets[i].length == 2
from_i.length == 3
to_i.length == 3

Name the technique and the memory hook. Then rebuild the solution.
column2:
Hook: Take the smallest ticket, write the airport down when stuck, then reverse.
Techniques: eulerian-path, hierholzer, dfs, post-order, graph-building, sorting, greedy, reverse-thinking

Approach: Hierholzer DFS with post-order append. Walk from JFK and always take the smallest unused ticket. When an airport has no unused tickets, append it to the route. Reverse the route at the end.

Rebuild:
  1. Build graph = defaultdict(list) from sorted(tickets, reverse=True), so each list ends with the smallest destination.
  2. Create an empty route list.
  3. Define visit(airport): while graph[airport] has tickets, call visit(graph[airport].pop()). The pop removes the smallest ticket, so each ticket is used once.
  4. After the while loop, append airport to route (post-order, the airport is stuck).
  5. Call visit("JFK") and return route[::-1].
Signals:
  • The task says to use every edge (ticket, pair, domino, connection) exactly once. This points to an Eulerian path, not a vertex search.
  • Vertices can repeat in the answer but edges cannot. Track used edges, not visited vertices.
  • Each item links an end of one item to the start of the next item. Model items as edges between endpoint values.
  • The start vertex is fixed and a valid answer is guaranteed. You can run Hierholzer from that start with no existence check.
Key insight: In an Eulerian path walk, the first vertex where you get stuck must be the final vertex of the path. So build the answer backward: append a vertex when it has no unused edges, then reverse. Any detour that the greedy walk skipped gets spliced in before the dead end, so greedy choice of the smallest edge never needs to be undone.
Approaches:
  • Brute force over ticket orders: O(E! * E) time, O(E) space (too slow)
  • Backtracking DFS with sorted adjacency: O(E^d) worst case, d = max out-degree time, O(E) space (too slow)
  • Hierholzer DFS with post-order (optimal): O(E log E) time, O(E) space
  • Hierholzer with min-heaps per airport: O(E log E) time, O(E) space
  • Iterative Hierholzer with an explicit stack: O(E log E) time, O(E) space
from collections import defaultdict
from typing import List


class Solution:
    def findItinerary(self, tickets: List[List[str]]) -> List[str]:
        graph = defaultdict(list)
        # Sort descending so pop() from the end gives the smallest destination.
        for src, dst in sorted(tickets, reverse=True):
            graph[src].append(dst)

        route = []

        def visit(airport: str) -> None:
            while graph[airport]:
                visit(graph[airport].pop())
            route.append(airport)  # post-order: append when stuck

        visit("JFK")
        return route[::-1]

Counting Bits (Bit Manipulation, Easy)

You get an integer n. Return an array ans of length n + 1. For each i with 0 <= i <= n, ans[i] is the number of 1 bits in the binary representation of i. Do not use a built-in popcount function (for example __builtin_popcount in C++).

Constraints:
0 <= n <= 10^5
Follow-up: It is very easy to come up with a solution with a runtime of O(n log n). Can you do it in linear time O(n) and possibly in a single pass?

Name the technique and the memory hook. Then rebuild the solution.
column2:
Hook: Drop the last bit, look it up, add the bit back.
Techniques: bit-manipulation, dp-1d-linear

Approach: DP on the right shift. The number i >> 1 is i without its last bit, and its answer is already in the table, so ans[i] = ans[i >> 1] + (i & 1).

Rebuild:
  1. Make a table ans = [0] * (n + 1); ans[0] = 0 is the base case.
  2. Loop i from 1 to n in increasing order.
  3. Drop the last bit: i >> 1 is smaller than i, so ans[i >> 1] is already filled.
  4. Add the dropped bit back: ans[i] = ans[i >> 1] + (i & 1), with parentheses around i & 1.
  5. Return ans.
Signals:
  • The output is a value for every integer from 0 to n, not for one number. Answers for small numbers can build answers for larger numbers.
  • The value is a property of the binary form of a number. Removing one bit (shift right, clear lowest set bit, or remove highest bit) gives a smaller number with a known answer.
  • The follow-up asks for O(n) when a per-item O(log n) method is obvious. This means each answer must come from an earlier answer in O(1).
  • The problem bans the built-in popcount and asks for linear time. A separate loop per number is then too slow, so the answers must share work through a recurrence.
Key insight: A bit operation that removes one known bit from i gives a smaller number. So the answer for i is the stored answer for that smaller number plus the removed bit.
Approaches:
  • Count bits of each number separately: O(n log n) time, O(1) extra space
  • Built-in popcount (not allowed by the statement): O(n log n) time, O(1) extra space
  • DP on the right shift (optimal, standard): O(n) time, O(1) extra (O(n) output) space
  • DP on the lowest set bit: O(n) time, O(1) extra (O(n) output) space
  • DP on the highest set bit (NeetCode offset): O(n) time, O(1) extra (O(n) output) space
class Solution:
    def countBits(self, n: int) -> List[int]:
        ans = [0] * (n + 1)
        for i in range(1, n + 1):
            # i >> 1 is i without its last bit; i & 1 is that last bit.
            ans[i] = ans[i >> 1] + (i & 1)
        return ans

column1:
Top K Frequent Elements (Arrays & Hashing, Medium)

You get an integer array nums and an integer k. Return the k elements that occur most often in nums. You can return the answer in any order. k is at least 1 and at most the number of distinct values in nums. The answer is guaranteed to be unique, so there is no tie at the boundary between the k-th and the (k+1)-th most frequent value.

Constraints:
1 <= nums.length <= 10^5
-10^4 <= nums[i] <= 10^4
k is in the range [1, the number of unique elements in the array].
It is guaranteed that the answer is unique.
Follow-up: Your algorithm's time complexity must be better than O(n log n), where n is the array's size.

Name the technique and the memory hook. Then rebuild the solution.
column2:
Hook: Bucket values by count, read buckets top down, take the first k.
Techniques: counting-frequency, bucket-sort, hash-map-lookup, heap-top-k

Approach: Count, then bucket sort by frequency and take the first k. Put each value into buckets[count], read the buckets from the highest count down into one list, and return the first k items of that list.

Rebuild:
  1. Count every value with count = Counter(nums).
  2. Make len(nums) + 1 empty buckets with a list comprehension, because a count can be as large as n.
  3. For each (num, freq) in count.items(), append num to buckets[freq].
  4. Start an empty list by_frequency.
  5. Loop freq from len(nums) down to 1. Extend by_frequency with buckets[freq].
  6. Return by_frequency[:k].
Signals:
  • The task asks for the k most frequent, k largest, or k best items, not a full ranking.
  • The output order is free, so you only need to select a set, not sort it.
  • The ranking key is a count, and a count is an integer between 1 and n. A bounded integer key allows bucket sort or counting sort.
  • A follow-up demands better than O(n log n). This rules out a full sort and points to a heap, bucket sort, or quickselect.
Key insight: When the ranking key is a small bounded integer, do not compare keys. Use the key as an array index. A frequency is always between 1 and n, so an array of n + 1 buckets sorts the values by frequency in linear time.
Optimal: The algorithm is the same bucket sort in O(n) time and O(n) space. The record's solution_code adds an early exit. It appends one value at a time and returns as soon as it has k values, so it skips the remaining low buckets. This saves only a constant factor. Use it if you want to stop the work early. The answer does not change.
Approaches:
  • Brute force: count each value by rescanning: O(n * m + m log m), m = number of distinct values time, O(m) space (too slow)
  • Hash map count + sort by frequency: O(n + m log m) time, O(m) space
  • Hash map count + min-heap of size k: O(n + m log k) time, O(m + k) space
  • Hash map count + bucket sort by frequency (optimal, standard): O(n) time, O(n) space
  • Hash map count + quickselect: O(n) average, O(n + m^2) worst case time, O(m) space
from collections import Counter
from typing import List


class Solution:
    def topKFrequent(self, nums: List[int], k: int) -> List[int]:
        count = Counter(nums)

        # buckets[f] holds the values that occur exactly f times.
        buckets = [[] for _ in range(len(nums) + 1)]
        for num, freq in count.items():
            buckets[freq].append(num)

        # Read the buckets from the highest frequency down.
        # This lists the values from most frequent to least frequent.
        by_frequency = []
        for freq in range(len(nums), 0, -1):
            by_frequency.extend(buckets[freq])

        return by_frequency[:k]

column1:
Design Twitter (Heap / Priority Queue, Medium)

Design a simplified version of Twitter. Users can post tweets and follow or unfollow another user. A user can see the 10 most recent tweets in the user's news feed. Implement the Twitter class. Twitter() initializes your twitter object. void postTweet(int userId, int tweetId) composes a new tweet with ID tweetId by the user userId. Each call to this function uses a unique tweetId. List<Integer> getNewsFeed(int userId) retrieves the 10 most recent tweet IDs in the user's news feed. Each item in the news feed must be posted by users who the user followed or by the user themself. Tweets must be ordered from most recent to least recent. void follow(int followerId, int followeeId): the user with ID followerId starts to follow the user with ID followeeId. void unfollow(int followerId, int followeeId): the user with ID followerId stops following the user with ID followeeId.

Constraints:
1 <= userId, followerId, followeeId <= 500
0 <= tweetId <= 10^4
All the tweets have unique IDs.
At most 3 * 10^4 calls will be made to postTweet, getNewsFeed, follow, and unfollow.

Name the technique and the memory hook. Then rebuild the solution.
column2:
Hook: Stamp each tweet with a global clock. Merge the timelines with a heap: one cursor per user, pop the newest, push that user's previous tweet, stop at ten.
Techniques: heap-k-way-merge, heap-top-k, design-data-structure, hash-map-lookup, hash-set-membership

Approach: Heap k-way merge with one cursor per user. Stamp each tweet with a global counter and append it to its author's list. For a feed, put the newest tweet of you and each followee in a max-heap, pop the newest 10 times, and after each pop push the next older tweet of that same user.

Rebuild:
  1. State: a counter time = 0, tweets = defaultdict(list) that holds (time, tweetId) per user, and following = defaultdict(set) per user.
  2. postTweet: append (time, tweetId) to tweets[userId]. Then add 1 to time.
  3. getNewsFeed seed: start an empty list heap. For each uid in following[userId] | {userId}, read user_tweets = tweets.get(uid). If it has tweets, append (-time, tweetId, uid, i) for its last index i. Then heapify the list.
  4. getNewsFeed merge: while the heap is not empty and the feed has fewer than 10 items, pop the top and append its tweetId to the feed.
  5. After each pop, if i > 0, read tweets[uid][i - 1] and push (-time, tweetId, uid, i - 1).
  6. Return the feed list.
  7. follow: if followerId is not followeeId, add followeeId to following[followerId].
  8. unfollow: discard followeeId from following[followerId]. discard does not raise an error for a missing item.
Signals:
  • The query asks for the k most recent or k best items, and k is a small fixed number.
  • The candidates come from many sources, and each source already keeps its items in sorted order.
  • Items arrive over time and are appended, so each per-source list is sorted by time for free.
  • Ranking is by recency, but the IDs carry no time order. This points to a global counter as a timestamp.
Key insight: The feed is a merge of several lists that are already sorted by time, and you need only the first 10 results. A heap that holds one cursor per list gives the next global item in O(log F), where F is the number of lists. So the read work depends on the number of sources and the output size, not on the total data size.
Approaches:
  • Global tweet log scan: O(1) post, follow, unfollow; O(T) getNewsFeed in the worst case, T = total tweets time, O(T + E), E = follow edges space (too slow)
  • Collect all relevant tweets and sort: O(N log N) per getNewsFeed, N = tweets of the user and followees time, O(T + E) plus O(N) per call space (too slow)
  • Last 10 per user, then select top 10: O(10F log 10) = O(F) per getNewsFeed, with up to 10F candidates; O(1) for other operations time, O(T + E) plus O(10F) per call space (too slow)
  • Heap k-way merge over per-user sorted lists (chosen): O(1) post, follow, unfollow; O(F + 10 log F) getNewsFeed, F = number of followees time, O(T + E) total; O(F) heap per call space
  • heapq.merge with reversed lists: O(F + 10 log F) per getNewsFeed time, O(F) per call space
  • Fan-out on write (push model): O(followers) post; O(10) getNewsFeed; O(F + 10 log F) rebuild on follow or unfollow time, O(T + E + 10U), U = users space
import heapq
from collections import defaultdict
from typing import List


class Twitter:

    def __init__(self):
        self.time = 0
        self.tweets = defaultdict(list)    # userId -> [(time, tweetId)], oldest first
        self.following = defaultdict(set)  # followerId -> set of followeeIds

    def postTweet(self, userId: int, tweetId: int) -> None:
        self.tweets[userId].append((self.time, tweetId))
        self.time += 1

    def getNewsFeed(self, userId: int) -> List[int]:
        # Seed the heap with the newest tweet of every relevant user.
        heap = []
        for uid in self.following[userId] | {userId}:
            user_tweets = self.tweets.get(uid)
            if user_tweets:
                i = len(user_tweets) - 1
                time, tweet_id = user_tweets[i]
                heap.append((-time, tweet_id, uid, i))
        heapq.heapify(heap)

        # K-way merge: pop the newest, then push the next older tweet of that user.
        feed = []
        while heap and len(feed) < 10:
            _, tweet_id, uid, i = heapq.heappop(heap)
            feed.append(tweet_id)
            if i > 0:
                time, next_id = self.tweets[uid][i - 1]
                heapq.heappush(heap, (-time, next_id, uid, i - 1))
        return feed

    def follow(self, followerId: int, followeeId: int) -> None:
        if followerId != followeeId:
            self.following[followerId].add(followeeId)

    def unfollow(self, followerId: int, followeeId: int) -> None:
        self.following[followerId].discard(followeeId)

column1:
Sum of Two Integers (Bit Manipulation, Medium)

Given two integers a and b, return the sum of the two integers without using the operators + and -.

Constraints:
-1000 <= a, b <= 1000

Name the technique and the memory hook. Then rebuild the solution.
column2:
Hook: XOR is the sum, AND shifted left is the carry. Repeat until no carry, mask to 32 bits, and fix the sign with ~(a ^ MASK).
Techniques: bit-manipulation, math, simulation

Approach: XOR sum plus shifted AND carry, masked to 32 bits. XOR adds each column without carry, AND shifted left by one gives the carry, and you repeat until the carry is zero, then convert bit 31 back to a negative sign.

Rebuild:
  1. Set MASK = 0xFFFFFFFF to emulate a 32-bit int.
  2. Loop while b != 0.
  3. In one tuple assignment, set a to (a ^ b) & MASK and b to ((a & b) << 1) & MASK. The tuple form makes both parts use the old a.
  4. After the loop, return a if a <= 0x7FFFFFFF.
  5. Otherwise return ~(a ^ MASK), which equals a minus 2^32 without the minus operator.
Signals:
  • The statement forbids the normal arithmetic operators. This points to building the arithmetic from bitwise operators.
  • The task asks for a basic arithmetic operation under an operator ban. Think of how a hardware circuit or the long-hand method computes it, one bit column at a time.
  • The inputs can be negative. This means two's complement matters, and in Python you must emulate a fixed word width with a mask.
  • The values fit in a fixed word width such as 32 bits. A loop over the bit positions then runs a constant number of times.
Key insight: Addition splits into two independent parts: a carry-free sum (XOR) and a carry (AND shifted left by one). Their sum equals the original sum, so you repeat the split until the carry is zero.
Approaches:
  • Built-in shortcut (sum([a, b]) or operator.add): O(1) time, O(1) space
  • Unit steps with bitwise increment and decrement: O(|b| * 32) time, O(1) space
  • Ripple-carry adder bit by bit: O(32) = O(1) time, O(1) space
  • XOR plus shifted AND carry loop with a 32-bit mask (optimal): O(32) = O(1) time, O(1) space
  • Sign case analysis without a mask (common reference form): O(log(max(|a|, |b|))) time, O(log(max(|a|, |b|))) recursion space
class Solution:
    def getSum(self, a: int, b: int) -> int:
        MASK = 0xFFFFFFFF          # keep 32 bits, like a C int
        while b != 0:
            # sum without carry, and the carry moved one column left
            a, b = (a ^ b) & MASK, ((a & b) << 1) & MASK
        # bit 31 set means negative: flip the low 32 bits, then flip all bits
        return a if a <= 0x7FFFFFFF else ~(a ^ MASK)

column1:
Combination Sum IV (Blind 75 extra, Medium)

You get an array nums of distinct positive integers and a positive integer target. Return the number of possible combinations of numbers from nums that add up to target. You can use each number any number of times. Different orders count as different combinations, so (1, 2) and (2, 1) are two separate ways. In other words, count the ordered sequences whose sum is exactly target. The test cases make sure that the answer fits in a 32-bit integer.

Constraints:
1 <= nums.length <= 200
1 <= nums[i] <= 1000
All the elements of nums are unique.
1 <= target <= 1000
Follow-up: What if negative numbers are allowed in the given array? How does it change the problem? What limitation we need to add to the question to allow negative numbers?

Name the technique and the memory hook. Then rebuild the solution.
column2:
Hook: Ways to make a total: try every last number, add the ways for what is left.
Techniques: dp-knapsack-unbounded, dp-1d-linear, memoized-dfs

Approach: Bottom-up DP over the total, split by the last number. ways[total] is the sum of ways[total - last] over every number last that fits, with ways[0] = 1.

Rebuild:
  1. Make a list ways of size target + 1 filled with 0.
  2. Set ways[0] = 1, because picking nothing is one way to make 0.
  3. Loop total from 1 to target in the outer loop.
  4. In the inner loop, try each number last in nums as the last pick.
  5. If last <= total, add ways[total - last] to ways[total].
  6. Return ways[target].
Signals:
  • The problem asks for the number of ways to reach an exact total, not for the list of ways. Counting points to DP, not backtracking.
  • Items can be reused without limit. This is an unbounded knapsack shape.
  • The statement says that different orders count as different. Order matters, so you count sequences, not multisets.
  • The target is small (at most 1000) and the values are positive integers. A table indexed by the running sum is cheap.
Key insight: To count ordered sequences that reach a total, condition on the last step. The count for total s is the sum of the counts for s - x over every allowed step x. The future depends only on the remaining amount, so a 1-D table over the amount replaces the exponential search. The loop order decides what you count: amount outside counts orderings, items outside counts multisets.
Approaches:
  • Brute-force enumeration (DFS over sequences): O(n^(target / min(nums))) time, O(target / min(nums)) space (too slow)
  • Top-down memoized DFS on remaining sum: O(n * target) time, O(target) space
  • Bottom-up DP over the sum (sum outer, nums inner): O(n * target) time, O(target) space
  • Bottom-up DP with sorted nums and early break: O(n log n + n * target) time, O(target) space
class Solution:
    def combinationSum4(self, nums: List[int], target: int) -> int:
        ways = [0] * (target + 1)
        ways[0] = 1  # one way to make 0: pick nothing
        for total in range(1, target + 1):
            for last in nums:  # try every number as the last pick
                if last <= total:
                    ways[total] += ways[total - last]
        return ways[target]

column1:
Partition Equal Subset Sum (1-D Dynamic Programming, Medium)

You get an integer array nums. Return true if you can split the elements into two subsets so that the sum of the elements in each subset is equal. Otherwise return false. Every element goes into exactly one subset.

Constraints:
1 <= nums.length <= 200
1 <= nums[i] <= 100

Name the technique and the memory hook. Then rebuild the solution.
column2:
Hook: Odd total means no. Otherwise grow the set of reachable sums and ask if half the total is in it.
Techniques: dp-knapsack-01, dp-1d-linear, memoized-dfs, hash-set-membership, bit-manipulation

Approach: Set of reachable sums. Start with {0} for the empty subset. For each number, add that number to every old sum and merge the results into the set. At the end, check if half of the total is in the set.

Rebuild:
  1. Compute total = sum(nums). If total is odd, return False.
  2. Start with sums = {0}, the sum of the empty subset.
  3. For each x in nums, do sums |= {s + x for s in sums}. Skip keeps the old sums, take adds x to them. The comprehension reads only the old sums, so x is used once.
  4. Return total // 2 in sums.
Signals:
  • The task asks if you can split items into two groups with equal sums. This is the same as asking if one subset reaches half of the total.
  • Each item is used at most once, and you only choose take or skip. This is a 0/1 knapsack decision.
  • The values are small positive integers and the count is small. So the total sum is small (here at most 20000), and a table indexed by sum is cheap.
  • The answer is yes or no about reachability, not an optimum. A boolean DP over reachable sums fits.
Key insight: Equal partition is a disguise for subset sum to half the total. Subsets that reach the same sum are interchangeable for the future, so you track which sums are reachable, not which subsets exist.
Optimal: The optimal solution_code stores the same reachable sums in a boolean list of size total / 2 + 1 and updates it in place. It must loop j from target down to x so that dp[j - x] still holds the value from before x. It also caps sums at the target and can return early when dp[target] becomes true. Use it when you need the classic 0/1 knapsack table, or when you need a counting or min/max version, for example target sum or coin change, because a set cannot store a count per sum. Both versions are O(n * total). In CPython both take under 0.2 s of CPU time at the maximum size.
Approaches:
  • Brute force over all subsets: O(2^n) time, O(n) space (too slow)
  • Memoized DFS on (index, remaining): O(n * target) time, O(n * target) space
  • 2-D bottom-up 0/1 knapsack table: O(n * target) time, O(n * target) space
  • Set of reachable sums (intuitive pick): O(n * target) time, O(target) space
  • 1-D boolean DP with reverse sum loop (chosen): O(n * target) time, O(target) space
  • Bitset shift: O(n * target / w) time, O(target / w) space
class Solution:
    def canPartition(self, nums: List[int]) -> bool:
        total = sum(nums)
        if total % 2:
            return False
        sums = {0}
        for x in nums:
            sums |= {s + x for s in sums}
        return total // 2 in sums

column1:
Pacific Atlantic Water Flow (Graphs, Medium)

There is an m x n rectangular island. The Pacific Ocean touches the left and top edges of the island. The Atlantic Ocean touches the right and bottom edges of the island. The island is a grid of square cells. You get an m x n integer matrix heights. heights[r][c] is the height above sea level of the cell at coordinate (r, c). The island receives a lot of rain. Rain water can flow from a cell to a neighbor directly north, south, east or west if the neighbor's height is less than or equal to the current cell's height. Water can flow from any cell next to an ocean into that ocean. Return a 2D list of grid coordinates result, where result[i] = [ri, ci] means that rain water can flow from cell (ri, ci) to both the Pacific and the Atlantic oceans. Note: the official text does not fix an output order. The examples list the cells in row-major order.

Constraints:
m == heights.length
n == heights[r].length
1 <= m, n <= 200
0 <= heights[r][c] <= 10^5

Name the technique and the memory hook. Then rebuild the solution.
column2:
Hook: Water flows down, so flood uphill from each ocean and keep the cells both floods reach.
Techniques: multi-source-bfs, reverse-thinking, grid-flood-fill, hash-set-membership

Approach: Use a reverse flood fill from each ocean. Seed a stack and a reached set with all border cells of one ocean. Step only to neighbors that are at least as high. Return the cells that both floods reach.

Rebuild:
  1. Read rows = len(heights) and cols = len(heights[0]).
  2. Write flood_uphill(starts). Set reached = set(starts) and stack = list(starts).
  3. While the stack is not empty, pop a cell (r, c).
  4. For each of the 4 neighbors, check that it is inside the grid, is not in reached, and has height >= heights[r][c].
  5. If all checks pass, add the neighbor to reached and push it. Return reached when the stack is empty.
  6. Set pacific = flood_uphill(the whole top row plus the whole left column).
  7. Set atlantic = flood_uphill(the whole bottom row plus the whole right column).
  8. Return [[r, c] for r, c in sorted(pacific & atlantic)].
Signals:
  • The question asks which cells or nodes can reach a fixed target set, such as a border, an exit or a gate.
  • Many sources share a few fixed targets. A separate search from each source repeats the same work.
  • A local rule between neighbors sets the move direction, such as height less than or equal. You can test the same rule backward from the target side.
  • The answer needs cells that meet two or more reachability conditions at the same time. This points to one search per condition and an intersection.
Key insight: When many sources ask whether they can reach a small fixed target set, reverse the edges and search once from all targets together. One reverse search answers the question for every source at the same time.
Optimal: The record's solution_code uses the same reverse search with the same O(m*n) time and O(m*n) space. It uses a collections.deque as a BFS queue instead of a list as a stack. It builds the result with a row-major scan of the grid instead of sorted(pacific & atlantic). The visit order does not change the reached sets, so both versions return the same cells in the same order.
Approaches:
  • Brute force: downhill search from every cell: O((m*n)^2) time, O(m*n) space (too slow)
  • Memoized downhill search per cell: O(m*n) with SCC condensation time, O(m*n) space
  • Reverse multi-source BFS from each ocean (optimal): O(m*n) time, O(m*n) space
  • Reverse DFS from each ocean (NeetCode style): O(m*n) time, O(m*n) space
from typing import List


class Solution:
    def pacificAtlantic(self, heights: List[List[int]]) -> List[List[int]]:
        rows, cols = len(heights), len(heights[0])

        def flood_uphill(starts):
            # Water flows down or level, so search backward from the ocean:
            # climb to neighbors that are at least as high.
            reached = set(starts)
            stack = list(starts)
            while stack:
                r, c = stack.pop()
                for nr, nc in ((r + 1, c), (r - 1, c), (r, c + 1), (r, c - 1)):
                    if (
                        0 <= nr < rows
                        and 0 <= nc < cols
                        and (nr, nc) not in reached
                        and heights[nr][nc] >= heights[r][c]
                    ):
                        reached.add((nr, nc))
                        stack.append((nr, nc))
            return reached

        top_and_left = [(0, c) for c in range(cols)] + [(r, 0) for r in range(rows)]
        bottom_and_right = [(rows - 1, c) for c in range(cols)] + [
            (r, cols - 1) for r in range(rows)
        ]
        pacific = flood_uphill(top_and_left)
        atlantic = flood_uphill(bottom_and_right)
        return [[r, c] for r, c in sorted(pacific & atlantic)]

Longest Repeating Character Replacement (Sliding Window, Medium)

You get a string s and an integer k. In one operation, you choose any character of s and change it to any other uppercase English letter. You can do this operation at most k times. Return the length of the longest substring that contains only the same letter after the operations. A substring is contiguous. You do not have to use all k operations.

Constraints:
1 <= s.length <= 10^5
s consists of only uppercase English letters.
0 <= k <= s.length

Name the technique and the memory hook. Then rebuild the solution.
column2:
Hook: Window length minus top count must be at most k.
Techniques: sliding-window-variable, counting-frequency, hash-map-lookup

Approach: Sliding window with exact max frequency. Grow the window one letter to the right. While window length minus the count of its most common letter is more than k, shrink the window from the left. Get that top count with max over the at most 26 letter counts.

Rebuild:
  1. Import Counter from collections. Make a Counter for the window, and set left = 0 and best = 0.
  2. For each right, ch in enumerate(s), add one to count[ch].
  3. While (right - left + 1) - max(count.values()) > k, subtract one from count[s[left]] and add one to left.
  4. After the while loop the window is valid, so set best = max(best, right - left + 1).
  5. After the for loop, return best.
Signals:
  • The task asks for the longest contiguous substring or subarray that satisfies a condition.
  • A budget of at most k changes, deletions or flips limits how many bad elements a window can hold.
  • The validity test of a window depends only on counts inside the window, so you can update it in O(1) when one element enters or leaves.
  • Validity is monotone: if a window is valid, every shorter window inside it is also valid. So you can shrink from the left without losing a valid answer.
Key insight: Reframe the cost of a window as a count expression: the minimum number of changes to make a window uniform is its length minus the count of its most frequent element. Then the problem is the longest window with length - max_freq <= k, a classic variable sliding window with a monotone validity condition.
Optimal: The optimal solution keeps max_freq as a running maximum that never goes down, so it does not scan the counts. This removes the factor of 26 and gives O(n). A stale max_freq can be too high, so the window can stay at a length that is not valid now. That length is never more than the length of a valid window found before, so the answer stays correct. The answer grows only when a letter count goes above the old max_freq. You need this trick only for a large alphabet, where a scan of all counts is too slow, or when the task requires strict O(n).
Approaches:
  • Brute force over all substrings: O(26 * n^2) time, O(26) space (too slow)
  • Binary search on the answer length: O(26 * n log n) time, O(26) space
  • One sliding window per target letter: O(26 * n) time, O(1) space
  • Sliding window with exact max frequency: O(26 * n) time, O(26) space
  • Sliding window with non-decreasing max frequency (optimal): O(n) time, O(26) space
from collections import Counter


class Solution:
    def characterReplacement(self, s: str, k: int) -> int:
        count = Counter()
        left = 0
        best = 0
        for right, ch in enumerate(s):
            count[ch] += 1
            # Changes needed = window length - count of its most common letter.
            while (right - left + 1) - max(count.values()) > k:
                count[s[left]] -= 1
                left += 1
            best = max(best, right - left + 1)
        return best

column1:
Non-overlapping Intervals (Intervals, Medium)

You get an array intervals where intervals[i] = [start_i, end_i]. Return the minimum number of intervals that you must remove so that the remaining intervals do not overlap. Intervals that only touch at a point do not overlap. For example, [1, 2] and [2, 3] do not overlap. Every interval has start_i < end_i.

Constraints:
1 <= intervals.length <= 10^5
intervals[i].length == 2
-5 * 10^4 <= start_i < end_i <= 5 * 10^4

Name the technique and the memory hook. Then rebuild the solution.
column2:
Hook: Sort by end, keep what fits, remove the rest.
Techniques: greedy, intervals-sort-sweep, sorting, reverse-thinking

Approach: Greedy, sort by end. Keep the interval that finishes first, skip every interval that starts before the last kept end, and return n minus the kept count.

Rebuild:
  1. Sort the intervals by their end value.
  2. Set kept = 0 and prev_end = negative infinity.
  3. For each start, end: if start >= prev_end, the interval fits. Touching intervals fit, so use >= and not >.
  4. When it fits, add one to kept and set prev_end = end.
  5. Return len(intervals) - kept.
Signals:
  • The task asks for the minimum number of items to remove so that the rest satisfy a pairwise compatibility rule. Rewrite it as the maximum number of items to keep.
  • The items are intervals on a line and the conflict is overlap. This is the classic activity selection or interval scheduling setup.
  • Every interval has the same value, and only the count of kept intervals matters. Equal values make the earliest-end greedy safe. Different values need DP.
  • The input size is up to 10^5, so the target is O(n log n) or better. That points to sort plus one linear pass.
Key insight: Minimum removals equals n minus the maximum set you can keep. To keep the most non-overlapping intervals, always keep the one that ends first. An early end leaves the most room for the rest, and an exchange argument shows this choice is never worse.
Approaches:
  • Brute force over subsets: O(2^n * n log n) time, O(n) space (too slow)
  • DP like longest increasing subsequence: O(n^2) time, O(n) space (too slow)
  • Weighted-scheduling DP with binary search: O(n log n) time, O(n) space
  • Greedy, sort by end (optimal, standard): O(n log n) time, O(n), because sort with a key function stores n keys and Timsort can use a merge buffer of up to n/2 items space
  • Greedy, sort by start (NeetCode variant): O(n log n) time, O(n) in the worst case for the Timsort merge buffer space
class Solution:
    def eraseOverlapIntervals(self, intervals: List[List[int]]) -> int:
        intervals.sort(key=lambda iv: iv[1])
        kept = 0
        prev_end = float("-inf")
        for start, end in intervals:
            if start >= prev_end:
                kept += 1
                prev_end = end
        return len(intervals) - kept

column1:
Target Sum (2-D Dynamic Programming, Medium)

You get an integer array nums and an integer target. Put exactly one symbol, '+' or '-', before each integer in nums, then concatenate all the integers to build an expression. For example, for nums = [2, 1], a '+' before 2 and a '-' before 1 give the expression "+2-1". Return the number of different expressions that you can build that evaluate to target. Two expressions are different when the sign at one or more positions is different, so +0 and -0 count as two expressions.

Constraints:
1 <= nums.length <= 20
0 <= nums[i] <= 1000
0 <= sum(nums[i]) <= 1000
-1000 <= target <= 1000

Name the technique and the memory hook. Then rebuild the solution.
column2:
Hook: Plus or minus each number, cache on (index, running sum).
Techniques: dp-knapsack-01, memoized-dfs, backtracking-subsets

Approach: Memoized DFS on (index, running sum). Try '+' and '-' for each number. Count the paths that end at target. Cache each (i, running_sum) pair so that equal prefixes are solved only once.

Rebuild:
  1. Inside findTargetSumWays, define ways(i, running_sum): the number of ways to sign nums[i:] so that the final sum equals target.
  2. Base case: at i == len(nums), return 1 if running_sum == target, else 0.
  3. Branch: return ways(i + 1, running_sum + nums[i]) + ways(i + 1, running_sum - nums[i]).
  4. Import cache from functools and put @cache on ways. Because ways is an inner function, each call of findTargetSumWays gets a new cache.
  5. Return ways(0, 0).
Signals:
  • Each item gets one of two choices (plus or minus, take or skip), and the question asks how many choice sequences hit an exact total.
  • The answer is a count of ways, not a single best value, so the DP adds counts instead of taking a max or min.
  • The sum of all values is small (here at most 1000), so a table indexed by partial sum is cheap.
  • The limit n <= 20 allows 2^n enumeration only in a fast language. In Python, plain 2^n recursion takes seconds per test. The small bound on the sum makes a DP over sums the safe choice.
Key insight: A plus/minus sign assignment is the same as picking a subset: the plus group P satisfies P - N = target and P + N = total, so P = (total + target) / 2. Counting sign assignments becomes counting subsets with a fixed sum, which is a standard 0/1 knapsack count.
Optimal: The optimal solution_code rewrites the signs as a subset. The '+' group must sum to P = (total + target) / 2. It then counts subsets with sum P in one 1-D array, dp[s] += dp[s - num], with s going from high to low. It has the same O(n * total) time. It uses O(total) memory, no recursion and no hashing, so it is faster by a constant factor. Use it when n is large enough to make recursion depth a risk, or when the problem asks for O(total) space. It is also the bridge to Partition Equal Subset Sum and Last Stone Weight II.
Approaches:
  • Brute force recursion over signs: O(2^n) time, O(n) space (too slow)
  • Memoized DFS on (index, running sum): O(n * total) time, O(n * total) space
  • Bottom-up layered counts of reachable sums: O(n * total) time, O(total) space
  • Subset-sum reduction with 1-D 0/1 knapsack count (optimal): O(n * total) time, O(total) space
  • Meet in the middle: O(2^(n/2)) time, O(2^(n/2)) space
from functools import cache
from typing import List

class Solution:
    def findTargetSumWays(self, nums: List[int], target: int) -> int:
        # ways(i, running_sum) = number of sign choices for nums[i:]
        # that turn running_sum into target.
        @cache
        def ways(i, running_sum):
            if i == len(nums):
                return 1 if running_sum == target else 0
            plus = ways(i + 1, running_sum + nums[i])
            minus = ways(i + 1, running_sum - nums[i])
            return plus + minus

        return ways(0, 0)

column1:
Coin Change II (2-D Dynamic Programming, Medium)

You get an integer array coins of distinct coin values and an integer amount. Return the number of combinations of coins that sum to exactly amount. A combination is unordered: 1+2 and 2+1 are the same combination. You can use each coin value an unlimited number of times. If no combination makes the amount, return 0. For amount 0 the answer is 1, because the empty combination counts. The final answer is guaranteed to fit in a signed 32-bit integer.

Constraints:
1 <= coins.length <= 300
1 <= coins[i] <= 5000
All the values of coins are unique.
0 <= amount <= 5000

Name the technique and the memory hook. Then rebuild the solution.
column2:
Hook: Coins outside, amounts going up inside: ways[a] += ways[a - coin].
Techniques: dp-knapsack-unbounded, dp-1d-linear, dp-2d-grid, memoized-dfs

Approach: 1-D counting DP, coins outside, amounts inside (unbounded knapsack). Keep ways[a] for every amount, and add one coin type at a time: ways[a] += ways[a - coin], with a going up from coin to amount.

Rebuild:
  1. Make ways = [0] * (amount + 1) and set ways[0] = 1 for the empty combination.
  2. Loop over each coin in the outer loop, so each combination is built in one fixed coin order.
  3. Loop a from coin up to amount in the inner loop, so the same coin can repeat.
  4. Add ways[a - coin] to ways[a]: old ways[a] skips the coin, ways[a - coin] adds one more of it.
  5. Return ways[amount].
Signals:
  • The problem asks for the number of ways to reach a target sum, so you count with a sum-of-ways DP and do not enumerate.
  • The word combinations means order does not matter, so you must fix one canonical order of choices to avoid counting the same multiset twice.
  • Each item has an infinite supply, which points to the unbounded knapsack pattern.
  • The target sum is a small integer (at most 5000) and there are at most 300 item types, so a table of item types times sums (about 1.5 million cells) is cheap. A small numeric target suggests a DP indexed by the sum.
Key insight: To count unordered combinations, process the item types in a fixed order in the outer loop. Then every multiset has exactly one build order and is counted once. Unlimited copies mean the 'take one more' transition stays on the same item, so in a 1-D array you sweep the target upward and read values that already include the current item.
Approaches:
  • Brute force: enumerate a count for each coin: O(product of (amount / c_i + 1)), exponential time, O(m) recursion depth space (too slow)
  • Memoized DFS take-or-skip (NeetCode): O(m * n) time, O(m * n) space (too slow)
  • 2-D DP that sums over the copy count: O(m * n + n^2 log m) time, O(m * n) space (too slow)
  • 2-D bottom-up DP: O(m * n) time, O(m * n) space
  • 1-D rolling DP (optimal): O(m * n) time, O(n) space
class Solution:
    def change(self, amount: int, coins: List[int]) -> int:
        # ways[a] = number of combinations that make a, using the coins seen so far
        ways = [0] * (amount + 1)
        ways[0] = 1  # one way to make 0: take nothing
        for coin in coins:  # one coin type at a time: each combination is built once
            for a in range(coin, amount + 1):  # go up: this coin can repeat
                ways[a] += ways[a - coin]  # ways without coin + ways that add one more coin
        return ways[amount]

column1:
Diameter of Binary Tree (Trees, Easy)

You get the root of a binary tree. Return the length of the diameter of the tree. The diameter is the length of the longest path between any two nodes in the tree. The length of a path is the number of edges on it, not the number of nodes. The path does not have to pass through the root. A tree with one node has diameter 0.

Constraints:
The number of nodes in the tree is in the range [1, 10^4].
-100 <= Node.val <= 100

Name the technique and the memory hook. Then rebuild the solution.
column2:
Hook: At each node, record left height + right height as a candidate for best, and pass 1 + the bigger height up. Deep tree: list parents first, then walk backward.
Techniques: tree-dfs-bottom-up

Approach: Bottom-up heights from a parents-first list. Collect the nodes with a stack so that each parent comes before its children, then walk the list backward. At each node, add the two child heights as a candidate path and store 1 + the larger height for the parent.

Rebuild:
  1. Make order = [] and stack = [root].
  2. While the stack is not empty, pop a node. If the node is not None, append it to order and push node.left and node.right. Every parent now comes before its children in order.
  3. Make height = {None: 0} and best = 0. The None key gives a missing child the height 0.
  4. Loop over reversed(order). Both children of each node then already have a height.
  5. Read left = height[node.left] and right = height[node.right].
  6. Set best = max(best, left + right). This sum is the edge count of the path that bends at node.
  7. Store height[node] = 1 + max(left, right).
  8. After the loop, return best.
Signals:
  • The statement asks for the longest path between any two nodes of a tree. Such a path goes up to one highest node and then goes down, so each node is a possible bend point.
  • The statement says the path may or may not pass through the root. This tells you that the answer can sit at any node, so you need a running global best, not only the value at the root.
  • The value at a node depends on results from both children, such as heights. This points to a postorder (bottom-up) DFS.
  • The node count goes up to 10^4 and the tree can be skewed. Recomputing heights for every node is O(n^2), so each node must be visited a constant number of times.
Key insight: Every path in a tree has a unique highest node where it bends. The longest path that bends at a node is the sum of the two longest downward chains from that node. Compute these chains bottom-up, record the two-sided sum as a candidate at each node, and pass only the one-sided chain up to the parent.
Optimal: The optimal solution_code is the recursive form of the same idea: height(node) returns 1 + max of the child heights and updates a nonlocal best with left + right. It is shorter and uses O(h) extra space instead of O(n). Both are O(n) time. Use the recursive form when the tree depth is small or the judge raises the recursion limit. For a skewed tree with 10^4 nodes it needs sys.setrecursionlimit above 10^4 in CPython.
Approaches:
  • All-pairs BFS on the undirected tree: O(n^2) time, O(n) space (too slow)
  • Separate height call at every node: O(n^2) worst case on a skewed tree, O(n log n) on a balanced tree time, O(h) space (too slow)
  • Single postorder DFS that returns height and updates a global best: O(n) time, O(h), where h is the tree height, up to O(n) for a skewed tree space
  • Iterative postorder with an explicit stack: O(n) time, O(n) space
  • Two traversals (farthest-node trick): O(n) time, O(n) space
class Solution:
    def diameterOfBinaryTree(self, root: Optional[TreeNode]) -> int:
        # 1. List the nodes so that every parent comes before its children.
        order = []
        stack = [root]
        while stack:
            node = stack.pop()
            if node:
                order.append(node)
                stack.append(node.left)
                stack.append(node.right)

        # 2. Walk the list backward, so both children are done before the parent.
        height = {None: 0}  # nodes on the longest downward chain
        best = 0
        for node in reversed(order):
            left = height[node.left]
            right = height[node.right]
            best = max(best, left + right)  # edges of the path that bends here
            height[node] = 1 + max(left, right)
        return best

Permutation in String (Sliding Window, Medium)

You get two strings s1 and s2. Return true if s2 contains a permutation of s1. Otherwise, return false. In other words, return true if one of the permutations of s1 is a substring of s2. A permutation is a rearrangement of all the characters of a string. A substring is a contiguous part of a string.

Constraints:
1 <= s1.length, s2.length <= 10^4
s1 and s2 consist of lowercase English letters.

Name the technique and the memory hook. Then rebuild the solution.
column2:
Hook: Slide a window of len(s1) over s2 and compare its letter counts to s1's counts.
Techniques: sliding-window-fixed, counting-frequency

Approach: Fixed sliding window with two count arrays. Keep the letter counts of s1 and the letter counts of the last k letters of s2, and return true when the two arrays are equal.

Rebuild:
  1. Set k = len(s1) and make two lists of 26 zeros: need and window.
  2. Count each letter of s1 into need with ord(ch) - ord('a').
  3. Loop r, ch over enumerate(s2) and add ch to window.
  4. If r >= k, remove s2[r - k] from window, so the window holds only the last k letters.
  5. If window == need, return True.
  6. After the loop, return False.
Signals:
  • The statement says permutation or anagram of a pattern. Order does not matter, so only the letter counts matter.
  • The target is a contiguous substring whose length is fixed by the pattern. This points to a fixed-size sliding window.
  • The window property is a comparison of two multisets. Letter counts support one add and one remove in O(1), so the state can slide instead of being rebuilt.
  • The alphabet is small and fixed (26 lowercase letters). A count array of size 26 is the window state, and a full compare of two states costs O(26).
Key insight: A permutation is identified only by its letter counts. Every candidate substring has the same length as the pattern. So slide a fixed-size window and update its counts with one letter in and one letter out. Do not rebuild the counts for each window.
Optimal: The optimal solution_code keeps one diff array and an integer bad that counts the letters with unequal counts. Only the entering letter and the leaving letter can change bad, so each step is O(1) instead of O(26). This removes the alphabet factor. Use it when the alphabet is large or unknown, for example Unicode letters in a dict. Also use it when the task asks for O(n) time that does not depend on the alphabet size. For 26 letters and n up to 10^4, the two-array compare is already fast.
Approaches:
  • Try every permutation of s1: O(k! * n * k) time, O(k! * k) space (too slow)
  • Sort every window: O((n - k + 1) * k log k) time, O(k) space (too slow)
  • Recount every window: O((n - k + 1) * k) time, O(1) space (too slow)
  • Fixed sliding window with two count arrays: O(k + 26 * n) time, O(1) space
  • Fixed sliding window with a mismatch counter (optimal): O(k + n) time, O(1) space
  • Multiset rolling hash: O(k + n) time, O(1) space
class Solution:
    def checkInclusion(self, s1: str, s2: str) -> bool:
        k = len(s1)
        need = [0] * 26     # letter counts of s1
        window = [0] * 26   # letter counts of the last k letters of s2
        for ch in s1:
            need[ord(ch) - ord("a")] += 1

        for r, ch in enumerate(s2):
            window[ord(ch) - ord("a")] += 1             # letter enters on the right
            if r >= k:
                window[ord(s2[r - k]) - ord("a")] -= 1  # letter leaves on the left
            if window == need:                          # same counts = permutation
                return True
        return False

Subtree of Another Tree (Trees, Easy)

You get the roots of two binary trees, root and subRoot. Return true if some subtree of root has the same structure and the same node values as subRoot. Otherwise return false. A subtree of a tree is one node of that tree together with all of its descendants. The whole tree also counts as a subtree of itself. So a match must cover every descendant down to the leaves. A match of only the top part of a subtree does not count.

Constraints:
The number of nodes in the root tree is in the range [1, 2000].
The number of nodes in the subRoot tree is in the range [1, 1000].
-10^4 <= root.val <= 10^4
-10^4 <= subRoot.val <= 10^4

Name the technique and the memory hook. Then rebuild the solution.
column2:
Hook: Try every node as a start, and ask Same Tree at each one. Both loops pop, skip the empty case, check, and push the children.
Techniques: tree-dfs-top-down, tree-dfs-bottom-up, tree-construction-serialization, grouping-by-canonical-key

Approach: DFS with a Same Tree check at every node, written with two explicit stacks. The outer stack visits every node of root as a possible start. At each start, a stack of node pairs checks if the tree there is identical to subRoot.

Rebuild:
  1. Write same_tree(a, b). Put the pair (a, b) in a list named pairs.
  2. While pairs is not empty, pop a pair (x, y).
  3. If x and y are both None, continue. This pair matches.
  4. If only one of them is None, or x.val != y.val, return False.
  5. Push the left pair (x.left, y.left) and the right pair (x.right, y.right).
  6. After the loop, return True. Every pair matched.
  7. In isSubtree, put root in a list named stack.
  8. While stack is not empty, pop a node. If the node is None, continue.
  9. If same_tree(node, subRoot) is True, return True.
  10. Push node.left and node.right.
  11. After the loop, return False. No start node matched.
Signals:
  • The question asks if one structure occurs inside another structure. This is pattern search, like substring search, but on trees.
  • The phrase 'a node and all of its descendants' means the match must end at the same leaves. A match of only the top part is not enough.
  • The node counts are small (2000 and 1000). Their product is 2 * 10^6, so an exact check at every node fits.
  • The check at one fixed start node is an 'are two trees identical' question (Same Tree). When a bigger question needs that equality check at every position, reuse the equality helper inside an outer traversal.
Key insight: A question of the form 'does pattern P occur inside structure S' splits into two parts. One part is an exact equality check that starts at a fixed position. The other part enumerates every position in S where P can start. For trees, the positions are the nodes, and the equality check is the Same Tree recursion.
Optimal: The record solution_code uses the same idea with recursion. same() recurses down both trees together, and isSubtree() recurses down root. It is shorter, and it is the usual textbook answer. Its base case 'return p is q' is a compact form of the two None rules. Both forms take O(n * m) time. The recursion depth of solution_code equals the height of root, so a skewed root of 2000 nodes makes it about 2000 levels deep. This is above the default CPython limit of 1000, so it raises RecursionError without sys.setrecursionlimit. A judge that raises the limit accepts it. Use the recursive form when the tree is shallow or when you want the shortest code.
Approaches:
  • Brute force: encode every subtree: O(n^2) time, O(n) space
  • DFS with a same-tree check at every node (standard): O(n * m) time, O(h), where h is the height of root, up to O(n) space
  • Preorder serialization with null markers plus string search: O(n + m) time, O(n + m) space
  • Canonical subtree ids (Merkle hashing): O(n + m) expected time, O(n + m) space
# Definition for a binary tree node.
# class TreeNode:
#     def __init__(self, val=0, left=None, right=None):
#         self.val = val
#         self.left = left
#         self.right = right
class Solution:
    def isSubtree(self, root: Optional[TreeNode], subRoot: Optional[TreeNode]) -> bool:
        def same_tree(a, b):
            pairs = [(a, b)]                    # node pairs still to compare
            while pairs:
                x, y = pairs.pop()
                if x is None and y is None:
                    continue                    # both empty: this pair matches
                if x is None or y is None or x.val != y.val:
                    return False                # one empty or different values
                pairs.append((x.left, y.left))
                pairs.append((x.right, y.right))
            return True

        stack = [root]                          # every node of root is a possible start
        while stack:
            node = stack.pop()
            if node is None:
                continue
            if same_tree(node, subRoot):
                return True
            stack.append(node.left)
            stack.append(node.right)
        return False

Task Scheduler (Heap / Priority Queue, Medium)

You get an array tasks of CPU tasks. Each task is an uppercase letter from A to Z. You also get an integer n. Each CPU interval either runs one task or stays idle. You can run the tasks in any order. Two tasks with the same label must have a gap of at least n intervals between them. Return the minimum number of CPU intervals needed to complete all tasks, idle intervals included.

Constraints:
1 <= tasks.length <= 10^4
tasks[i] is an uppercase English letter.
0 <= n <= 100

Name the technique and the memory hook. Then rebuild the solution.
column2:
Hook: Fill each window of n + 1 with the most frequent different tasks. Only the last window has no idle tail.
Techniques: heap-greedy-simulation, counting-frequency, greedy, simulation, math-number-theory

Approach: Round-by-round max-heap greedy. Each round is one cooldown window of n + 1 slots. You fill the window with the most frequent different tasks. A full window costs n + 1. The last round costs only the tasks that ran.

Rebuild:
  1. Count the tasks. Put the negated counts in a list and heapify it, so the heap gives the largest count first. Set time to 0.
  2. While the heap is not empty, start a round with an empty list named ran.
  3. Pop up to n + 1 counts and stop early if the heap is empty. Add 1 to each count to run one copy, and append it to ran.
  4. Push back each count in ran that is not zero.
  5. If the heap still has work, add n + 1 to time. Else add len(ran), because this is the last round.
  6. After the loop, return time.
Signals:
  • The problem asks for a minimum total time to schedule jobs that have a cooldown or minimum gap between repeats of the same kind.
  • Only the count of each job kind matters, not the input order, so you can compress the input to a frequency table.
  • The alphabet is small (26 kinds), so a heap or a scan over kinds costs a constant per step.
  • At each step you pick one available item, and the item with the most remaining copies is the safest pick. A repeated 'pick the largest available' choice points to a max-heap.
Key insight: The most frequent item is the bottleneck in a cooldown schedule. Always run the available item with the most remaining copies, and hold used items in a FIFO queue until their cooldown ends. Idle time appears only when every remaining item is cooling. The total length is (m - 1) * (n + 1) + ties, where m is the top count. If the other items fill all gaps, no idle occurs and the length equals the number of tasks.
Optimal: The record's solution_code runs the same greedy one interval at a time. It keeps a FIFO queue of cooling tasks with their ready times and jumps over idle runs. That event-simulation form extends directly to tasks with different cooldowns, because the queue then becomes a min-heap keyed by ready time. The round method can also print a valid schedule if the heap holds (negated count, label) pairs and full rounds get idle padding. The closed form max(N, (m - 1) * (n + 1) + ties) is O(N) with no heap, and it is the fastest to type once you trust it. All three cost O(N log 26) or less on these constraints.
Approaches:
  • Exhaustive search over schedules: O(exponential in number of kinds and counts) time, O(number of states) space (too slow)
  • Step-by-step greedy with a linear scan: O(T * 26), where T is the answer, up to about 1e6 time, O(26) space (too slow)
  • Max-heap plus cooldown queue simulation (chosen): O(N log 26) = O(N) time, O(26) space
  • Closed-form counting (greedy frames): O(N) time, O(26) space
import heapq
from collections import Counter
from typing import List


class Solution:
    def leastInterval(self, tasks: List[str], n: int) -> int:
        heap = [-count for count in Counter(tasks).values()]  # max-heap of counts
        heapq.heapify(heap)
        time = 0
        while heap:
            # One round = one cooldown window of n + 1 slots.
            # Run the most frequent different tasks in it.
            ran = []
            while heap and len(ran) < n + 1:
                ran.append(heapq.heappop(heap) + 1)  # run one copy
            for count in ran:
                if count:  # copies remain
                    heapq.heappush(heap, count)
            # A full window if work remains, else only the tasks that ran.
            time += n + 1 if heap else len(ran)
        return time

Palindromic Substrings (1-D Dynamic Programming, Medium)

Given a string s, return the number of palindromic substrings in it. A string is a palindrome when it reads the same backward as forward. A substring is a contiguous sequence of characters within the string.

Constraints:
1 <= s.length <= 1000
s consists of lowercase English letters.

Name the technique and the memory hook. Then rebuild the solution.
column2:
Hook: Every palindrome has a middle: expand from each middle, odd and even, and count each match.
Techniques: expand-around-center, dp-palindrome-substrings, dp-interval

Approach: Expand around center with a helper. For each index i, call expand(i, i) for odd-length palindromes and expand(i, i + 1) for even-length palindromes, and add one for each matching pair as the two ends move outward.

Rebuild:
  1. Set n to len(s).
  2. Define expand(left, right). Set count to 0.
  3. While left >= 0, right < n and s[left] == s[right], add one to count. Then move left down by one and right up by one.
  4. Return count from expand.
  5. Set total to 0. Loop i over every index of s.
  6. Add expand(i, i) for odd-length palindromes centered on s[i].
  7. Add expand(i, i + 1) for even-length palindromes centered between s[i] and s[i + 1].
  8. Return total.
Signals:
  • The task asks to count or find substrings that are palindromes.
  • The target pieces are symmetric around a middle point. So each one grows outward from that middle one matching pair at a time.
  • The string length is at most about 1000 to 3000. So O(n^2) work is fine and O(n^3) work is risky.
  • The answer counts positions, not distinct texts. So each (start, end) pair that is a palindrome adds one.
Key insight: A palindrome is defined by its center and its radius. Growing outward from a fixed center gives one new palindrome per matching pair. The first mismatch ends all longer candidates at that center. So each center costs one step per palindrome it produces plus at most one failed check. The total work is O(n + answer), which is O(n^2) in the worst case.
Optimal: The algorithm and the complexity are the same: O(n^2) time and O(1) extra space. The record code puts both center types into one loop over 2n - 1 centers with left = c // 2 and right = left + c % 2. This is only a compact form. Use it when you want one loop and no helper. For n of 10^5 or more, use Manacher's algorithm for O(n) time.
Approaches:
  • Brute force: O(n^3) time, O(n) space (too slow)
  • Interval DP table: O(n^2) time, O(n^2) space
  • Expand around center: O(n^2) time, O(1) space
  • Manacher's algorithm: O(n) time, O(n) space
class Solution:
    def countSubstrings(self, s: str) -> int:
        n = len(s)

        def expand(left, right):
            # Grow outward while the two ends match. Each match is one palindrome.
            count = 0
            while left >= 0 and right < n and s[left] == s[right]:
                count += 1
                left -= 1
                right += 1
            return count

        total = 0
        for i in range(n):
            total += expand(i, i)      # odd length: center on s[i]
            total += expand(i, i + 1)  # even length: center between s[i] and s[i+1]
        return total

Valid Parenthesis String (Greedy, Medium)

You get a string s that contains only three types of characters: '(', ')' and '*'. Return true if s is valid, else return false. These rules define a valid string. Any left parenthesis '(' must have a corresponding right parenthesis ')'. Any right parenthesis ')' must have a corresponding left parenthesis '('. A left parenthesis '(' must come before its corresponding right parenthesis ')'. A '*' can act as a single right parenthesis ')', a single left parenthesis '(', or an empty string. Each '*' makes its own choice. So s is valid if at least one choice for all the '*' characters gives a valid string.

Constraints:
1 <= s.length <= 100
s[i] is '(', ')' or '*'.

Name the technique and the memory hook. Then rebuild the solution.
column2:
Hook: Range of open counts: fail if the most goes below zero, clamp the fewest at zero, and end with fewest == 0.
Techniques: greedy, prefix-suffix-accumulation, stack-matching-parsing, memoized-dfs, dp-interval

Approach: Range of open counts (lo, hi). Keep the fewest and the most unmatched '(' that are possible after each character, and at the end check that zero open is possible.

Rebuild:
  1. Set lo = hi = 0, the fewest and the most unmatched '(' so far.
  2. Loop over each character c of s.
  3. For '(' add 1 to both. For ')' subtract 1 from both.
  4. For '*' subtract 1 from lo and add 1 to hi, because it can close or open.
  5. If hi < 0, return False, because even all '*' as '(' cannot cover the ')'.
  6. Set lo = max(lo, 0), because an open count is never negative.
  7. After the loop, return lo == 0, because then zero open brackets is possible.
Signals:
  • The input is a bracket sequence, so validity reduces to a running balance that never goes negative and ends at zero.
  • A wildcard symbol can take one of several values, and the question asks whether at least one assignment works.
  • Each wildcard changes a counter by a run of consecutive amounts, here -1, 0 or +1. This keeps the set of reachable counter values contiguous.
  • The answer is only true or false, so you do not need to build the assignment. You only need to prove that one exists.
Key insight: When each uncertain choice changes a counter by -1, 0 or +1, the set of reachable counter values stays a contiguous range. So you can replace an exponential set of choices with two numbers: the minimum and the maximum reachable value.
Approaches:
  • Brute force over all wildcard assignments: O(3^k * n), k = number of '*' time, O(n) space (too slow)
  • Interval DP over substrings: O(n^3) time, O(n^2) space
  • Memoized DFS over (index, open count): O(n^2) time, O(n^2) space
  • Two stacks of indices: O(n) time, O(n) space
  • Two-pass balance check: O(n) time, O(1) space
  • Greedy range of open counts (optimal): O(n) time, O(1) space
class Solution:
    def checkValidString(self, s: str) -> bool:
        lo = hi = 0  # fewest and most unmatched '(' we could have now
        for c in s:
            if c == "(":
                lo += 1
                hi += 1
            elif c == ")":
                lo -= 1
                hi -= 1
            else:  # '*' may close one, open one, or do nothing
                lo -= 1
                hi += 1
            if hi < 0:  # too many ')' even if every '*' opens
                return False
            lo = max(lo, 0)  # an open count can never be negative
        return lo == 0  # zero open brackets is reachable

Redundant Connection (Graphs, Medium)

In this problem, a tree is an undirected graph that is connected and has no cycles. You get a graph that started as a tree with n nodes labeled from 1 to n, with one additional edge added. The added edge has two different vertices chosen from 1 to n, and it was not an edge that already existed. The graph is an array edges of length n, where edges[i] = [ai, bi] means that there is an edge between nodes ai and bi. Return an edge that you can remove so that the resulting graph is a tree of n nodes. If there are multiple answers, return the answer that occurs last in the input.

Constraints:
n == edges.length
3 <= n <= 1000
edges[i].length == 2
1 <= ai < bi <= edges.length

Name the technique and the memory hook. Then rebuild the solution.
column2:
Hook: Same root already? That edge closes the cycle.
Techniques: union-find, cycle-detection

Approach: Plain union-find over edges in input order. Add edges one by one, and return the first edge whose two endpoints already have the same root.

Rebuild:
  1. Make parent = list(range(len(edges) + 1)). There are n = len(edges) nodes, labeled 1 to n. Each node starts as its own root. Index 0 is not used.
  2. Write find(x): while parent[x] != x, set parent[x] = parent[parent[x]] and move x up. Return x.
  3. Loop for a, b in edges and compute root_a = find(a) and root_b = find(b).
  4. If the roots are equal, return [a, b]. This edge closes the cycle.
  5. Else set parent[root_a] = root_b to join the two groups.
  6. After the loop, return []. The loop always returns first, because the input has exactly one cycle.
Signals:
  • The input is an undirected edge list and the question asks which edge creates a cycle or breaks the tree property.
  • The graph has n nodes and n edges, so it is a tree plus exactly one extra edge and has exactly one cycle.
  • The answer depends on the order of the edges in the input, which suggests processing edges one by one and stopping at the first conflict.
  • Each step asks the same question: are these two nodes already connected? Repeated connectivity queries under edge insertions point to union-find.
Key insight: When you add edges to an undirected graph one at a time, an edge creates a cycle exactly when its two endpoints are already in the same connected component. Union-find answers that question in near-constant time. The first edge that fails this test is also the last cycle edge in input order, because a cycle closes only when its last edge arrives.
Optimal: The optimal solution_code adds union by size: it keeps a size array and attaches the smaller tree under the larger one. Together with path halving, this makes each operation almost O(1) in the worst case, O(n alpha(n)) total. Without union by size, path halving alone still gives O(log n) amortized per operation, which is far below the limit for n <= 1000. Add union by size when inputs are very large or when an interviewer asks for the tight bound.
Approaches:
  • Remove each edge and test for a tree: O(n^2) time, O(n) space
  • Incremental DFS reachability check: O(n^2) time, O(n) space
  • Find the cycle, then pick the last cycle edge: O(n) time, O(n) space
  • Union-find over edges in input order (optimal, standard): O(n alpha(n)) time, O(n) space
from typing import List


class Solution:
    def findRedundantConnection(self, edges: List[List[int]]) -> List[int]:
        parent = list(range(len(edges) + 1))  # every node starts as its own root

        def find(x: int) -> int:
            while parent[x] != x:
                parent[x] = parent[parent[x]]  # path halving keeps chains short
                x = parent[x]
            return x

        for a, b in edges:
            root_a, root_b = find(a), find(b)
            if root_a == root_b:
                return [a, b]  # already connected, so this edge closes the cycle
            parent[root_a] = root_b  # union: join the two groups
        return []

Max Area of Island (Graphs, Medium)

You get an m x n binary matrix grid. A cell with value 1 is land. A cell with value 0 is water. An island is a group of land cells that connect 4-directionally (up, down, left, right). Diagonal cells do not connect. All four edges of the grid are surrounded by water. The area of an island is the number of cells with value 1 in that island. Return the maximum area of an island in grid. If there is no island, return 0.

Constraints:
m == grid.length
n == grid[i].length
1 <= m, n <= 50
grid[i][j] is either 0 or 1.

Name the technique and the memory hook. Then rebuild the solution.
column2:
Hook: Scan for land. Sink on push, count on pop, keep the max.
Techniques: grid-flood-fill, union-find

Approach: Scan and flood fill with a stack. Scan every cell. When you find land, call a helper that flood fills that island with an explicit stack. The helper sinks each cell to 0 when it pushes the cell, counts each pop and returns the count. Keep the largest count.

Rebuild:
  1. Get rows and cols from the grid.
  2. Write island_size(r, c). Sink grid[r][c] to 0, put (r, c) on a stack, and set size to 0.
  3. While the stack is not empty, pop a cell and add 1 to size.
  4. For each of the 4 neighbors, check that it is in bounds and equals 1. Then sink it to 0 and push it.
  5. When the stack is empty, return size.
  6. Set best to 0. Scan every cell. When a cell equals 1, set best to max(best, island_size(r, c)).
  7. Return best.
Signals:
  • The input is a 2D grid of cells, and cells connect to their 4 neighbors. Treat the grid as an implicit graph.
  • The problem talks about groups, regions, islands or blobs of same-valued cells. These are connected components.
  • The question asks for a property of each component (size, perimeter, shape) and then a max, min or total over components. Or it asks for the number of components.
  • The grid can hold up to a few thousand cells, and one component can cover all of them. A traversal that visits each cell once fits. A recursive traversal can get as deep as the cell count, so plan for an explicit stack in Python.
Key insight: An island is a connected component of an implicit grid graph. Flood fill each component exactly once from its first unvisited cell, and count cells as you visit them. Marking cells visited makes the whole scan linear, because no cell starts or joins a second traversal.
Optimal: The intuitive solution uses the same algorithm as solution_code. It only moves the flood fill into a helper function. Both run in O(m*n) time and use O(m*n) extra space for the stack in the worst case.
Approaches:
  • Fresh search from every land cell: O((m*n)^2) time, O(m*n) space (too slow)
  • Recursive DFS flood fill (NeetCode reference): O(m*n) time, O(m*n) space
  • Iterative DFS or BFS flood fill with in-place sinking (chosen): O(m*n) time, O(m*n) space
  • Union-find with component sizes: O(m*n * alpha(m*n)) time, O(m*n) space
class Solution:
    def maxAreaOfIsland(self, grid: List[List[int]]) -> int:
        rows, cols = len(grid), len(grid[0])

        def island_size(r, c):
            # Flood fill one island with a stack. Sink each cell when you push it.
            grid[r][c] = 0
            stack = [(r, c)]
            size = 0
            while stack:
                i, j = stack.pop()
                size += 1
                for x, y in ((i + 1, j), (i - 1, j), (i, j + 1), (i, j - 1)):
                    if 0 <= x < rows and 0 <= y < cols and grid[x][y] == 1:
                        grid[x][y] = 0
                        stack.append((x, y))
            return size

        best = 0
        for r in range(rows):
            for c in range(cols):
                if grid[r][c] == 1:
                    best = max(best, island_size(r, c))
        return best

Kth Largest Element in a Stream (Heap / Priority Queue, Easy)

Design a class KthLargest. The story frames the values as test scores in a university admissions office, and the kth highest score acts as a dynamic cut-off mark. The constructor KthLargest(k, nums) receives an integer k and an initial list of integer scores nums. The method add(val) adds the integer val to the stream. It then returns the kth largest value among all values so far, which are the initial nums plus every added value. The kth largest is the kth element of the list of all values sorted in descending order. Duplicates count separately, so it is not the kth distinct value. k stays fixed for the object. Values are only added and never removed. nums can be empty and k can equal nums.length + 1, so the object can hold fewer than k values before the first add. After each add, at least k values exist.

Constraints:
0 <= nums.length <= 10^4
1 <= k <= nums.length + 1
-10^4 <= nums[i] <= 10^4
-10^4 <= val <= 10^4

Name the technique and the memory hook. Then rebuild the solution.
column2:
Hook: Keep the top k in a min-heap. Every value goes through add: push, pop if over k, return the root.
Techniques: heap-top-k, design-data-structure

Approach: Min-heap of size k with one gate for every value. The constructor feeds each initial number through add. add pushes the value. If the heap then holds more than k values, add pops the smallest value. add returns the root.

Rebuild:
  1. Import heapq. Store k and start an empty list top_k that acts as a min-heap.
  2. In the constructor, call self.add(num) for each num in nums.
  3. In add, heappush the value onto top_k.
  4. If len(top_k) > k, heappop to remove the smallest value.
  5. Return top_k[0], which is the smallest of the k largest values.
Signals:
  • The question asks for the kth largest or kth smallest value, not for the whole sorted order.
  • Values arrive one at a time and a query follows each arrival, so the answer must update online.
  • The collection only grows. Nothing is deleted, and no window slides.
  • k is fixed for the lifetime of the structure, so a container of fixed size k is enough.
Key insight: When you only insert and need the kth largest, the answer never decreases. So a value below the current kth largest can never become the answer again, and you can discard it. Keep a min-heap of exactly k values. The heap holds the k largest values, and its root is the smallest of them. A new value must beat the root to enter, and the root is the answer.
Optimal: Same technique and same per-add cost of O(log k). Only the constructor differs. The record's solution_code copies nums, calls heapify in O(n), and pops until the size is k. That build costs O(n + (n - k) log n). The intuitive version costs O(n log k) for the build. At the maximum input size both builds take a few milliseconds, so the difference does not matter here. Use the heapify form only when the initial list is very large and k is close to n.
Approaches:
  • Sort on every add: O(N log N) per add, where N is the number of values so far. Timsort on a list that stays sorted drops this to about O(N), which is still too slow in total. time, O(N) space (too slow)
  • Sorted list with binary insertion: O(n log n) build, O(N) per add time, O(N) space
  • Quickselect on every add: O(N) average per add, O(N^2) worst case time, O(N) space (too slow)
  • Min-heap of size k (optimal, standard): O(n + (n - k) log n) build, O(log k) per add time, O(n) during build because of the copy, then O(k) space
  • Fenwick tree over the value range: O(n log V) build, O(log V) per add, where V = 20001 time, O(V) space
import heapq
from typing import List


class KthLargest:

    def __init__(self, k: int, nums: List[int]):
        self.k = k
        self.top_k = []  # min-heap that keeps the k largest values seen so far
        for num in nums:
            self.add(num)  # every value goes through the same gate

    def add(self, val: int) -> int:
        heapq.heappush(self.top_k, val)
        if len(self.top_k) > self.k:
            heapq.heappop(self.top_k)  # drop the weakest, it can never be the answer again
        return self.top_k[0]  # the smallest of the top k is the kth largest
